name: Adam and Eve
text: Eating from the tree God forbade. Adam received the command not to eat of the forbidden tree. The serpent contradicted its warning of death, the woman took and ate and gave to her husband, and he ate also. They covered themselves and hid, then answered God's inquiry by shifting blame. Judgment brought sorrow, toil, mortality, and expulsion; God clothed them before driving them out. The command and the contradiction stand against each other. God told Adam that eating of the forbidden tree would bring death; the serpent told the woman that they would not surely die (Genesis 2:16-17; Genesis 3:4-5). The temptation offered wisdom while denying the consequence of disobedience. Its doctrine was that the commandment could be broken without the judgment God had spoken. The fruit of lies is the spiritual danger: a word received becomes a deed performed (Hosea 10:13). Eve saw what was desirable, took, ate, and gave to her husband, and he ate also (Genesis 3:6). Paul warns of minds corrupted as the serpent beguiled Eve, and of Satan appearing as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:3,14). The promise of enlightenment did not make the teaching true. Adam's charge was that he hearkened to his wife against the command given to him (Genesis 3:17); another person's persuasion did not remove his responsibility. Their covering and hiding could not answer God's inquiry. Job speaks of covering transgressions as Adam, and Lamentations joins exposed nakedness to grievous sin (Job 31:33; Lamentations 1:8). The call, Where art thou, brought the man to account. Adam pointed to the woman God had given him, and she pointed to the serpent, but each still had to answer for the deed (Genesis 3:9-13). The serpent was cursed and brought low, and enmity was appointed between his seed and the woman's seed (Genesis 3:14-15). The promise reaches to Christ's destruction of the devil's works and the bruising of Satan under the saints' feet (1 John 3:8; Romans 16:20). To the woman came multiplied sorrow; to Adam, toil upon cursed ground until his return to dust (Genesis 3:16-19). The lie had promised escape from death, but the sentence established the opposite. God clothed them with coats of skins before driving them out (Genesis 3:21-24). The covering points toward the need for an atonement they could not supply by hiding; the Lamb is the provision named in Revelation 13:8. Mercy in their clothing did not cancel their expulsion. The guarded way to the tree of life left them unable to take for themselves what disobedience had forfeited.

name: Abel
text: Bringing the firstlings of his flock and the fat thereof. Abel brought the firstlings of his flock and the fat thereof, and the Lord had respect unto him and his offering. Hebrews witnesses to his faith, and Christ names him righteous Abel. His brother slew him, but his blood cried from the ground and his faith remained a testimony. Abel brought the firstlings of his flock and the fat thereof, and the Lord had respect unto Abel and his offering (Genesis 4:4). His gift was not described merely by its presence at the altar: the firstlings and the fat are specifically named. The later commands concerning the firstborn and the Lord's portion of the fat give precepts for the honour shown in that offering (Exodus 13:12; Leviticus 3:16). Hebrews supplies the decisive testimony: by faith Abel offered a more excellent sacrifice than Cain and obtained witness that he was righteous (Hebrews 11:4). His obedience cannot be reduced to the material of the gift while forgetting the man who brought it. John likewise distinguishes the brothers by their works: Cain's were evil and Abel's righteous (1 John 3:12). Worship and conduct belonged to the same account before God. God testified of Abel's gifts, and Christ named him righteous Abel (Hebrews 11:4; Matthew 23:35). His brother's violence did not reverse that judgment. The man rejected by Cain was accepted by God, and the blood shed in the field was not beyond God's hearing (Genesis 4:8-10). Being dead, he yet speaks. Hebrews preserves his faith as a witness after his life was taken; Genesis preserves the cry of his blood. The blessing was a righteous standing before God, not immunity from the wickedness of another. His case condemns envy without making the victim's death evidence against his obedience. Christ places Abel at the beginning of the blood of the prophets shed from the foundation of the world (Luke 11:49-51). His witness therefore reaches beyond the offering itself: righteous works drew his brother's hatred, and the murder of the righteous became a pattern repeated against God's messengers (1 John 3:12). Cain silenced his brother's voice in the field, but could not silence the testimony God gave of him.

name: Cain
text: Murder of his brother Abel. Cain brought of the fruit of the ground and Abel brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. The Lord had respect unto Abel and to his offering, and not unto Cain's, and Cain was very wroth. He was called to repent, and warned that if he did not, sin lay at the door. He talked with Abel in the field and slew him, then answered God with a lie and a taunt. When God did not regard Cain's offering, Cain became very wroth and his countenance fell. Before the murder, God addressed him: if he did well, he would be accepted; if not, sin lay at the door (Genesis 4:3-7). The warning made room for repentance. Rejection of the offering did not require him to become a murderer. Cain answered his brother's righteousness with violence. In the field he rose against Abel and slew him, then denied knowledge of him and asked whether he was his brother's keeper (Genesis 4:8-9). John names the motive plainly: Cain was of that wicked one, and slew his brother because his own works were evil and his brother's righteous (1 John 3:12). He would destroy the man whose conduct exposed his own instead of doing the good set before him. The warning of sin at the door and Peter's warning of the devouring adversary belong together (Genesis 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8). Anger nourished rather than corrected becomes an opening for further evil. The offering, the fallen countenance, the killing, and the lie show a course of refusal, not an unavoidable act forced upon him by God's rebuke.

name: Lamech
text: Killing a man and boasting of it; claiming seventy-sevenfold vengeance. Lamech of Cain's line told his wives Adah and Zillah of a killing and claimed seventy-sevenfold vengeance for himself against Cain's sevenfold. His declaration is preserved without a separate sentence executed upon him. Protection pronounced by God over Cain had become a man's boast about his own vengeance. Lamech of Cain's line took two wives, Adah and Zillah, and addressed them concerning a man he had slain to his wounding and a young man to his hurt (Genesis 4:19,23). His speech culminated in a claim of vengeance: if Cain were avenged sevenfold, Lamech would be seventy and sevenfold (Genesis 4:24). The protection God had pronounced over Cain became the measure of his own boast. God had restrained others from killing Cain; Lamech spoke as though that restraint authorized an even greater claim for himself. He made no recorded appeal for repentance or forgiveness. Vengeance was being treated as a man's possession to enlarge, although the Lord declares that vengeance belongs to him (Deuteronomy 32:35). A divine limit upon retaliation cannot rightly be turned into permission to threaten more of it. Genesis gives no separate sentence executed upon this Lamech. His speech is preserved as testimony to the violence and self-exaltation within Cain's genealogy, before the account turns to Seth and those who called upon the Lord (Genesis 4:23-26). The absence of a narrated punishment does not make his claim God's promise. Romans 12:19 commands the hearer not to avenge himself but to leave recompense to the Lord. Lamech's seventy-sevenfold is his own declaration; it is not the Lord extending Cain's protection by a new command.

name: Enoch
text: Walking with God three hundred years. Enoch walked with God, begat sons and daughters, and was not, for God took him. Hebrews says he was translated that he should not see death and had testimony that he pleased God. Jude preserves his warning of judgment upon ungodly deeds and speeches. Enoch walked with God after the birth of Methuselah for three hundred years and begat sons and daughters (Genesis 5:21-24). The testimony describes a sustained course amid the responsibilities of a household. Walking with God was not confined to a single occasion of danger or a single offering. Jude names him as the seventh from Adam and preserves his prophecy of the Lord coming with ten thousands of his saints to execute judgment upon ungodly deeds and hard speeches (Jude 1:14-15). His walk included testimony against the evil around him. The standard was not the approval of his generation, but the judgment of the Lord he proclaimed. Genesis says that he was not, for God took him. Hebrews explains that by faith he was translated that he should not see death, and that before his translation he had testimony that he pleased God (Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5). His disappearance was not presented as failure or abandonment, but as God's taking of the faithful man. The next verse makes the principle available to the hearer: without faith it is impossible to please God, and those who come to him must believe that he rewards those who diligently seek him (Hebrews 11:6). Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) calls Enoch an example of repentance to all generations (Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 44:16). His particular deliverance remains God's act, while the call to seek and please God continues beyond his generation.

name: The sons of God and the giants
text: Leaving their proper estate; taking wives of the daughters of men. The sons of God took wives of all whom they chose, seeing that the daughters of men were fair. The account follows Adam's genealogy and proceeds to the earth's corruption and violence. Mighty men of renown did not preserve that world from judgment. The Lord declared that his spirit would not always strive with man. After the genealogy of Adam through Seth, Genesis records the sons of God taking wives of all whom they chose because the daughters of men were fair (Genesis 5:1-3; Genesis 6:1-2). The sequence sets the lineage entrusted with godly responsibility beside choices governed by outward attraction. The distinction of a holy calling was not to be surrendered to whatever the eye desired. The angels are reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day. The giants and the world they filled with violence went under the Flood; Noah alone was carried through.

name: Noah
text: Doing according to all that God commanded him. In a world where every imagination of man's heart was only evil continually, one man was just and perfect in his generations and walked with God. He was told to build an ark and did it exactly, and he and his house were the only ones saved through the flood. Noah found grace in the Lord's eyes, was just and perfect in his generations, and walked with God while the earth was corrupt and filled with violence (Genesis 6:8-13). He was given a work whose form was specified: the ark's material, rooms, covering, dimensions, door, and stories (Genesis 6:14-16). His faith took the shape of carrying out what he had been told. He also had to gather food and bring living creatures into the ark. Genesis 7 distinguishes the clean beasts taken by sevens from the unclean taken by two (Genesis 6:19-22; Genesis 7:2-5). The distinctions were part of the command, not details he was free to discard. Twice the account records that he did according to all the Lord commanded him. Hebrews says he was warned of things not seen as yet and moved with fear to prepare for the saving of his house (Hebrews 11:7). Peter calls him a preacher of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5). Preparation and testimony belonged together: he acted upon the warning instead of waiting for the destruction to prove it true. The Lord called Noah's household into the ark and shut him in; Noah and those with him were preserved when the judgment overtook the earth (Genesis 7:1,16,23). His household benefited from a faith expressed in sustained work. Hebrews calls him an heir of the righteousness which is by faith, not merely a survivor of danger. Afterward he built an altar and offered of the clean beasts and fowls. God established the covenant with Noah, his seed, and every living creature, promising that a flood would not again destroy all flesh and setting the bow in the cloud as its token (Genesis 8:20-22; Genesis 9:8-17). The renewed earth also carried commands: replenish it, abstain from blood, and reckon with God's requirement of human life (Genesis 9:1-6). Deliverance opened a continuing duty, not freedom from God's rule.

name: The generation of the Flood
text: Corruption and violence filling the earth. A whole world under judgment. The earth was filled with violence and every imagination of the heart was continually evil, so God resolved to blot out what he had made, sparing only Noah's household. God saw that the wickedness of man was great and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. The earth was corrupt before him and filled with violence (Genesis 6:5-13). The judgment addressed both inward intention and outward harm: corrupt thoughts had become a corrupt way of life. Christ later recalled people eating, drinking, and marrying until the day Noah entered the ark (Matthew 24:37-39). Ordinary activity continued around an extraordinary warning. The danger was not that a meal or marriage was itself the offense named in Genesis, but that people continued without heeding the judgment coming upon their wickedness. God's longsuffering while the ark was preparing did not mean that the warning had been withdrawn (1 Peter 3:20).

name: Ham and the curse on Canaan
text: Seeing his father's nakedness and telling his brothers. Noah planted a vineyard, drank of the wine, was drunken, and was uncovered within his tent. Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father and told his two brethren without. Shem and Japheth took a garment on both their shoulders, went backward, and covered their father, and their faces were backward so that they saw not his nakedness. When Noah awoke he cursed Canaan. Noah drank wine, became drunken, and lay uncovered within his tent. Ham saw his father's nakedness and told his brothers outside. Shem and Japheth took a garment upon their shoulders, went backward, and covered him without looking upon his nakedness (Genesis 9:20-23). Their conduct supplies the contrast: they met the exposure with a covering rather than making it an occasion to look and tell. The duty to honour father and mother remains when a parent's weakness is visible (Exodus 20:12). Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) warns that a man's glory comes from the honour of his father and that parental dishonour is a reproach to the children (Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 3:10-11). Noah's recorded righteousness did not require concealing the account of his drunkenness, and his drunkenness did not give his son permission to treat his exposure without honour. The brothers showed what respectful action required in that moment. Awaking from his wine and knowing what his younger son had done, Noah pronounced the curse upon Canaan: a servant of servants would he be unto his brethren (Genesis 9:24-25). The text names Canaan, not all of Ham's descendants, as the object of this sentence. Neither a curse upon every African people nor a statement about skin colour is written here. Noah blessed the Lord God of Shem and spoke of Japheth's enlargement and dwelling in Shem's tents, repeating Canaan's servitude (Genesis 9:26-27). The different parties must remain distinct. The account gives the conduct, the contrasting honour of the brothers, and Noah's words, without explaining every reason why the curse fell upon Canaan. What is withheld cannot be supplied by expanding the sentence beyond the person it names.

name: The builders of Babel
text: Building a tower to make themselves a name and resist being scattered. The whole earth was of one language and one speech, and journeying from the east they found a plain in the land of Shinar and dwelt there. They said, let us build us a city and a tower whose top may reach unto heaven, and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth. The Lord came down, confounded their language, and scattered them. The builders at Shinar shared one language and proposed a city and a tower, naming their purpose themselves: make us a name, lest we be scattered over the earth (Genesis 11:1-4). Their unity was directed toward securing their own name and resisting dispersion. This stands against the charge to Noah's sons to be fruitful, multiply, and replenish the earth (Genesis 9:1). The Lord saw the people as one, with one language, and declared that nothing would be restrained from what they imagined to do (Genesis 11:6). Agreement alone was no proof of righteousness. The people could combine skill and labour while pursuing an end contrary to God's ordering. Nimrod's kingdom began in Babel and the same land of Shinar (Genesis 10:8-10); the name and place belong to the growth of human power, not an authority above God's judgment.

name: Abraham
text: Obeying the Lord's voice; keeping his charge, his commandments, his statutes, and his laws. Told to leave country, kindred and father's house for a land he would be shewed, he went. Told to offer his only son, he rose early in the morning. The Lord's own account of him, given to Isaac, is the law kept: Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws. Three great tests display a faith that acts upon the command. He left country, kindred and father's house for a destination he was not told (Genesis 12:1). He circumcised every male of his house on the day he was commanded (Genesis 17:23), at ninety-nine years old, receiving in his flesh the token of the covenant God had explained to him (Genesis 17:10-14; Genesis 17:24). And when the son through whom the whole promise ran was demanded, he rose early in the morning (Genesis 22:3), which is the detail the record chooses to report. Genesis 18 adds that he was expected to command his household after him to keep the way of the Lord (Genesis 18:19) and to do justice and judgment, and the Lord's own summary in Genesis 26 states the standard he met (Genesis 26:5): he kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws. He believed the Lord, and it was counted to him for righteousness (Genesis 15:6). That faith did not end in agreement with a promise. Hebrews explains that, when Isaac was required, Abraham accounted God able to raise him even from the dead (Hebrews 11:17-19). The angel stopped his hand, and he offered the ram provided in his son's stead (Genesis 22:11-13). James joins the offering to the earlier faith: faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect (James 2:21-23).

name: Pharaoh and Abimelech, who took Sarah
text: Taking another man's wife into the king's house. Twice Abraham called Sarah his sister, and twice a king took her. Pharaoh's household was plagued; Abimelech was warned in a dream and required to restore her. God expressly testified that he had kept Abimelech from touching her. The marriage stood despite the account given of it. In Egypt, Pharaoh's princes commended Sarai and she was taken into Pharaoh's house (Genesis 12:15). In Gerar, Abimelech sent and took Sarah (Genesis 20:2). Both acted on Abraham's word that she was his sister, and Abimelech pleaded the integrity of his heart (Genesis 20:5); the Lord acknowledged his integrity and said that he had withheld him from sinning (Genesis 20:6). Yet Sarah remained another man's wife. Once that was revealed, Abimelech was required to restore her; ignorance was not permission to keep her. The Lord plagued Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai. To Abimelech he came in a dream: thou art but a dead man, for the woman is a man's wife. The Lord had closed up every womb of the house of Abimelech, and opened them only when Sarah was restored and Abraham, the prophet, prayed for him.

name: Hagar, and the God who seeth
text: Returning and submitting when the angel sent her back; and calling him Thou God seest me. An Egyptian bondwoman given to Abram by her mistress, despised her when she conceived and was dealt with hardly until she fled. The angel of the Lord found her by a fountain in the wilderness, called her by name and by her station, told her to return and submit, and gave her a promise for her son. She named the Lord that spake unto her and called the well Beer-lahai-roi. Sent away years later with bread and a bottle of water, she was met again when the water was spent. She was told to go back to a house she had run from and to a mistress who had dealt hardly with her (Genesis 16:6), and she went. The angel gave her both a command to return and a promise that her seed would be multiplied beyond numbering (Genesis 16:9-10). Her son would be called Ishmael because the Lord had heard her affliction; his life and relations with his brethren were foretold before his birth (Genesis 16:11-12). The record does not conceal her fault either, that when she saw she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes, so the case is of a woman corrected and restored rather than of one wronged only. The angel found her by a fountain in the wilderness and addressed the servant whom the household dispute had driven away (Genesis 16:7-8). She answered the encounter with the name, Thou God seest me (Genesis 16:13). The well was called after it (Genesis 16:14) and was still known by that name when the account was written. When the bread and the water were gone and she had set the child down and lifted up her voice and wept, God heard the voice of the lad, renewed the promise that he would become a great nation, and opened her eyes to a well of water (Genesis 21:17-19). She filled the bottle and gave him drink, and God was with him as he grew (Genesis 21:20-21). The covenant inheritance was appointed through Isaac, but Ishmael was not forgotten: God had also promised Abraham a nation from this son (Genesis 21:12-13).

name: Sodom and Gomorrah
text: Grievous sin; inhospitality and violence against strangers. Cities whose sin was grave enough that its cry reached heaven. When two visitors lodged with Lot, the men of the city surrounded the house demanding them. Judgment fell the next morning. The prophets later name the fuller charge: pride, fullness of bread, careless ease, and no help for the poor and needy (Ezekiel 16:49-50), a hardness that showed itself in the mob at Lot's door. The cry against the cities was great before the messengers reached Lot's house (Genesis 18:20-21). The men then surrounded it, demanded the guests, threatened Lot when he resisted, and pressed upon the door. Even after the angels struck them with blindness, they wearied themselves seeking the entrance (Genesis 19:4-11). Abundance had not produced mercy, and correction did not turn the mob from its purpose. Abraham had pleaded that the righteous not be destroyed with the wicked; the Judge of all the earth distinguished the household brought out from the city overthrown (Genesis 18:23-25; Genesis 19:29).

name: Lot
text: A righteous man vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked; sheltering the strangers at his door. He chose the plain of Sodom and lived to regret it, but Peter calls him just Lot, vexed from day to day with the unlawful deeds of the city. He took the two strangers into his house and stood in his door against the men of the city. The angels took him by the hand and led him out before the fire fell. The obedience is genuine and the man is compromised, and the case is more useful for holding both. He chose the plain and ended sitting in the gate of Sodom as one of its men (Genesis 19:1). But when two strangers arrived he pressed them to lodge with him and fed them, and when the city surrounded the house he went outside (Genesis 19:6) and shut the door behind him rather than surrender guests he had taken in (Genesis 19:6). Peter's verdict, that he was a righteous man vexed from day to day by what he saw and heard (2 Peter 2:8), is the New Testament's reading of a life the record itself shows to be badly placed (2 Peter 2:6-9). His reception of the strangers must not conceal his offer of his two daughters to the mob (Genesis 19:8). Protecting guests did not make his daughters available for violence. The angels, not that offer, stopped the attack: they drew Lot inside and shut the door. When he warned his sons in law, they treated the warning as mockery (Genesis 19:10-14). The urgency of leaving exposed how little authority his warning carried within the city he had chosen.

name: Lot's wife
text: Looking back toward Sodom against the angel's command. The angels told Lot's household to escape for their lives and not look behind them. His wife looked back from behind him and became a pillar of salt. Christ made her a proverb in three words. The command was given with the rescue and it was specific: escape for thy life, look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain, escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed (Genesis 19:17). She had been taken out by the hand, along with her husband and her two daughters, the Lord being merciful unto them (Genesis 19:16), so mercy had already brought her beyond the city's walls. The command required her to continue the escape, neither looking back nor remaining in the plain. What the city she was leaving had become is set out in the same chapter. The men of Sodom compassed the house, both old and young, all the people from every quarter, and demanded the two men, saying, bring them out unto us, that we may know them (Genesis 19:4-5). To know in scripture is to lie with: Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived (Genesis 4:1), and Rebekah was a virgin, neither had any man known her (Genesis 24:16). So the demand was that the guests be handed over to be raped, by the whole male population of the city, and Lot's own answer, I pray you, brethren, do not so wickedly (Genesis 19:7),  shows this was already wickedness in Genesis, long before the law was written at Sinai, where it is named abomination (Leviticus 18:22). The same demand in the same words is made at Gibeah by certain sons of Belial, bring forth the man that came into thine house, that we may know him (Judges 19:22), and Jude names what the cities were doing, giving themselves over to fornication and going after strange flesh (Jude 1:7). She looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26). The account records no further warning between the backward look and its consequence. Christ raises her case by name as a warning to those who will turn back on the day of his revealing, in the day when he which shall be upon the housetop and his stuff in the house is told not to come down to take it away: Remember Lot's wife (Luke 17:31-32). Wisdom keeps the standing pillar as a memorial of an unbelieving soul (Wisdom of Solomon 10:7). Christ places the warning beside the temptation to return for possessions and the effort to save one's life only to lose it (Luke 17:31-33). Being led out was not the end of obedience. Her case warns against turning back after deliverance has begun, without requiring an invented account of what she was thinking when she looked.

name: Jacob, deceiving Isaac for the blessing
text: Putting on his brother's raiment and the skins of the kids, and saying to his blind father, I am Esau thy firstborn. The word had been given before either child was born: two nations are in thy womb, and the elder shall serve the younger. Esau afterwards sold the birthright for a meal and despised it. When Isaac, whose eyes were dim, sent Esau for venison to bless him, Rebekah dressed Jacob in his brother's clothes with kid skins on his hands and neck and sent him in with the meat. He said he was Esau, took the blessing, and had to leave the country. He served twenty years for a father in law who changed his wages ten times, and was given the elder daughter in place of the younger. The outcome was settled before the act and before the men. The Lord told Rebekah, two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels, and the one people shall be stronger than the other people, and the elder shall serve the younger (Genesis 25:23). Paul takes that as the plain case of a thing determined apart from conduct: the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth, it was said unto her, The elder shall

name: Esau
text: Despising his birthright; marrying Hittite wives; purposing to kill his brother. The firstborn of Isaac sold his birthright for a single meal, took wives of the Canaanites to his parents' grief, and when the blessing went to Jacob resolved to kill him. The prophets and apostles treat him as the pattern of the profane man. Hebrews names it (Hebrews 12:16-17): a fornicator or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright (Hebrews 12:16). His marriages were a grief of mind to Isaac and Rebekah (Genesis 26:35). His hatred of Jacob was murder in the heart (Genesis 27:41). He found no place of repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears. Malachi: I hated Esau, and laid his mountains and his heritage waste. Obadiah sentences his house for its violence against Jacob: the house of Esau shall be for stubble.

name: Isaac
text: Dwelling in the land the Lord told him of, and not going down into Egypt in the famine. A famine came, and the natural road was Egypt, where his father had gone. The Lord appeared and said, Go not down into Egypt; sojourn in this land, and I will be with thee. Isaac stayed in Gerar, sowed in a famine year, and reaped an hundredfold. The obedience is a refusal to take the obvious road. Famine came, Egypt was where his father had gone in the same circumstances, and the Lord told him not to go. He stayed, and then sowed a crop in a famine year in a land not yet his (Genesis 26:12). A quieter pattern appears in the disputes over wells: when the herdsmen of Gerar seized the wells he had dug, he did not contest them but moved and dug again, until at Rehoboth no one strove with him (Genesis 26:22). He surrendered a legitimate claim rather than fight for it, twice. The instruction to remain carried the promise of God's presence and the oath sworn to Abraham; Isaac dwelt in Gerar in obedience to that word (Genesis 26:2-6). At Esek and Sitnah the herdsmen strove, but at Rehoboth he acknowledged that the Lord had made room for them (Genesis 26:20-22). He did not have to seize every disputed well in order for the promise to stand. He reaped an hundredfold in the year of the famine (Genesis 26:12) and grew great enough that the king of the country came to him seeking terms (Genesis 26:26-29). The reason Abimelech gives is the point of the case: we saw certainly that the Lord was with thee (Genesis 26:28). The blessing was public and legible to outsiders, and it came to the man who had declined to take by force what was his. Peace did not require him to pretend that he had been treated well. He asked Abimelech why men who hated him and sent him away had now come to him. After they acknowledged the Lord's presence with him, he made a feast, exchanged an oath, and sent them away in peace (Genesis 26:27-31). Blessing strengthened him without making retaliation his answer.

name: Laban and the changed wages
text: Changing his hired servant's wages ten times, and giving the elder daughter in place of the younger. He took seven years' work for Rachel and delivered Leah, then charged another seven. He changed the wages ten times over twenty years. When Jacob left, he pursued him seven days with his brethren, and God came to him in a dream by night and told him to speak neither good nor bad. He searched the tents for his gods, found nothing, and went home having made a covenant at the heap. Two statutes are engaged. The substitution of Leah was fraud in a contract already performed, and his justification, that it must not be so done in our country to give the younger before the firstborn (Genesis 29:26), is a rule he had known before he took the seven years (Genesis 29:18). The changed wages are the graver charge because they were continuous (Genesis 31:7): Jacob's account, which Laban does not deny, is that thou hast changed my wages ten times (Genesis 31:41), and that but for the God of his father he would have been sent away empty (Genesis 31:42). Deuteronomy 24 forbids oppressing a hired servant that is poor and needy (Deuteronomy 24:14) and requires his wages the same day (Deuteronomy 24:14-15). Laban himself acknowledged that the Lord had blessed him for Jacob's sake, and Jacob recalled how little Laban had before his arrival (Genesis 30:27-30). He recognized the benefit of Jacob's service, yet continued changing the terms. The second seven years did not mean that Jacob waited fourteen years to receive Rachel. After completing Leah's week, he received Rachel also and served the further seven years (Genesis 29:27-30). The wrong lay in changing the agreement after the first service was performed. Jacob's later testimony joins the two periods of marriage service to six years for the cattle, amid heat, frost, sleeplessness, and repeated changes of wages (Genesis 31:38-41).

name: Rachel and the stolen teraphim
text: Stealing her father's images, and hiding them under her while she sat upon them. Rachel stole her father's images and hid them beneath the camel's furniture. Laban searched without finding them, while Jacob, unaware of her act, declared that whoever was found with them should not live. No divine sentence for the theft is announced. The household later put away its strange gods before going to Bethel. She took household gods out of a house she was leaving (Genesis 31:19) and carried them into a covenant family, which is the offense underneath the theft. The concealment compounded it: she placed the images in the camel's furniture, sat upon them, and said she could not rise because the custom of women was upon her (Genesis 31:34-35). The excuse concealed what she had taken; Genesis does not say that she invoked a statute or describe Laban's reasoning about uncleanness. Jacob's ignorance is stated by the record, for Jacob knew not that Rachel had stolen them (Genesis 31:32), which is why his oath was unwitting. No divine sentence for the theft is recorded. Jacob had pronounced that with whomsoever thou findest thy gods (Genesis 31:32), let him not live, without knowing that Rachel was the one who had taken them. She was not found and no judgment is announced. She died bearing Benjamin on the way to Ephrath (Genesis 35:19), but the account does not identify her death as punishment for the theft. Jacob afterwards required the whole household to put away the strange gods that were among them (Genesis 35:2) and buried what the household surrendered under the oak at Shechem (Genesis 35:4). That cleansing addressed the strange gods among them; the passage does not inventory Rachel's stolen images separately.

name: Jacob at Peniel
text: I will not let thee go, except thou bless me. Left alone at the ford Jabbok the night before he had to face the brother he had cheated, he wrestled with a man until the breaking of the day. The hollow of his thigh was put out of joint and he did not let go. Asked his name, he gave it, and was given another. He called the place Peniel, for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved, and he passed over halting upon his thigh. The obedience is a refusal to release, sustained after the hollow of his thigh had been put out of joint and after he had been told to let go because the day was breaking. What the case turns on is the question he was asked and the answer he gave. He had once stood before a blind father and said I am Esau thy firstborn; now he was asked what is thy name, and said Jacob, which means supplanter. The contrast is sharp: before Isaac he had claimed Esau's name; here he gives his own name and asks for a blessing (Genesis 27:19; Genesis 32:26-28). Before the wrestling, Jacob confessed that he was not worthy of the mercies already shown him, asked deliverance from Esau, and appealed to God's promise concerning his seed (Genesis 32:9-12). His persistence was therefore joined to dependence, not a claim that his own strength could compel God.

name: Shechem son of Hamor
text: Defiling Dinah, daughter of Jacob. Dinah went out to see the daughters of the land, and Shechem the son of Hamor, prince of the country, saw her, took her, and lay with her and defiled her. His soul clave unto her afterwards, and his father came to Jacob asking her in marriage and proposing that the two peoples intermarry and become one. Jacob's sons answered deceitfully, requiring every male of the city to be circumcised, and on the third day Simeon and Levi took the city with the sword. Dinah went out to see the daughters of the land; Shechem took her and defiled her (Genesis 34:1-2). Genesis does not say she went alone, and her visit does not make her responsible for his violence. The father waketh for the daughter when no man knoweth, and the care for her taketh away sleep, in her virginity, lest she should be defiled (Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 42:9-10), and marriage is a weighty responsibility (Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 7:25). These precepts charge a household to care for its daughters, not to rename a violated daughter the offender. Shechem then did it backwards, taking first and loving after: his soul clave unto Dinah, and he loved the damsel, and spake kindly unto her, when he had already defiled her (Genesis 34:3). Affection afterward did not undo the defilement. The sons of Jacob were grieved and very wroth, because he had wrought folly in Israel in lying with Jacob's daughter, which thing ought not to be done (Genesis 34:7): the law was in force and known long before it was written in stone at Sinai, which later guarded the daughters of Israel against prostitution (Deuteronomy 23:17). That prohibition is not a charge of prostitution against Dinah. Then Hamor proposed the exact reverse of the law: make ye marriages with us, and give your daughters unto us, and take our daughters  unto you, and dwell with us, and we will become one people (Genesis 34:9-10, 16). The proposal to intermarry anticipates the alliances Moses would forbid (Deuteronomy 7:3). The city's own reasoning is recorded and it was not love either: shall not their cattle and their substance and every beast of theirs be ours (Genesis 34:23). On the third day, when they were sore, Simeon and Levi took each man his sword and came upon the city boldly and slew all the males, and Hamor and Shechem with them, and took Dinah out of Shechem's house (Genesis 34:25-26). Judith's prayer identifies the vengeance as a sword given by God: O Lord God of my father Simeon, to whom thou gavest a sword to take vengeance of the strangers, who loosened the girdle of a maid to defile her (Judith 9:2). It goes further and credits the outcome to God, that thou gavest their rulers to be slain, and smotest the servants with their lords (Judith 9:3), and names the brothers as being moved with thy zeal, and abhorred the pollution of their blood (Judith 9:4). Jacob immediately objected to the danger brought upon his household: ye have troubled me to make me to stink among the inhabitants of the land, and I being few in number (Genesis 34:30). The brothers answered with the question the case turns on, and the chapter closes with their question: should he deal with our sister as with an harlot (Genesis 34:31). Jacob held it against them to his deathbed and divided them in Israel (Genesis 49:5-7), and the tribe of Levi afterwards carried that same sword lawfully at the calf and at Peor, both of which are entered in this volume. The two testimonies must remain together: Judith invokes God's judgment against those who defiled the maid, while Jacob's later words condemn the brothers' fierce anger and cruel wrath (Judith 9:2-4; Genesis 49:5-7). Shechem's desire to marry Dinah did not acquit him, and the judgment upon him did not prevent Jacob from judging the conduct of his own sons.

name: Simeon and Levi at Shechem
text: Deceitful covenant; slaughter of a city for one man's crime. After Dinah's defilement, Jacob's sons answered Shechem deceitfully and required circumcision. Simeon and Levi slew the males while they were sore, and the city was plundered. Judith remembers the sword as vengeance for Dinah; Jacob condemned his sons' fierce anger and pronounced their division in Israel. They answered Shechem and Hamor deceitfully (Genesis 34:13). They offered union on the condition that every male be circumcised, then attacked while the men were sore (Genesis 34:14-25). Hamor and Shechem were slain, Dinah was taken out, and the sons of Jacob spoiled the city and carried off its households (Genesis 34:26-29). The circumcision proposed as the beginning of peace became the occasion of the sword. Judith's prayer remembers Simeon's sword as vengeance granted by God for the defilement of the maid (Judith 9:2-4). Jacob nevertheless refused to unite his honour with his sons' assembly and condemned their cruelty. The offense against Dinah was real; so was the anger for which the brothers were answerable. Their zeal cannot be described without the judgment Jacob later pronounced upon it.

name: Reuben
text: Lying with Bilhah, his father's concubine. Jacob's firstborn went up to his father's bed and lay with Bilhah, and Israel heard of it. Nothing more is said until the deathbed, where it cost Reuben the birthright. The nakedness of thy father's wife shalt thou not uncover (Leviticus 18:8), later a capital offense in the law. Chronicles states the consequence plainly (1 Chronicles 5:1-2): because he defiled his father's bed, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph (1 Chronicles 5:1). Bilhah was his father's concubine, and Israel heard what Reuben had done (Genesis 35:22). The brief report is not an acquittal by silence. When Jacob gathered his sons, he first named the dignity and power that belonged to Reuben and then named the deed that cost him that excellence (Genesis 49:3-4). Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel. The double portion went to Joseph, the rule to Judah. Firstborn status did not shelter him from the consequence of defiling his father's bed (Genesis 49:3-4). Chronicles distinguishes the birthright from rulership: Joseph's sons received the birthright, while Judah prevailed above his brethren and from him came the chief ruler (1 Chronicles 5:1-2). Reuben remained a son and a tribe of Israel, but did not retain the privilege his place of birth had given him.

name: Joseph's brothers
text: Conspiracy to murder; selling a brother; deceiving their father with a bloodied coat. Joseph's brothers envied him, conspired against him, sold him for twenty pieces of silver, and used his bloodied coat to deceive their father. Years later famine brought them before Joseph in Egypt. They confessed their guilt, Judah offered himself for Benjamin, and Joseph preserved the household instead of taking vengeance. At seventeen Joseph brought his father the evil report of his brethren (Genesis 37:2). The law distinguishes bearing necessary witness from concealing known iniquity  (Leviticus 5:1), but Genesis does not reproduce the report or describe a formal demand for testimony. It records the brothers' hatred, their father's favour, and the dreams that increased their envy. The record then names the root twice, and it is not the coat: his brethren envied him (Genesis 37:11), and the envious man hath a wicked eye (Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 14:8). Envy grew into conspiracy, they said one to another, behold, this dreamer cometh, come now therefore, and let us slay him (Genesis 37:19-20), and conspiracy into man-stealing, which the law makes capital: he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, shall surely be put to death (Exodus 21:16). Twenty pieces of silver is what they took for him (Genesis 37:28). The cover-up endured for years through a lie told with a garment and the blood of a kid (Genesis 37:31-33), recalling the garment and the kids used to deceive Isaac, and it brought Jacob to say he would go down into the grave unto his son mourning (Genesis 37:35). Their own verdict on themselves, spoken in Egypt before they knew who was listening, is the one the case records: we are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear (Genesis 42:21). The brothers did not all act alike. Reuben sought to deliver Joseph back to his father, while Judah proposed selling him instead of shedding his blood (Genesis 37:21-27). The sale spared Joseph from their intended murder but still handed their brother into bondage. Years later Judah's willingness to remain a bondman for Benjamin reversed his earlier willingness to send a brother away.

name: Er and Onan
text: Wickedness before the Lord; refusing to raise up seed to a dead brother. Judah took a Canaanite wife, the daughter of Shuah, and had Er, Onan and Shelah. He took Tamar for Er his firstborn, and Er was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord slew him. Judah told Onan to go in unto his brother's wife and raise up seed to his brother. Onan knew the seed should not be his, and spilled it on the ground, and the thing which he did displeased the Lord, and he slew him also. Er's particular wickedness is not named: the record says only that he was wicked in the sight of the Lord (Genesis 38:7). Onan's act is described together with its purpose: he deliberately prevented seed from being raised to his dead brother. The act cannot be separated from the duty he was evading. The text states his motive before it states his method: Onan knew that the seed should not be his, and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother's wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother (Genesis 38:9). He took the wife and kept the use of her, and withheld the one thing the arrangement existed for. What he refused was later written into the law: her husband's brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband's brother unto her, that the firstborn she beareth may succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel (Deuteronomy 25:5-6). Both died at the Lord's hand, not by any court. The duty Onan refused was later written into the law of the kinsman: the firstborn she bears shall succeed in the name of his brother that is dead.

name: Judah and Tamar
text: Withholding Shelah from his brother's widow; going in to a woman he took for a harlot. Judah promised Tamar his third son and never gave him, then lay with her himself on the road to Timnath. When her pregnancy came to light he ordered her burned, until she produced his signet, bracelets and staff. He judged himself: she hath been more righteous than I. After Er and Onan died, Judah sent Tamar to her father's house to wait for Shelah (Genesis 38:11), and let her wait. Tamar covered her face and sat in an open place (Genesis 38:14), and Judah, taking her for a harlot, went in to her for the price of a kid, leaving his signet, bracelets, and staff as a pledge (Genesis 38:18). Three months later he was told his daughter in law was with child by whoredom (Genesis 38:24), and said, Bring her forth, and let her be burnt. Tamar had seen that Shelah was grown and that she was still not given to him (Genesis 38:14). Judah had feared losing another son but left her bound to an expectation he did not fulfil. When the pregnancy was reported, he condemned her before confronting his own part in it. The pledge supplied the identification his accusation lacked. No sentence fell on Tamar; Judah stopped it himself when the pledge was laid before him (Genesis 38:25-26), confessed that the fault was his for withholding Shelah, and knew her again no more. She bore Pharez and Zarah, and Pharez stands in the line of David and of Christ. The confession names the withheld duty: she hath been more righteous than I, because that I gave her not to Shelah my son (Genesis 38:26). Judah's comparative judgment does not need to be enlarged into a declaration that every act was faultless. It exposes his own failure and halts the destruction he had ordered. The house did not end with the deaths of Er and Onan. Tamar bore Pharez and Zarah, and the line through Pharez is preserved in the genealogy of David and Christ (Ruth 4:18-22; Matthew 1:3). The record preserves the fault and its acknowledgment alongside the continuation of the family.

name: Joseph
text: Refusing his master's wife: how can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?. Sold by his brothers, bought by Potiphar, tempted daily by his master's wife, Joseph refused, fled, and was jailed on her lie. The Lord was with him in the pit, in the prison, and in the palace, and he became the man through whom the whole house of Israel was kept alive. The refusal is not a single moment of resistance but a daily one: she spake to Joseph day by day, and he hearkened not unto her. His stated ground is the one the case turns on. He names his master's trust first and then goes past it to the real bar, sinning against God, before Sinai, while serving as a Hebrew sold into Egypt (Genesis 39:8-10). Her repeated pressure did not make adultery less wicked. Genesis does not record a hearing at which he answered her accusation; it does record his later insistence that he had done nothing deserving imprisonment (Genesis 40:15). When she caught his garment, he left it in her hand and fled (Genesis 39:11-12). Escape from the sin cost him the appearance of innocence in her story, but he did not recover the garment by surrendering to the demand. In prison he continued serving, noticed the distress of the other prisoners, and directed the interpretation of their dreams to God (Genesis 40:4-8). Faithfulness continued before deliverance came.

name: Potiphar's wife
text: Soliciting her husband's servant day by day, and bearing false witness against him when he fled. She asked Joseph to lie with her and he refused, telling her it would be a great wickedness and a sin against God. When she caught him by the garment and he left it in her hand and fled, she kept the garment and turned it into evidence against him. The record gives her offense and the statute it breaks, and never gives her sentence. His master's wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said, Lie with me (Genesis 39:7), and she spake to Joseph day by day, and he hearkened not unto her (Genesis 39:10), so the solicitation was sustained and not a moment's impulse. His refusal names the offense before any law was written at Sinai: there is none greater in this house than I, neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife; how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God (Genesis 39:9). Adultery was known to be sin from the beginning. Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws (Genesis 26:5), and even a heathen king rebuked Isaac on the same ground, one of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us (Genesis 26:10), so the nations themselves knew it carried guilt. Then, on a day when none of the men of the house were within, she caught him by his garment, and he left it in her hand  and fled (Genesis 39:11-12), which is the example the wise man commands: flee from sin as from the face of a serpent, for if thou comest too near it, it will bite thee, the teeth  thereof are as the teeth of a lion (Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 21:2). The solicitation was followed by false witness. She called the men of her house and said, he hath brought in an Hebrew unto us to mock us, he came in unto me to lie with me, and I cried with a loud voice, and she laid up the garment by her until his lord came home (Genesis 39:14-16). The same mouth that had flattered him turned and accused him: the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil, but her end is bitter as wormwood, and her ways are moveable (Proverbs 5:3-6), and more bitter than death is the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and her hands as bands, whoso pleaseth God shall escape from her (Ecclesiastes 7:26). The later law requires diligent inquiry and directs that a false witness receive the consequence intended for the accused (Deuteronomy 19:16-19). That statute identifies the gravity of false accusation; Genesis does not say an Israelite court applied it in Egypt. The judgment recorded falls on the innocent man. His master's wrath was kindled, and he took Joseph and put him into the prison, a place where the king's prisoners were bound (Genesis 39:19-20). No inquiry or hearing of Joseph's defence is described. Proverbs warns of the force of a husband's jealousy: jealousy is the rage of a man, therefore he will not spare in the day of vengeance, he will not regard any ransom (Proverbs 6:34-35). Against the woman no later sentence is recorded. Her offense is double under the law, the solicitation and then the false witness, and both stand written with no penalty set against them. What the record does report is where the favour went: the Lord was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison (Genesis 39:21), and the psalm carries it on, whose feet they hurt with fetters, he was laid in iron, until the time that his word came, the word of the Lord tried him (Psalms 105:18-19). The prison became part of the road to government, but Joseph's eventual deliverance did not make the accusation true.

name: Job
text: Perfect and upright, fearing God and eschewing evil; sinning not with his lips in all his loss. Job of Uz feared God and eschewed evil. Under a trial limited by God's command, he lost his substance, his children, and then his health, yet held fast his integrity. When God answered, Job humbled himself and repented of words beyond his understanding. He prayed for his accusing friends, and the Lord restored him. The commendation is given by God before the trial and repeated after it began: hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God and escheweth evil (Job 1:8), and still he holdeth fast his integrity, although thou movedst me against him to destroy him without cause (Job 2:3). The obedience is not endurance only. He acted as a priest for his own household: when the days of their feasting were gone about, and every one had kept his day, Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all, for Job said, it may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts; thus did Job continually (Job 1:5). His defence recalls practical righteousness: when he went out to the gate through the city, the young men saw him and hid themselves, the aged arose and stood, the princes refrained talking, and the nobles held their peace (Job 29:7-10). He delivered the poor that cried and the fatherless, was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame, searched out a cause he did not know before judging it, and broke the jaws of the wicked and plucked the spoil out of his teeth (Job 29:12-17). He also made a covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1). His righteousness included investigation, not merely sympathy: he sought the facts and rescued the oppressed from the wicked. That stands against his friends' readiness to explain his suffering by accusing him without establishing their charge. Satan's charge was that the obedience  was bought: doth Job fear God for nought, hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side (Job 1:9-10). The trial has limits set by God. Satan asked leave and was given it in limits both times: all that he hath is in thy power, only upon himself put not forth thine hand (Job 1:12), and then, behold, he is in thine hand, but save his life (Job 2:6). And when the property, the servants and all ten children were taken in a single day, he worshipped and said, the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away, blessed be the name of the Lord; in all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly (Job 1:20-22). After his body was afflicted, his wife urged him to abandon his integrity: dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die (Job 2:9), and he answered her, thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh; what, shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips (Job 2:10). The Lord turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends: also the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before. So the Lord blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning. He had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, seven sons and three daughters, and in all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job; and he saw his sons' sons, even four generations. James: ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.

name: Job's three friends
text: Speaking of God the thing that is not right; condemning the righteous. Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite made an appointment together to come and mourn with Job and to comfort him. They wept, rent their mantles, and sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights without a word. Then they argued for thirty chapters that his suffering proved hidden sin, and Eliphaz at last invented the sins outright. When the Lord answered out of the whirlwind he answered them too, and required them to bring sacrifice to the man they had condemned. Their first response was compassion. They heard of the evil that was come upon him and came every one from his own place, having made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him (Job 2:11); they wept, rent their mantles, and sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him, for they saw  that his grief was very great (Job 2:12-13). Their presence in his grief was not itself the fault. The fault is in what they concluded and would not abandon. Eliphaz began from a rule that is not always true: who ever perished, being innocent, or where were the righteous cut off (Job 4:7). Bildad argued from God's justice to Job's guilt, doth God pervert judgment, or doth the Almighty pervert justice (Job 8:3), which is a true question put to a false use. Zophar spoke a heavy precept and misapplied it, that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth (Job 11:6), treating unproved guilt as something already established. Then Eliphaz stopped My wrath is kindled against thee and against thy two friends, for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath. They were ordered to bring seven bullocks and seven rams to Job and have him pray for them, lest I deal with you after your folly. He did, and the Lord accepted Job.

name: Pharaoh of the Exodus
text: Oppressing Israel; drowning their sons; refusing the Lord's command. The king who did not know Joseph enslaved Israel, ordered their male infants thrown into the river, and when Moses came in the Lord's name answered, Who is the Lord? He hardened his heart through ten plagues and drowned in the sea he pursued Israel into. The policy was deliberate and it is quoted: come on, let us deal wisely with them, lest they multiply, and it come to pass, that, when there falleth out any war, they join also unto our enemies (Exodus 1:10). What followed was forced labour with rigour, and lives made bitter with hard bondage, in morter and in brick and in all manner of service in the field (Exodus 1:13-14), and when the affliction only increased them he moved to infanticide by decree, every son that is born ye shall cast into the river (Exodus 1:22). To the Lord's command he answered, Who is the Lord, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go? I know not the Lord, neither will I let Israel go (Exodus 5:2). Then the pattern that gives him his sentence: each time a plague lifted he hardened his heart and would not let the people go, and he broke his word repeatedly with the evidence in front of him. Paul reads the outcome as appointed, for the scripture saith unto Pharaoh, even for this same purpose have I raised thee up, that I might shew my power in thee, and that my name might be declared throughout all the earth (Romans 9:17). Ten plagues came upon the country, and they were not random: against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment, I am the Lord (Exodus 12:12), and the record confirms it was carried out, upon their gods also the Lord executed judgments (Numbers 33:4). Each stroke shamed a thing Egypt worshipped, the river, the beasts, the light, and the last of them took the firstborn of every house from the throne to the dungeon, and there was not a house where there was not one dead (Exodus 12:29-30). He let them go and pursued them, and the waters returned and covered the chariots and the horsemen, and all the host of Pharaoh that came into the sea after them; there remained not so much as one of them (Exodus 14:27-28). Wisdom's summary is that a strange death found them, and that the element of the sea, which had let Israel pass, drowned the pursuers (Wisdom of Solomon 19:1-5).

name: Shiphrah and Puah, the midwives
text: Fearing God and not doing as the king of Egypt commanded them. Pharaoh ordered the Hebrew midwives to kill every son at the birthstool. They feared God more than the king and saved the men children alive. God dealt well with them, and because they feared God, he made them houses. They were given a direct order by the head of state, backed by his power to kill them: when ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women, if it be a son, then ye shall kill him (Exodus 1:16). They disobeyed it, and the text states the reason without embellishment: but the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive (Exodus 1:17). That is the rule the apostles afterwards stood on, we ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), and the standard Proverbs sets, if thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain; if thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not, doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it (Proverbs 24:11-12). Called to account, they answered that the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women, for they are lively, and are delivered ere the midwives come in unto them (Exodus 1:19), which is a statement about the daughters of Israel and not about the nations, and the record neither corrects it nor rebukes them for it. Therefore God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied, and waxed very mighty (Exodus 1:20), and the reason is given again so that it cannot be mistaken for reward of policy: and it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that he made them houses (Exodus 1:21). Two women at the bottom of an empire were given households of their own, which is the currency this account values, and the increase they had risked their lives to protect is recorded in the same breath. The whole nation that came out of Egypt came through the hands they refused to use. Their names are written and the Pharaoh who commanded them is not, which is itself the verdict.

name: Moses, and the Egyptian in the sand
text: Slaying an Egyptian and hiding him in the sand. Moses went out to his brethren, saw an Egyptian smiting a Hebrew, looked this way and that, and slew him. He supposed his brethren would have understood that God by his hand would deliver them; they understood not, and the man who did the wrong threw the killing in his face. Forty years in Midian were the sentence. He knew whose son he was before he struck anyone. Raised in Pharaoh's house and called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, he went out unto his brethren and looked on their burdens, and the account calls the man he defended one of his brethren (Exodus 2:11), so the lineage was never in doubt to him. Acts gives what he was thinking: he supposed his brethren would have understood how that God by his hand would deliver them, but they understood not (Acts 7:25). The deliverance was the right end and the means and the timing were his own. The record's own witness that he knew it was unlawful is in the two details it bothers to keep: he looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no man, he slew the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand (Exodus 2:12). A man who is executing judgment does not check whether he is being watched, and does not bury the body. The next day two Hebrews strove, and he that did the wrong said, Who made thee a prince and a judge over us? intendest thou to kill me, as thou killedst the Egyptian? And Moses feared, and said, Surely this thing is known. Pharaoh heard the thing and sought to slay Moses, and Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh and dwelt in the land of Midian, a stranger, where he begat two sons. He came back at eighty to the work he had tried to begin at forty.

name: Moses and the uncircumcised son
text: Neglecting the sign of the covenant in his own house. Sent back to Egypt with the rod of God in his hand, Moses took his wife and his sons and went. He had just been given the message for Pharaoh: Israel is my son, even my firstborn; let my son go, and if thou refuse, I will slay thy son, even thy firstborn. By the way in the inn the Lord met him and sought to kill him, because his own son was uncircumcised. Zipporah took a sharp stone and circumcised the child and cast the foreskin at his feet, and said, Surely a bloody husband art thou to me. So he let him go. Circumcision was not a Sinai ordinance. It was given to Abraham centuries earlier as the token of the covenant, every man child among you shall be circumcised, and he that is eight days old shall be circumcised among you, every man child in your generations (Genesis 17:10-12), with the penalty written into it: the uncircumcised man child whose flesh of his foreskin is not circumcised, that soul shall be cut off from his people, he hath broken my covenant (Genesis 17:14). That is why the deliverer of Israel was worthy of death on the road, and it is why the case belongs in this volume as evidence that the law was in force long before it was written in stone. Two things sharpen it. Egypt did not practise it, and Israel was afterwards told plainly, after the doings of the land of Egypt, wherein ye dwelt, shall ye not do (Leviticus 18:3), so a man raised in Pharaoh's house had taken up the omission of the country he was raised in. And the errand he was carrying makes it intolerable: he had just been given the words, Israel is my son, even my firstborn; let  my son go, and if thou refuse, I will slay thy son, even thy firstborn (Exodus 4:22-23). He was going to demand another man's firstborn on pain of death while his own son bore no token of the covenant he was invoking. The Lord met him and sought to kill him (Exodus 4:24), which is the sentence of Genesis 17:14 falling on the head of the house rather than on the child. The remedy was immediate and it was performed by his wife: then Zipporah took a sharp stone, and cut off the foreskin of her son, and cast it at his feet, and said, Surely a bloody husband art thou to me (Exodus 4:25). So he let him go; then she said, A bloody husband thou art, because of the circumcision (Exodus 4:26), and the record explains her own words so that they are not mistaken for a complaint about anything else. The record gives no further comment, and the placing is the comment: the thing had to be set right in his own house before he could carry a word from God into Pharaoh's. The same neglect cost the next generation as well, for all the people born in the wilderness had not been circumcised, and Joshua had to make sharp knives and circumcise them again the second time before they took the land (Joshua 5:2-5). The token was never withdrawn: Abraham was ninety years old and nine when he was circumcised  (Genesis 17:24), and Paul took and circumcised Timothy because of the Jews which were in those quarters (Acts 16:3). Circumcision verily profiteth, if thou keep the law (Romans 2:25), and the circumcision of the heart is commanded alongside it and not instead of it, circumcise yourselves to the Lord, and take away the foreskins of your heart (Jeremiah 4:4).

name: The magicians of Egypt
text: Withstanding Moses with their enchantments, and hardening Pharaoh in his refusal. Pharaoh called the wise men and the sorcerers, and they matched the rod and the blood and the frogs with their enchantments. At the lice they could not, and said, This is the finger of God. At the boils they could not so much as stand before Moses, because the boil was upon them. Pharaoh called the wise men and the sorcerers, and the magicians of Egypt did in like manner with their enchantments (Exodus 7:11), and what they did was witchcraft, which the law puts under death and names among the abominations for which the nations were cast out (Deuteronomy 18:10-12; Exodus 22:18). But mark the limit of the craft: they could copy a plague and they could not lift one. They turned water into blood and could not turn it back clear, and the fish still died and the river still stank; they brought up frogs and could not remove a frog. Every imitation therefore added to the affliction of their own country while giving the king a reason to refuse, and the record gives that reason each time: and Pharaoh's heart was hardened, neither did he hearken unto them, as the Lord had said (Exodus 7:22). The use of the craft was to hold a king in his sin, and it was practised on a people who were suffering for it. Aaron's rod swallowed up their rods before the contest had properly begun (Exodus 7:12). At the third plague the craft ran out: the magicians did so with their enchantments to bring forth lice, but they could not, and they said unto Pharaoh, This is the finger of God (Exodus 8:18-19), and even that confession did not move the king. At the sixth they could not so much as stand in the room, for the boil was upon the magicians, and upon all the Egyptians (Exodus 9:11). The whole contest was a judgment on what they served, for the Lord had said, against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment: I am the Lord (Exodus 12:12), and Numbers records that it was done, upon their gods also the Lord executed judgments (Numbers 33:4). Paul names the two and gives the standing sentence on every imitator after them: as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth, but they shall proceed no further, for their folly shall be manifest unto all men (2 Timothy 3:8-9).

name: Israel at the first Passover
text: Doing as the Lord commanded Moses and Aaron: the lamb, the blood on the door, the unleavened bread. On the night the destroyer went through Egypt, every house of Israel that did as it was told was passed over. The children of Israel went away, and did as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron, so did they. The ordinance was made perpetual on the spot. Take you a lamb according to the house of your fathers; kill it in the evening; take of the blood and strike it on the two side posts and on the upper door post; eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, in haste; none of you shall go out at the door of his house until the morning. And the children of Israel went away, and did as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron, so did they. By faith he kept the passover, and the sprinkling of blood, lest he that destroyed the firstborn should touch them. The blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you. At midnight the Lord smote all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, and against the children of Israel not so much as a dog moved his tongue. He brought them forth also with silver and gold: and there was not one feeble person among their tribes. Thus did all the children of Israel; as the Lord commanded Moses and Aaron, so did they. And it came to pass the selfsame day.

name: Amalek
text: Attacking Israel's stragglers on the way out of Egypt. Amalek came out against Israel at Rephidim and, as Deuteronomy records, smote the hindmost, the feeble and faint and weary, and feared not God. Israel prevailed while Moses' hands were held up. This was not a stranger's war. Amalek was of Esau: Timna was concubine to Eliphaz Esau's son, and she bare to Eliphaz Amalek (Genesis 36:12), and his house were dukes in the land of Edom. So the first nation to come against Israel after the sea was a nation of their own brother's seed, which is the standing on which Edom is judged elsewhere in this volume. The manner of the attack is the charge, and Moses set it down forty years later so that it could not be forgotten: remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt, how he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God (Deuteronomy 25:17-18). He did not meet the mighty men at the front. He went to the back, where the women, the children and the old were, and took the ones who could not answer him. The Lord swore a war without end: the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation (Exodus 17:16), and the sentence was written for a memorial in a book and rehearsed in the ears of Joshua, for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven (Exodus 17:14). Balaam pronounced the same, that Amalek was the first of the nations, but his latter end shall be that he perish for ever (Numbers 24:20). Centuries later Saul was sent by Samuel to execute it and spared Agag, and the failure is entered separately in this volume. The war then ran on exactly as sworn: David smote them and recovered all (1 Samuel 30:17-18), the sons of Simeon smote the rest that were escaped in the days of Hezekiah (1 Chronicles 4:42-43), and in Persia Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite (Esther 3:1), of the seed Saul had let live, rose to destroy the whole nation and was hanged on his own gallows. Generation to generation is what was sworn and what the record shows.

name: Moses
text: Refusing to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter; faithful in all the Lord's house; very meek, above all the men upon the face of the earth. He gave up the court of Egypt to be counted with slaves, and led them forty years through a wilderness that murmured against him at every turn. The Lord's testimony on him is unmatched: my servant Moses, who is faithful in all mine house; with him will I speak mouth to mouth. He was buried by God. The record puts the first act at the point of choice rather than at the burning bush. Grown, and with the court of Egypt open to him, he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter (Hebrews 11:24) and chose to be counted with slaves, esteeming reproach greater riches than the treasures of Egypt (Hebrews 11:26). What follows is forty years of a specific and unglamorous obedience: building the tabernacle to specification, so that as the Lord commanded Moses, so did he is repeated through the whole account of it, and enduring a congregation that murmured against him at every stage (Exodus 33:7). Numbers gives the character in one line that he did not write about himself, that he was very meek above all men on the face of the earth (Numbers 12:3). His own failure at Meribah is a separate case, and its inclusion here would be dishonest. The commendation given to him is unlike any other in the Old Testament. Where a prophet receives visions and dreams, God says of Moses that he is faithful in all mine house (Numbers 12:7), and that he will speak with him mouth to mouth (Numbers 12:8), apparently, and not in dark speeches. He spoke as a man speaks to his friend. He asked to be blotted out of the book rather than see the nation destroyed and was not rebuked for asking. He was refused the land for the one failure and buried by God himself in a grave no man knows, and he stands on the mount with Elijah at the transfiguration, so that the man barred from the land is seen standing in it.

name: The manna hoarders
text: Keeping manna overnight; going out to gather on the Sabbath. Told to gather only a day's portion, some kept manna until morning and it bred worms and stank. Told there would be none on the seventh day, some went out to gather anyway and found nothing. The manna was given as a test and the terms of the test were stated when it was given: the people shall go out and gather a certain rate every day, that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no (Exodus 16:4). The murmuring that preceded it, would to God we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots (Exodus 16:3), was answered with the reminder that murmuring against the men the Lord sends is murmuring against the Lord: your murmurings are not against us, but against the Lord (Exodus 16:8). Two failures followed and both were failures to trust a daily portion. Moses said, let no man leave of it till the morning, notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moses, but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and stank (Exodus 16:19-20). Then on the seventh day there went out some of the people for to gather, and they found none (Exodus 16:27), though they had been told the day before that the sixth day's double portion was for the rest of the holy sabbath, and had been told to bake and seethe on the sixth day for it (Exodus 16:23). The hoarded bread rotted and Moses was wroth with them (Exodus 16:20). The sabbath gatherers went out and found nothing, and the Lord answered them through Moses with the question that measures the whole wilderness: how long refuse ye to keep my commandments and my laws (Exodus 16:28), and the rule of the day was restated, abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day (Exodus 16:29). The sentences are small and exact, a stink and an empty basket, and they are recorded so that the sabbath and the daily portion would be understood before the greater tests came. An omer of the manna was laid up before the testimony, to be kept for the generations that would not see it (Exodus 16:32-34), so that the provision that proved them was kept as evidence.

name: Bezaleel and Aholiab
text: Making all that the Lord commanded, and no more; and teaching others to do it. Two men were called by name and filled with the spirit of God in wisdom, understanding, knowledge and all manner of workmanship, to devise the work of the tabernacle in gold, silver, brass, stone and timber. They made every piece to the pattern shewed in the mount, and Moses looked upon all the work and blessed them. God also put in their hearts that they might teach.
