The obedience is exactness in craft, which the record treats as seriously as any other obedience in the volume. They worked to a pattern given on the mount and are commended for adding nothing to it: according to all that the Lord commanded Moses, so the children of Israel made all the work (Exodus 39:42). Bezaleel was of Judah and Aholiab of Dan, one of the least of the tribes, which the account sets side by side without comment (Exodus 31:2,6). The same chapter that lists their filling with the spirit lists it as being for cutting stones and carving timber (Exodus 31:5), so the first men in scripture said to be filled with the spirit of God were filled for manual work (Exodus 31:3). Moses did look upon all the work, and behold, they had done it as the Lord had commanded (Exodus 39:43), even so had they done it: and Moses blessed them. The glory of the Lord filled the tent they had made (Exodus 40:34). They were also given the capacity to teach, so the skill was not held privately, and the tabernacle they built stood for four centuries and every case in Leviticus and Numbers takes place inside or around it.

name: Aaron and Israel at the golden calf
text: Idolatry within weeks of the covenant. While Moses was on the mountain receiving the law that forbade it, the people made a golden calf and worshipped it. The covenant was broken almost before the ink was dry. Not forty days had passed since they heard the voice from the mount. When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down, they gathered themselves together unto Aaron and said, up, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, we wot not what is become of him (Exodus 32:1). Any time deliverance did not come when Israel wanted it, the nation turned, and it turned toward what it had carried out of Egypt: the spirit that was in Israel in Egypt was still in Israel when they left, and it corrupted them the moment the man was out of sight. Aaron's part is the heavier for who he was. He had seen every plague and stood before Pharaoh and been set apart to the priesthood, and he received the gold and fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf, and they said, these be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt (Exodus 32:4). Then he built an altar before it and proclaimed, to morrow is a feast to the Lord (Exodus 32:5), which is the offence named in the second commandment performed under the name of the first. They rose up early, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play (Exodus 32:6), and the Lord's own verdict was given before Moses had seen any of it: they have turned aside quickly out of the way which I commanded them (Exodus 32:8), and, I have seen this people, and, behold, it is a stiffnecked people (Exodus 32:9). Moses ground the calf to powder and made them drink it. The Levites, called to the Lord's side, put about three thousand to the sword, and the Lord sent a plague on the people. Aaron was spared but not excused.

name: The sons of Levi at the golden calf
text: Answering, Who is on the Lord's side? and executing the sentence on their own brethren. When Moses stood in the gate of the camp and asked who was on the Lord's side, all the sons of Levi gathered to him, took their swords, and went through the camp. Three thousand fell. For that day the priesthood and the service of the sanctuary were given to the tribe, and Moses' last blessing names it. Moses stood in the gate of the camp with the calf ground to powder (Exodus 32:20) and put a question rather than an order: who is on the Lord's side? The whole tribe came to him (Exodus 32:26). What they were then commanded was the hardest thing in the law, to execute the sentence on apostates without regard to kinship, slay every man his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbour (Exodus 32:27). Deuteronomy 13 states the statute they were applying, that a brother or a son or the wife of thy bosom who entices to other gods is not to be spared or concealed (Deuteronomy 33:8-11). Three thousand fell, and the account is careful that the sword did not fall on strangers. Moses read the day as a consecration: consecrate yourselves today to the Lord, even every man upon his son and upon his brother (Exodus 32:29), that he may bestow upon you a blessing this day. The priesthood and the whole service of the sanctuary were given to the tribe (Numbers 3:31), and the Levites were taken instead of the firstborn of Israel (Numbers 3:12). Moses' final blessing on Levi names the cause exactly (Numbers 3:17), that they observed God's word and kept his covenant (Deuteronomy 33:9), and did not acknowledge their own brethren nor know their own children. Malachi holds the covenant with Levi up centuries later as what a priesthood is supposed to be (Malachi 2:4-7).

name: Nadab and Abihu
text: Offering strange fire not commanded. Two priests, sons of Aaron, offered fire before the Lord that he had not commanded. Fire came out from the Lord and consumed them on the spot. The instructions for the incense had already been given, and given to their own father: Aaron was to burn sweet incense every morning and at even, a perpetual incense before the Lord throughout the generations, and ye shall offer no strange incense thereon (Exodus 30:7-9). So the fault is not an error of enthusiasm but the offering of a thing expressly excluded. They took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not (Leviticus 10:1). The office itself was guarded to this degree: Aaron and his sons were appointed to wait on the priest's office, and the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death (Numbers 3:10), so nearness to the altar was the most closely regulated standing in Israel and these two held it. There went out fire from the Lord and devoured them, and they died before the Lord (Leviticus 10:2). The record notes what fire it was: the same that had come out from before the Lord and consumed the burnt offering upon the altar in the chapter before, while the people shouted and fell on their faces (Leviticus 9:24). The fire that had accepted the lawful offering consumed the unlawful one. Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar were then forbidden to uncover their heads or rend their clothes lest they die and wrath come upon all the people, and the mourning was given to the whole house of Israel instead (Leviticus 10:6). The father was not permitted to mourn his own sons, because they died in the midst of the sin, and the sentence pronounced over it is the standing rule of the sanctuary: I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me, and before all the people I will be glorified (Leviticus 10:3).

name: The blasphemer in the camp
text: Blaspheming the Name in a quarrel. In a fight within the camp, a man blasphemed the Name and cursed. He was held until the Lord's mind was made known, and his case set the statute for all Israel. He is identified by his lineage before his act, and the lineage is the first thing the case teaches. The son of an Israelitish woman, whose father was an Egyptian, went out among the children of Israel, and this son of the Israelitish woman and a man of Israel strove together in the camp (Leviticus 24:10). His mother was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan (Leviticus 24:11), so the mother was named and the tribe was named, and he was conceived in Egypt while Israel dwelt among the Egyptians; there is no half Israel, and he was counted with his mother's people. In the strife the Israelitish woman's son blasphemed the name of the Lord, and cursed (Leviticus 24:11). The offence was against God directly, in the camp, spoken aloud and heard. The Lord commanded that the whole congregation stone him outside the camp, the witnesses laying their hands on his head. From his case came the law: whoever blasphemes the Name shall be put to death.

name: The complainers at Taberah and the lusters at Kibroth-hattaavah
text: Murmuring against the Lord; lusting after flesh and despising the manna. The people complained and the fire of the Lord burned in the outskirts of the camp. Days later the mixed multitude fell to lusting and Israel wept for the meat of Egypt. Quail came, and with the quail a plague. The first sentence names the whole offence: when the people complained, it displeased the Lord, and the Lord heard it, and his anger was kindled (Numbers 11:1). Egypt had been destroyed for them, its firstborn, its army, its land, and at the first trial on the far side of the sea they murmured. Nothing spoken is hidden, and the wise man's warning is the  precept the case sits on: beware of murmuring, which is unprofitable, and refrain your tongue from backbiting, for there is no word so secret that shall go for nought, and the mouth that belieth slayeth the soul (Wisdom of Solomon 1:11). The second stage came from outside the nation before it came from inside it: the mixt multitude that was among them fell a lusting, and the children of Israel also wept again (Numbers 11:4). The nations sprinkled in among Israel lusted first, and Israel followed them, as it always has, and wept for the fish they did eat in Egypt freely, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, and the garlick (Numbers 11:5), the diet of the house of bondage, weeks after the bondage ended. They had just watched the Lord consume the complainers in the uttermost parts of the camp and went back and did the same thing, and the psalm names it: they tempted God in their heart by asking meat for their lust, and they spake against God (Psalms 78:18-19). Fire consumed the complainers at Taberah until Moses prayed. At Kibroth-hattaavah, while the flesh was yet between their teeth, the Lord smote the people with a very great plague; the place is named for the graves of the lusters. Paul: these things were our examples.

name: Eldad and Medad
text: Prophesying in the camp when the spirit rested on them, and being defended by Moses. Seventy elders were gathered to the tabernacle to be given of the spirit that was on Moses. Two of the written men stayed in the camp, and the spirit rested on them there, and they prophesied. A young man ran and told Moses, and Joshua said, My lord Moses, forbid them. Moses answered, Enviest thou for my sake? would God that all the Lord's people were prophets. They were of the written number but they were not at the tent. Nothing in the account says they refused to go, and the record does not accuse them; what it records is that the spirit rested on them where they were (Numbers 11:25), and that they did not conceal it or wait for permission before speaking. The complaint against them came from the camp and from Moses' own servant (Numbers 11:27), and the two men are not shown answering it. Moses refused to silence them and turned the rebuke on the man who wanted it done: enviest thou for my sake? would God that all the Lord's people were prophets (Numbers 11:29), and that the Lord would put his spirit upon them. The case is entered because the blessing was defended by the one person whose standing it might have threatened, and because the wish Moses expressed is the thing Joel later prophesies and Peter cites at Pentecost as fulfilled. Two men who were not in the room are the volume's earliest evidence that the gift is not confined to the appointed place.

name: Aaron and Miriam
text: Speaking against Moses; challenging his authority. Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses, using his marriage as a pretext to ask whether the Lord had not also spoken through them. God summoned all three and answered plainly. The occasion is named and it was a pretext: Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married (Numbers 12:1). That is Zipporah, the daughter of the priest of Midian, whom he had married in the forty years outside Egypt and whom the Lord had allowed him; they had said nothing about her when he was bringing them out of Egypt, nor when he set Aaron over the men and Miriam over the women. What they actually said is the charge: hath the Lord indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us? And the Lord heard it (Numbers 12:2). It was a claim of equality with the man God had set over them, and Miriam is named first because she led it. The record answers it before the Lord does, with the one line Moses did not write about himself: now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth (Numbers 12:3). The Lord called all three to the tabernacle and came down in the pillar of the cloud, and declared the difference to their faces: to a prophet I make myself known in a vision, and speak in a dream; my servant Moses is not so, who is faithful in all mine house, with him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches; wherefore then were ye not afraid to speak against my servant Moses (Numbers 12:6-8). The anger of the Lord was

name: The ten spies
text: Bringing an evil report; making the congregation to murmur. Twelve men searched Canaan forty days. Ten came back and told the people the land eats its inhabitants and the giants made them as grasshoppers. Caleb and Joshua said the Lord would bring them in. The people believed the ten. They were sent as rulers of their tribes, and they searched the land forty days (Numbers 13:2, 25), and their report did not deny the land was good, for they carried back one cluster of grapes borne between two upon a staff and said, surely it floweth with milk and honey (Numbers 13:23, 27). What they denied was that God could give it, and they said it in the presence of the whole congregation: we be not able to go up against the people, for they are stronger than we (Numbers 13:31). Then they brought up an evil report of the land, calling it a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof, and there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight (Numbers 13:32-33). Ten rulers who had watched Egypt destroyed and the sea part measured themselves against men, and the evil report spread its spirit through the whole camp in a night. Caleb had already answered them in front of the people: let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it (Numbers 13:30). Because of the report the whole congregation wept that night, said one to another, let us make a captain, and let us return into Egypt (Numbers 14:4), and bade stone Caleb and Joshua with stones, and the glory of the Lord appeared in the tabernacle before all the children of Israel (Numbers 14:10). The men that brought up the evil report died by the plague before the Lord (Numbers 14:37), the ten of them, while Joshua and Caleb, of the men that went to search the land, lived still (Numbers 14:38). The nation's sentence is entered separately, but it is measured from this act: after the number of the days in which ye searched the land, even forty days, each day for a year, shall ye bear your iniquities (Numbers 14:34). Forty-five years later Caleb, at eighty-five, asked for the mountain the ten had feared and took it (Joshua 14:10-12), and Mattathias on his deathbed put the two together as the pattern for his sons: Caleb for bearing witness before the congregation received the heritage of the land, and Joshua for fulfilling the word was made a judge in Israel (1 Maccabees 2:55-56).

name: Caleb and Joshua
text: Wholly following the Lord when ten spies and the whole congregation would not. Twelve men saw the same land, the same cities and the same giants. Ten said, We be not able. Two said, The Lord is with us: fear them not. The ten died of the plague; the whole generation died in the wilderness; and Caleb and Joshua were the only two of six hundred thousand who walked into the land. Twelve men walked the same ground, saw the same walled cities and the same giants (Numbers 13:28), and came back with the same facts (Numbers 13:26). The difference was not information. Ten reported that the people were stronger (Numbers 13:31); two reported that the Lord was with them, and their fear is departed from them (Numbers 14:9). Caleb and Joshua rent their clothes (Numbers 14:6) and stood before a congregation that was reaching for stones (Joshua 14:6-14). The formula the Lord uses of Caleb is the exact standard of the case: he hath followed me fully, and again, he wholly followed the Lord God of Israel (Joshua 14:14). The obedience was not silence under pressure but public contradiction of a settled majority. Of six hundred thousand men numbered from twenty years old and upward (Numbers 14:29), these two entered the land. Every other man of that generation died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:2), and the sentence was measured to the offense at a year for a day. Caleb at eighty-five asked for the mountain with the giants on it rather than an easier portion, and got it, and Hebron became his inheritance because he wholly followed the Lord (Joshua 14:14). Joshua succeeded Moses and divided the land he had been the first to say could be taken (Joshua 14:6-14).

name: The generation that died in the wilderness
text: Ten provocations; unbelief at Kadesh-barnea. Those numbered from twenty years old who had seen the signs in Egypt and at the sea, and had tempted the Lord ten times, were sentenced at Kadesh to wander until every one of them had fallen in the wilderness. Only Caleb and Joshua of that generation entered the land. The charge is a count, and God gave the number himself: all those men which have seen my glory, and my miracles, which I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and have tempted me now these ten times, and have not hearkened to my voice (Numbers 14:22). At the sea, at Marah, over the manna, at Rephidim, at the calf, at Taberah, at Kibroth-hattaavah, and at last at the border of the land itself, when the whole congregation wept and said, would God that we had died in the land of Egypt, or in this wilderness (Numbers 14:2), and proposed a captain to lead them back to a country whose army was at the bottom of the sea. Told the sentence, they mourned greatly, rose early, and presumed to go up unto the hill top, though the ark of the covenant of the Lord and Moses departed not out of  the camp (Numbers 14:40, 44), so that the last act of the generation was disobedience in the opposite direction. Hebrews names the root of the whole sequence, that they could not enter in because of unbelief (Hebrews 3:19), and puts the question that fixes the case: with whom was he grieved forty years? was it not with them that had sinned, whose carcases fell in the wilderness (Hebrews 3:17). Forty years, a year for each day of the search. Your carcases shall fall in this wilderness. Sirach counts them: the six hundred thousand footmen gathered together in the hardness of their hearts, whom he pitied not.

name: The man gathering sticks on the Sabbath
text: Working on the Sabbath. A man was found gathering sticks on the Sabbath day and was held because it had not been declared what should be done to him. The Lord then gave Moses the instruction for this case. The sabbath had already been given as the sign and its breach already carried death: ye shall keep the sabbath therefore, for it is holy unto you, every one that defileth it shall surely be put to death (Exodus 31:14), and, whosoever doeth any work in the sabbath day, he shall surely be put to death (Exodus 31:15). It is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that ye may know that I am the Lord that doth sanctify you (Exodus 31:13), and keeping it is what marks Israel as his; the nations do not have it. The work in question is not obscure. Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day (Exodus 35:3), and gathering sticks is gathering fuel to kindle it. Bake that which ye will bake to day, and seethe that ye will seethe (Exodus 16:23) is the rule of the day before: the cooking is done on the sixth day, the sabbath meal is what was laid up. While the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man that gathered sticks upon the sabbath day (Numbers 15:32), and they that found him brought him unto Moses and Aaron, and unto all the congregation (Numbers 15:33). The case is entered as a warning against every man excusing his own trade on that day. The Lord instructed Moses that the man must be put to death by stoning outside the camp, and the congregation carried out that command. Numbers 15:34 describes uncertainty about what should be done to this man; it should not be read as saying that no Sabbath death penalty had previously been stated.

name: Korah, Dathan, and Abiram
text: Rebellion against God-appointed authority. Korah led 250 leaders in a challenge to Moses and Aaron, claiming the whole congregation was holy and needed no mediator. The earth answered the claim. The company is counted exactly: Korah of Levi, with Dathan, Abiram and On of Reuben, and two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown (Numbers 16:1-2). What they claimed was equality, that all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the Lord is among them, wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the congregation of the Lord (Numbers 16:3). Moses answered by naming what they already held and what they were reaching for: seemeth it but a small thing unto you that the God of Israel hath separated you from the congregation of Israel, to bring you near to himself to do the service of the tabernacle, and ye seek the priesthood also (Numbers 16:9-10). They were Levites, and the service of the tabernacle was theirs and no one else's, and it was not enough. Dathan and Abiram would not even come when called, and charged Moses with bringing them out of a land flowing with milk and honey to kill them in the wilderness and making himself altogether a prince over them (Numbers 16:12-13). The test was the censers, since the dispute was over who might come near: take you censers, and put fire therein, and put incense in them before the Lord, and the man whom the Lord doth choose, he shall be holy (Numbers 16:6-7). The ground clave asunder and swallowed Korah's company with their houses and all their goods, and they went down alive into the pit (Numbers 16:31-33). Fire came out from the Lord and consumed the two hundred and fifty men that offered incense (Numbers 16:35). The next day the whole congregation murmured, saying, ye have killed the people of the Lord, and a plague killed fourteen thousand seven hundred more until Aaron ran with a censer and stood between the dead and the living (Numbers 16:46-48). The censers of the dead were beaten into plates for a covering of the altar, a memorial that no stranger which is not of the seed of Aaron come near to offer incense (Numbers 16:39-40).

name: The congregation, the day after Korah
text: Murmuring that Moses and Aaron had killed the people of the Lord. The earth had swallowed Korah's company the day before, and fire had consumed the two hundred and fifty. The next morning the whole congregation gathered against Moses and Aaron and called the dead the people of the Lord. The plague began before the sentence was finished being spoken. The earth had opened the day before and the fire had consumed two hundred and fifty men with censers in their hands, and on the very next day the nation took the side of the dead: but on the morrow all the congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron, saying, ye have killed the people of the Lord (Numbers 16:41). The judgment they had watched became the grievance. They gathered against the two men again, and the glory of the Lord appeared (Numbers 16:42), which is the same sign that had answered Korah, and this time there was no test of censers and no warning; wrath went out from the Lord and the plague was begun (Numbers 16:46). The glory of the Lord appeared and wrath went out from him; the plague was begun. Moses sent Aaron running into the congregation with a censer to make an atonement, and he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stayed. Fourteen thousand and seven hundred died, beside them that died about the matter of Korah.

name: Moses at the waters of Meribah
text: Failing to honor God as holy before the people. Told to speak to the rock so it would give water, Moses instead struck it twice and spoke rashly to the people. The water came, but so did a sentence: he would not enter the promised land. The command was exact and it was small: take the rod, gather the assembly, and speak ye unto the rock before their eyes, and it shall give forth his water (Numbers 20:8). What Moses did instead is two things, and the first is the graver. He said, Hear now, ye rebels; must we fetch you water out of this rock (Numbers 20:10). That we is how the record shows he was out of the spirit: he put himself and Aaron in the place of the one who was giving the water. Then he lifted up his hand and smote the rock twice with his rod, when he had been told to speak to it (Numbers 20:11). The provocation was real and the  account does not hide it. There was no water, the congregation gathered against him, and they chode with him, which is a loud and angry thing: would God that we had died when our brethren died before the Lord, and wherefore have ye brought up the congregation into this wilderness, that we and our cattle should die there (Numbers 20:3-4). He was carrying twelve tribes at once. The provocation explains the anger and does not excuse the word. The water still came out abundantly, and the congregation drank, and their beasts also (Numbers 20:11), so the people lost nothing by it and only the two men did. The sentence is pronounced immediately and the ground given is precise: because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore ye shall not bring this congregation into the land which I have given them (Numbers 20:12). Forty years of carrying the nation ended with the leader kept out of the country for one sentence spoken in anger. The place was named Meribah, which is strife, because the children of Israel strove with the Lord, and he was sanctified in them (Numbers 20:13). The psalm reads it the same way, that they angered him also at the waters of strife, so that it went ill with Moses for their sakes, because they provoked his spirit, so that he spake unadvisedly with his lips (Psalms 106:32-33).

name: Israel and the fiery serpents
text: Speaking against God and against Moses; loathing the bread from heaven. Discouraged on the way around Edom, the people spoke against God and Moses: there is no bread, no water, and our soul loatheth this light bread. The Lord sent fiery serpents, and much people of Israel died. Edom had refused them passage and the way round was long, and the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way (Numbers 21:4). Then the people spake against God, and against Moses, wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? for there is no bread, neither is there any water, and our soul loatheth this light bread (Numbers 21:5). The bread they loathed was angels' food, rained from heaven every morning (Psalms 78:25), and the complaint is aimed at both the provision and the deliverer in a single breath. Paul files it as tempting Christ: neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted, and were destroyed of serpents (1 Corinthians 10:9). No other people in the record takes its food so seriously or complains of it so readily, and it is one of the marks by which this nation is known. The Lord sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people, and much people of Israel died (Numbers 21:6). The biting brought them back into the spirit at once: we have sinned, for we have spoken against the Lord, and against thee; pray unto the Lord,  that he take away the serpents from us. And Moses prayed for the people (Numbers 21:7). The serpents were not taken away. Moses was told to make a fiery serpent and set it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived (Numbers 21:9). Wisdom says they were troubled for a  small season, that they might be admonished, having a sign of salvation, and that he that turned toward it was not saved by the thing that he saw, but by thee that art the Saviour of all (Wisdom of Solomon 16:6-7). The brass serpent was for Israel, to heal the Israelites bitten for rebelling against God and Moses, and Christ took it as the figure of his own death when speaking to a ruler of the Jews: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life (John 3:14-15). The brass serpent itself became an idol centuries later and Hezekiah broke it in pieces, which is entered under his name in this volume.

name: Sihon and Og
text: Refusing Israel passage and coming out to battle against them. Israel asked only to pass through on the king's highway, turning neither to the right nor to the left. Sihon gathered his people and came out to fight, and Og after him. Both kingdoms were given into Israel's hand, and the land east of Jordan became the first inheritance. Moses sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites with words of peace (Deuteronomy 2:26): let me pass through thy land (Numbers 21:22); we will not turn into the fields or the vineyards. Sihon would not suffer Israel to pass, but gathered all his people and fought at Jahaz (Numbers 21:23). Og king of Bashan came out against them at Edrei (Deuteronomy 3:1), the last of the remnant of giants (Deuteronomy 3:11). Israel smote Sihon with the edge of the sword (Numbers 21:24) and possessed his land from Arnon to Jabbok. Of Og the Lord said, Fear him not, for I have delivered him into thy hand (Numbers 21:34); they smote him and his sons and all his people until none was left him alive (Numbers 21:35). The psalms remember it as mercy that endureth for ever (Psalms 136:17): who smote great kings, and gave their land for an heritage (Psalms 136:21).

name: Balaam
text: Divination for hire; counseling Moab to seduce Israel into idolatry. Hired by Balak to curse Israel, Balaam could only bless. So he taught Balak a surer way: draw Israel into fornication and the feasts of Baal-peor and let their own God judge them. It worked, and it killed him. Balak sent for him to curse Israel and the answer was given him at the first asking: thou shalt not go with them, thou shalt not curse the people, for they are blessed (Numbers 22:12). He asked again when the princes came back with more honour, and the going was permitted in anger, and the angel of the Lord stood in the way for an adversary against him with a drawn sword, and his ass saw what the prophet could not (Numbers 22:22-23). Peter names the spirit: Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness, but was rebuked for his iniquity, the dumb ass speaking with man's voice forbad the madness of the prophet (2 Peter 2:15-16). He could not curse them, and blessed them four times against his will, so he found another way to bring the curse. Moses names it after the war: these caused the children of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam, to commit trespass against the Lord in the matter of Peor (Numbers 31:16), and Christ  names it in the churches: the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed unto idols, and to commit fornication (Revelation 2:14). The offence was not the failed curse. It was teaching the enemy how to make Israel curse itself. He was killed in the war his own counsel caused. Israel slew the kings of Midian, Evi, and Rekem, and Zur, and Hur, and Reba, five kings of Midian, and Balaam also the son of Beor they slew with the sword (Numbers 31:8), so the man who would not go home when the angel stood in the road died among the kings he had advised. Joshua sets him among the slain and calls him the soothsayer (Joshua 13:22). Jude gives the sentence on everyone who follows him: they ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the gainsaying of Core (Jude 1:11), and his own words are left standing in the record as the verdict on his life, let me die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like his (Numbers 23:10), which was the one thing he did not get.

name: Israel at Baal-peor
text: Fornication with the daughters of Moab; sacrificing to their gods. In Shittim the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab, who called them to the sacrifices of their gods. Israel ate, bowed down, and joined himself unto Baal-peor. The plague took twenty-four thousand. It was Balaam's counsel executed. He could not curse a people God had blessed, so he taught Balak the one thing that works: put another god in front of Israel and send the women to bring them to it (Numbers 31:16; Revelation 2:14). Israel abode in Shittim, and the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab (Numbers 25:1), and they called the people unto the sacrifices of their gods, and the people did eat, and bowed down to their gods (Numbers 25:2). The whoredom and the worship were not two sins but one; the rite of Baal-peor was whoredom, and Israel joined himself unto Baal-peor (Numbers 25:3), joined as a man is joined to a wife. Hosea gives the verdict on the whole affair: they went to Baal-peor, and separated themselves unto that shame, and their abominations were according as they loved (Hosea 9:10), and the psalm adds what they ate: they joined themselves also unto Baal-peor, and ate the sacrifices of the dead (Psalms 106:28). It was the golden calf again, for the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play, and that play was the same play (1 Corinthians 10:7-8). The Lord's sentence began with the leadership: take all the heads of the people, and hang them up before the Lord against the sun, that the fierce anger of the Lord may be turned away from Israel (Numbers 25:4), and Moses said unto the judges of Israel, slay ye every one his men that were joined unto Baal-peor (Numbers 25:5), every judge by his rank  taking the men under him. A plague ran through the camp while the sentence was being carried out, and it was stayed by the javelin of Phinehas, which is entered separately as a blessing, and those that died in the plague were twenty and four thousand (Numbers 25:9). Paul, counting the day itself, says three and twenty thousand fell in one day (1 Corinthians 10:8). Moses set the outcome before the next generation as a thing their own eyes had seen: all the men that followed Baal-peor, the Lord thy God hath destroyed them from among you, but ye that did cleave unto the Lord your God are alive every one of you this day (Deuteronomy 4:3-4). Then the judgment turned outward against the nation that had supplied the women, which is entered under the Midianites.

name: The Midianites, in the matter of Peor
text: Beguiling Israel with their wiles into fornication and the worship of Baal-peor. Balaam could not curse Israel, so he taught Balak how to make Israel curse itself. The daughters of Midian and Moab drew the people to Peor, and twenty-four thousand died in the plague. The Lord then told Moses to avenge Israel of the Midianites before he was gathered to his people. On Balaam's counsel the women of Midian invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods (Numbers 25:2); the people ate, and bowed down, and joined themselves to Baal-peor (Numbers 25:3). Cozbi, the daughter of a prince of Midian, was brought into the camp itself (Numbers 31:12). They vexed Israel with their wiles, wherewith they beguiled you in the matter of Peor (Numbers 25:18). Vex the Midianites, and smite them. Israel warred against Midian as the Lord commanded Moses and slew all the males (Numbers 31:7), the five kings of Midian, and Balaam the son of Beor with the sword (Numbers 31:8). Moses was angry that the women who had caused the trespass were kept alive (Numbers 31:15), and the sentence was carried through on them also.

name: Phinehas
text: Zealous for his God at Peor; making an atonement for the children of Israel. While the congregation wept at the door of the tabernacle and the plague was running, a prince of Simeon walked a Midianite woman into the camp in front of them. Phinehas took a javelin and went in after them, and the plague was stayed at twenty-four thousand. The Lord gave him the covenant of an everlasting priesthood. The plague was already running and the congregation was weeping at the door of the tabernacle when a prince of Simeon brought a Midianite woman past them all into the camp (Numbers 25:6). It was done in the sight of Moses and the whole assembly, which makes it a public defiance rather than a private sin, and no one moved. Phinehas rose from among the congregation (Numbers 25:7), took a javelin, and followed them in. The act was summary and without trial, and the record neither disguises that nor apologises for it. What the text emphasises is the standing of the man and the state of the camp: a priest, in a time of open apostasy, executing a sentence the law already prescribed on parties taken in the act. The plague was stayed at twenty-four thousand (Numbers 25:9), and the account attributes the stopping to the act. God's own reading of the motive is given: he was zealous for my sake among them, so that I consumed not the children of Israel in my jealousy (Numbers 25:11). He received a covenant of peace and of an everlasting priesthood for himself and his seed (Numbers 25:13), and the high priesthood ran in his line down to the captivity. The psalm files it under the language of the law court, that it was counted unto him for righteousness unto all generations (Psalms 106:31), which is a phrase used elsewhere only of Abraham's faith (Psalms 106:28-31).

name: Zimri and Cozbi
text: Bringing a Midianite woman into the camp in the sight of the congregation. While the congregation wept at the tabernacle door over the plague, Zimri, a prince of Simeon, walked a Midianite princess past them into his tent. Phinehas followed with a javelin and thrust them both through. The act was public and it was done in the middle of a national mourning. The people had already joined themselves unto Baal-peor, called to the sacrifices of their gods and eating and bowing down, and the anger of the Lord was kindled (Numbers 25:2-3), so the worship and the whoredom were one thing and not two. Then, while the whole congregation was weeping before the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, one of the children of Israel brought a Midianitish woman unto his brethren in the sight of Moses and in the sight of all the congregation (Numbers 25:6). It was a man who did not care about his own people while everyone around him mourned. Both are named afterwards, which the record does deliberately: Zimri the son of Salu, a prince of a chief house among the Simeonites, and Cozbi the daughter of Zur, head over a people of a chief house in Midian (Numbers 25:14-15). Both died on the javelin, and the plague was stayed. God gave Phinehas a covenant of everlasting priesthood because he was zealous for his God and made an atonement. Sirach ranks him third in glory; the Maccabees claim him as father.

name: The daughters of Zelophehad
text: Asking rightly for their father's inheritance, and marrying within their tribe as commanded. Five sisters with no brother came to the door of the tabernacle and asked why their father's name should be done away from among his family because he had no son. The Lord said, The daughters of Zelophehad speak right, and made a statute of judgment for all Israel. They then married as they were told, and kept the inheritance in Manasseh. Five women with no brother came to the door of the tabernacle and made a legal argument, and the record names them, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, and names their tribe, Manasseh (Numbers 27:1). They did not ask for pity and they did not accuse anyone. They set out the facts: our father died in the wilderness, and he was not in the company of them that gathered themselves together against the Lord in the company of Korah, but died in his own sin, and had no sons (Numbers 27:3). Then the question, and it was the question of the lineage: why should the name of our father be done away from among his family, because he hath no son? give unto us therefore a possession among the brethren of our father (Numbers 27:4). They brought a gap in the law to the only authority who could fill it, in the proper form and at the proper place, and Moses did not answer out of his own judgment: Moses brought their cause before the Lord (Numbers 27:5). When the answer created a second question, that an inheritance might pass out of the tribe by marriage, the chief fathers of Gilead brought that too (Numbers 36:1-4), and the daughters accepted the further ruling and married within their father's tribe as commanded (Numbers 36:10-12). The Lord did not merely grant the request; he endorsed the reasoning: the daughters of Zelophehad speak right, thou shalt surely give them a possession of an inheritance among their father's brethren (Numbers 27:7). Their case became the order of inheritance for the whole nation: if a man die, and have no son, then ye shall cause his inheritance to pass unto his daughter, and if he have no daughter, to his brethren, and if no brethren, to his father's brethren, and if his father have no brethren, to his kinsman that is next to him of his family, and it shall be unto the children of Israel a statute of judgment (Numbers 27:8-11). The second ruling set the rule on marriage where an

name: Rahab
text: Receiving the spies with peace, and believing that the Lord had given Israel the land. A harlot of Jericho hid two Israelite spies under the flax on her roof, confessed that the Lord their God is God in heaven above and in earth beneath, and asked for her father's house. She bound the scarlet line in the window. When the wall fell, hers was the one house left, and she is in the line of Christ. She was a Canaanite, a harlot, and a resident of a city under the ban, and her faith came by report before it came by sight: we have heard how the Lord dried up the water of the Red sea for you, and what ye did unto the two kings of the Amorites, Sihon and Og (Joshua 2:10). She said what the report had done to the city, and to her: as soon as we had heard these things, our hearts did melt, neither did there remain any more courage in any man (Joshua 2:11). Faith and fear went together in her. What she feared was not the king of Jericho, who could have had her killed for hiding the men, but the judgment of the God she had heard of, and that fear is what gave her the faith to put her life on the line. Her confession is complete and it is in her own mouth: the Lord your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath (Joshua 2:11). She hid the men on the roof under the flax, answered the king's men with truth in part and misdirection in the rest, and sent the pursuers toward Jordan after men who had gone nowhere (Joshua 2:4-7). Then she bargained, as one who had something to sell: swear unto me by the Lord, since I have shewed you kindness, that ye will also shew kindness unto my father's house (Joshua 2:12-13). James selects her as the standing example that faith which does not act is dead, and pairs her with Abraham (James 2:25). The spies answered, our life for yours, if ye utter not this our business (Joshua 2:14), so the covenant was conditional: if she uttered it, they would be quit of the oath (Joshua 2:20). The token was the line of scarlet thread bound in the window she had let them down by, and the terms were that everyone in the house behind it would live and anyone who went out of the doors into the street would answer for himself (Joshua 2:18-19). She said, according unto your words, so be it, and bound the scarlet line in the window (Joshua 2:21). When the wall fell down flat, her house stood, and Joshua sent the two spies to bring her out with her father, her mother, her brethren, and all that she had (Joshua 6:22-23). Everything else in the city was devoted. Joshua saved Rahab the harlot alive, and her father's household, and she dwelleth in Israel even unto this day, because she hid the messengers (Joshua 6:25). Hebrews lists her among those who perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace (Hebrews 11:31), and Matthew places her in the direct line of David and of Christ, Salmon begat Booz of Rachab (Matthew 1:5), so that the woman spared from the ban became an ancestor of the one who ends it.

name: Achan
text: Taking devoted spoil from Jericho. Jericho's spoil was placed under the ban, devoted wholly to God. Achan took a garment, silver, and a wedge of gold and hid them in his tent. Israel's next battle failed because of it. The first sentence of the chapter names the party, and it is not one man: the children of Israel committed a trespass in the accursed thing, for Achan the son of Carmi took of the accursed thing, and the anger of the Lord was kindled against the children of Israel (Joshua 7:1). The record charges the nation for what one man did in secret in his own tent, which is the point of the case and the reason it is entered under Israel as well as under Achan. His own confession gives the sequence: I saw, I coveted, I took, and hid them in the earth in the midst of my tent (Joshua 7:21). Every step of it was private, and the sin the nation carried was a sin nobody in the nation knew about. Three thousand men went up against Ai and fled, and the men of Ai smote about thirty and six of them and chased them from before the gate, and the hearts of the people melted and became as water (Joshua 7:4-5). That melting is itself the sentence written in the law for disobedience, that the Lord shall send faintness into their hearts, and the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them, and they shall flee as fleeing from a sword when none pursueth (Leviticus 26:36). Israel could not stand before its enemies until the accursed thing was destroyed from among them, and Joshua was told the nation could not be with him until then (Joshua 7:12-13). The man was taken by lot, tribe by family by household, and he and all that he had were brought up to the valley of Achor and stoned and burned (Joshua 7:24-25). The Lord turned from the fierceness of his anger only after that, and the place keeps the name to this day.

name: The Gibeonites, and Israel's oath
text: Obtaining a covenant by fraud; Israel making it without asking counsel of the Lord. The Gibeonites came to Joshua in old clothes with moldy bread claiming to be from a far country, and Israel made peace with them. Three days later the fraud was found out. The oath stood anyway. Two offenses, and the record weighs Israel's as the heavier. The Gibeonites were Hivites, one of the nations named for destruction in the same chapter (Joshua 9:1, 7), and their only hope was to pretend they were not, so they did work wilily, with old sacks upon their asses, wine bottles old and rent, old shoes and old garments, and bread dry and mouldy (Joshua 9:4-5), and said, we be come from a far country, now therefore make ye a league with us (Joshua 9:6). They leaned on the fame of the Most High to sell it: from a very far country thy servants are come because of the name of the Lord thy God, for we have heard the fame of him, and all that he did in Egypt (Joshua 9:9). The props sold the story. Israel's fault is set down in one clause and it is the whole of it: and the men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the Lord (Joshua 9:14). They were suspicious, they asked the right questions, and then they reasoned it out among themselves instead of inquiring, which is exactly what the proverb forbids: trust in the Lord with all thine heart, and lean not unto thine own understanding, in all thy ways acknowledge him (Proverbs 3:5-6). The league the law forbade with the inhabitants of the land (Exodus 23:32; Deuteronomy 20:16-17) was made through not asking, and it became a snare and a trap to the nation for centuries after. Because the princes had sworn by the Lord, the Gibeonites could not be killed, but were made hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and the altar. Centuries later, when Saul broke that oath, God sent famine on Israel for it.

name: The five kings at Makkedah
text: Confederating against Gibeon for making peace with Israel. Five Amorite kings joined to punish Gibeon for coming to terms with Joshua. Israel came up all night from Gilgal, the Lord cast great stones from heaven on them, and the sun stood still. The five fled into a cave at Makkedah. Joshua had great stones rolled on the mouth of it and posted men, finished the battle, and then brought them out, had the captains put their feet on their necks, and hanged them on five trees until evening. The attack was on Gibeon rather than on Israel (Joshua 10:1), and Gibeon's only offense was making peace. The record gives their motive as fear, because Gibeon was a great city and the men of it mighty (Joshua 10:2), and states the aggression plainly: they came up and encamped against Gibeon, and made war against it. Israel was bound by an oath to defend the city, an oath obtained by deceit and entered separately in this volume, so the campaign is Israel keeping a covenant it had been tricked into. The Lord discomfited them, and more died from the hailstones than Israel killed with the sword (Joshua 10:11). They were taken alive from the cave, and the treading on their necks was done in front of the army with the words spoken over it, fear not, nor be dismayed, be strong and of good courage, for thus shall the Lord do to all your enemies (Joshua 10:25). They were hanged on five trees and taken down at sundown (Joshua 10:26), which is Deuteronomy 21 kept exactly in the middle of a war, and the stones that had shut them in the cave were rolled back over their bodies (Deuteronomy 21:22-23).

name: Othniel and Achsah
text: Taking Kirjath-sepher at Caleb's word; and asking for the springs as well as the land. Caleb offered his daughter to whoever would smite Kirjath-sepher and take it. His younger brother's son Othniel took it and was given her. As she came to him she moved him to ask her father for a field, and lighted off her ass, and Caleb said, What wouldest thou? She asked for a blessing: thou hast given me a south land, give me also springs of water. He gave her the upper springs and the nether springs. Othniel became the first judge of Israel. Two obediences, one of arms and one of speech. Othniel took a fortified city on the strength of a word rather than a strategy (Joshua 15:17). Achsah's is the more instructive: she had been given a portion in the dry south (Joshua 15:19), which was a lawful gift and an insufficient one, and rather than resent it she got down off the ass and asked, framing the request as a blessing rather than a complaint, thou hast given me a south land, give me also springs of water. She asked the right person, at the right moment, for the thing the land actually needed. He gave her the upper springs and the nether springs (Joshua 15:19), which is more than she asked for, and the detail is repeated in Joshua and in Judges so that the record carries it twice (Joshua 15:16-19). Othniel afterwards had the Spirit of the Lord come upon him (Judges 3:9), judged Israel, went out to war, and the land had rest forty years (Judges 3:11). The first deliverer in the book of Judges came out of a household in (Judges 1:1) which a daughter asked well and a father gave more than was requested (Joshua 15:13).

name: Adoni-bezek
text: Mutilating seventy kings. Judah defeated the Canaanite king Adoni-bezek and cut off his thumbs and great toes. He said it himself: seventy kings with thumbs and toes cut off had gathered their meat under my table; as I have done, so God hath requited me. Judah went up first at the Lord's word, with Simeon his brother, and the Lord delivered the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand, and they slew ten thousand men in Bezek (Judges 1:1-4). The king who fled from that field had made a practice of mutilation and counted it as his glory. He says the number himself: threescore and ten kings, having their thumbs and their great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table (Judges 1:7). Seventy kings maimed so that they could neither hold a sword nor stand in a rank, kept alive to eat scraps as a display of his power. The law of Israel limits punishment to measure, breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, as he hath caused a blemish in a man, so shall it be done to him again (Leviticus 24:19-20); he had exceeded all measure seventy times. They pursued after him, and caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his great toes (Judges 1:6): the same mutilation, once. The verdict is pronounced by the condemned man himself, and the record leaves it in his mouth: as I have done, so God hath requited me (Judges 1:7). A Canaanite king recognised the measure of the God of Israel from his own case and named it as justice. They brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died (Judges 1:7). Christ states the rule he fell under as a rule for everyone: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again (Matthew 7:2).

name: Israel in the days of the Judges
text: Serving Baalim and Ashtaroth; intermarrying with the Canaanites; every man doing right in his own eyes. After Joshua's generation died a generation arose that knew not the Lord. They forsook him for the gods of the peoples round about, took their daughters as wives, and were sold into the hands of Mesopotamia, Moab, Canaan, Midian, Ammon, and the Philistines in turn. Israel's fall began with a command they had heard, not a law they had never received. They were to overthrow the altars of the inhabitants and make no covenant with their gods. Instead, they left the altars standing, made leagues, and settled among the very snares against which they had been warned (Judges 2:1-3). When they became strong, they put the inhabitants to tribute rather than finish what had been commanded (Judges 1:27-35). Profit did not make that substitution obedience. The marriages followed the settlement, and the worship followed the marriages: they took their daughters, gave their own daughters, and served their gods (Judges 3:5-7). Deuteronomy 7:3-4 had already joined those things together, warning that the son would be turned from following the Lord. Exodus 23:32-33 called the gods of the land a snare. What Israel accepted into its households became what Israel bowed before. They could not preserve the covenant by keeping the land while adopting the worship of its inhabitants. Joshua's generation had seen the works of the Lord, but the generation after them knew neither him nor those works (Judges 2:7-10). The departure was also from instruction: they would not hearken to their judges and returned to their own stubborn way (Judges 2:17-19). Proverbs 3:5-6 commands trust in the Lord instead of leaning on one's own understanding. Every man doing right in his own eyes was not liberty from judgment; it was the abandonment of the rule by which Israel was to live. The Lord delivered them to spoilers and sold them into the hands of their enemies. Wherever they went, his hand was against them, as he had sworn (Judges 2:14-15). The nations did not suddenly become greater than the God who brought Israel out of Egypt. Israel had departed from him, and the covenant's curses followed them into the inheritance. The land itself did not shelter a disobedient people. Yet the Lord heard their groaning and raised up judges to deliver them. His mercy was shown repeatedly, but the rest was repeatedly misused: when the judge died, they corrupted themselves more than their fathers (Judges 2:18-19). Nehemiah 9:26-28 rehearses the same history—disobedience, enemies, a cry from trouble, saviours, rest, and another return to evil. Mercy gave opportunity to return; it was not permission to resume the sin. In the days before Jephthah, the Lord told them to cry to the gods they had chosen. Israel then confessed, put away the strange gods, and served him (Judges 10:10-16). Repentance had to reach what they kept and what they did. Hosea 5:15 joins affliction to acknowledging the offense and seeking his face. The nations left among Israel proved whether they would hearken to the commandments: the answer was to be given in obedience, not in tears alone (Judges 2:20-23; 3:1-4).

name: Eglon king of Moab
text: Possessing the city of palm trees and taking tribute of Israel eighteen years. The Lord strengthened Eglon against Israel because Israel did evil, and for eighteen years Israel served him. When they cried, the Lord raised up Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite with a message from God, and the message was a dagger. The first cause named is Israel's evil: the Lord strengthened Eglon king of Moab against them (Judges 3:12). Eglon gathered Ammon and Amalek, smote Israel, possessed the city of palm trees, and received their service for eighteen years (Judges 3:13-14). The king's dominion was real, but it was not power outside the Most High's hand. Israel's disobedience had placed them beneath the oppressor. The reversal is plain beside Rahab's testimony. When Israel approached the land, she said the inhabitants' hearts had melted at the report of what the Lord had done to Egypt and to Sihon and Og (Joshua 2:9-11). Now the Lord strengthened an enemy against Israel. The issue was not whether he still had power, but whether his people walked with him. The God who made the nations afraid could also give them strength to chastise his own people. When Israel cried, the Lord raised up Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite. Othniel had come from Judah; the next deliverer came from Benjamin (Judges 3:9, 15). Deliverance was the Lord's appointment, not the possession of one household. Ehud carried the tribute with a two-edged dagger hidden on his right thigh, then returned to Eglon with a secret errand (Judges 3:16-19). Eglon dismissed his attendants. Alone with the king, Ehud declared that he had a message from God and struck him with the dagger. He locked the parlour doors and escaped while the servants delayed, supposing their master required privacy (Judges 3:20-26). The chamber in which the king expected security became the place of his death. Receiving Israel's tribute could not secure him when the Lord raised a deliverer. Ehud did not leave the matter at the king's death. He sounded a trumpet, gathered Israel, and led them to seize the fords of Jordan. About ten thousand Moabites fell, and none escaped; Moab was subdued and the land rested eighty years (Judges 3:27-30). The same Lord who strengthened Eglon removed his dominion. Israel's cry was answered by the overthrow of the power under which they had served.

name: Jabin and Sisera
text: Mightily oppressing Israel twenty years with nine hundred chariots of iron. Jabin reigned in Hazor and Sisera commanded his host, and for twenty years they mightily oppressed the children of Israel. Deborah sent for Barak, the Lord discomfited the chariots at Kishon, and Sisera died in a tent with a nail through his temples. After Ehud died, Israel again did evil, and the Lord sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan. Sisera, his captain, commanded nine hundred chariots of iron and oppressed Israel mightily for twenty years (Judges 4:1-3). The iron chariots explain the terror of the servitude; they do not explain away the Lord's government of it. Israel had returned to sin after rest, and the enemy was again given the upper hand. The song describes what oppression did to ordinary life. Highways lay unoccupied, travellers used byways, and village life ceased until Deborah arose (Judges 5:6-7). It then names the departure beneath the disorder: Israel chose new gods, and war was in the gates (Judges 5:8). Their worship and their public condition were not separate matters. The people who would not be ruled by the Lord found themselves ruled by the force of Canaan. The Lord appointed the place of the confrontation. Deborah told Barak to draw ten thousand men toward Mount Tabor; the Lord would draw Sisera, his chariots, and his multitude to the river Kishon and deliver him into Barak's hand (Judges 4:6-7). The enemy's gathering was therefore not an interruption of the promise. It brought the host to the place where the promise would be fulfilled. At Deborah's word Barak descended, and the Lord discomfited Sisera's army. The captain abandoned his chariot and fled on foot, while Barak pursued the host until none remained (Judges 4:14-16). Judges 5:20-21 names the stars fighting and Kishon sweeping the enemy away. Deuteronomy 20:1 had forbidden Israel to fear horses, chariots, and a greater people when the Lord was with them. What appeared to establish Sisera's superiority could not preserve him against that word. Sisera reached Jael's tent, but did not reach safety. She killed him there, fulfilling Deborah's declaration that the honour of taking him would go to a woman (Judges 4:9, 17-22). Jabin's destruction followed as Israel's hand grew stronger against him (Judges 4:23-24). The song ends with Sisera's household expecting spoil while the captain never returns, and with forty years of rest for Israel (Judges 5:28-31). The oppressor's expectation and the Lord's judgment were opposite things.

name: Deborah
text: Judging Israel under the palm tree; going up with Barak when he would not go alone. Deborah, a prophetess to whom Israel came for judgment, delivered the Lord's command to Barak and went with him. The Lord defeated the Canaanite host, Jael took Sisera, and Deborah and Barak sang of the deliverance. The land rested forty years. Deborah was a prophetess, and Israel came to her for judgment under the palm tree between Ramah and Bethel (Judges 4:4-5). In a time when the people had chosen new gods and the highways had become unsafe, she arose as a mother in Israel (Judges 5:6-8). Her service was not merely to comfort an afflicted people. She brought the Lord's command to bear upon their condition. She sent for Barak and told him what the Lord had commanded: gather ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun, draw toward Tabor, and meet the host that the Lord would deliver into his hand (Judges 4:6-7). Deborah gave the prophetic direction; Barak gathered and commanded the army. When he made his going dependent upon hers, she accompanied him but did not soften the word concerning the honour he would lose (Judges 4:8-10). Encouragement did not require withholding correction. At the moment of battle she called him to rise because the Lord had gone before him (Judges 4:14). Her confidence rested on the command and promise already given. She did not leave Barak measuring ten thousand men against nine hundred chariots as though those numbers settled the matter. Faithful instruction turned his attention to who had appointed the battle. The Lord fulfilled the word: Barak defeated the host, Jael took Sisera, and Jabin was subdued (Judges 4:15-24). Deborah and Barak then sang praise to the Lord. The song begins with the people willingly offering themselves, and her heart is toward the governors who did the same (Judges 5:1-2, 9). Willing service had also marked those who brought offerings for the tabernacle (Exodus 35:21-22). In each service, the heart had to move with the work. The song did not commend everyone without distinction. It remembered Zebulun and Naphtali risking their lives, named the tribes that remained behind, and pronounced the curse upon Meroz for refusing help (Judges 5:15-18, 23). Thanksgiving preserved the judgment as well as the victory. The willing were to be remembered, and the absent were not to borrow their honour. The land rested forty years (Judges 5:31). Deborah's place in the deliverance is established by the work itself: she judged, instructed, accompanied, strengthened, and gave the glory to the Lord. A mother in Israel helped call the nation out of fear and back into service.

name: Barak
text: Going down into the valley on the word of a prophetess against nine hundred chariots of iron. Called by Deborah and told the Lord had commanded him to draw toward Tabor with ten thousand men, he answered that he would go if she went with him and not otherwise. She went, and told him the honour of the day would go to a woman. At her word he went down from Tabor and the Lord discomfited Sisera and all his chariots, and there was not a man left. He is named among the faithful in Hebrews. Barak received a command before he saw a victory. The Lord directed him to gather ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun at Tabor and promised to deliver Sisera's host into his hand (Judges 4:6-7). His answer added a condition: he would go if Deborah went, and would not go if she did not. She agreed to accompany him, but declared that Sisera would be sold into a woman's hand (Judges 4:8-9). The promise of victory stood; the honour attached to his part in it was diminished. He nevertheless gathered the men and went up. When Deborah told him that the day had come and the Lord had gone before him, Barak descended from the mountain with the ten thousand after him (Judges 4:10, 14). His hesitation did not remain his last act. The command required movement toward the enemy, and he moved. Deuteronomy 20:1 directs Israel not to fear chariots or a greater host when the Lord is with them; Barak had to act upon that confidence. Zebulun and Naphtali are remembered for jeopardizing their lives in the high places of the field (Judges 5:18). Their willingness stands against the long deliberations of Reuben and the remaining behind of Gilead, Dan, and Asher (Judges 5:15-17). Discussion of a duty is not its performance. Barak and the men with him entered the battle while others stayed where they were. The Lord discomfited Sisera and all his host. Barak pursued the chariots and army to Harosheth, and none of that host remained (Judges 4:15-16). Judges 5:20-21 describes the stars fighting and the river Kishon sweeping the enemy away. The fighting was real, but the power that made the pursuit victorious belonged to the Lord. When Barak reached Jael's tent, she showed him Sisera dead (Judges 4:22). Both words had been fulfilled: the host was delivered, and the captain's death brought honour to a woman. Barak could not claim the part assigned to another, but neither was the deliverance withheld from Israel because of his earlier hesitation. Hebrews 11:32-34 names Barak among the faithful and speaks of weakness made strong and armies put to flight. His history holds correction and faith together. He was corrected in the honour of the journey, yet obeyed the command to go; the Lord gave the victory, and Barak joined Deborah in praising him (Judges 5:1-2).

name: Jael
text: Blessed above women in the tent: the nail, the hammer, and Sisera. Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Heber the Kenite, whose house was at peace with Jabin. Jael covered him with a mantle, gave him milk, and when he slept drove a tent nail through his temples into the ground. Deborah's song puts the blessing on her twice over. Sisera fled from the defeated host to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite. He chose that refuge because there was peace between Jabin and Heber's house (Judges 4:17). The agreement gave him confidence in the household, but it did not overturn the word already spoken: the Lord would sell Sisera into a woman's hand (Judges 4:9). Jael invited him in and covered him. When he asked for water, she gave him milk; he then asked her to stand at the door and deny that a man was within (Judges 4:18-20). The captain who had commanded nine hundred iron chariots now depended upon a woman to conceal him. His military strength had left him, and his expectation of safety rested on her cooperation. She took a tent nail and a hammer and killed him while he slept (Judges 4:21). The decisive act came inside a tent, not at the head of an army. Jael did not need Sisera's rank or equipment to fulfil the part that brought his oppression to an end. When Barak arrived in pursuit, she brought him in to see the fallen captain (Judges 4:22). Deborah and Barak's song pronounces Jael blessed above women in the tent and recounts the milk, the nail, the hammer, and Sisera's fall (Judges 5:24-27). The blessing is attached to her deed in Israel's deliverance. The honour Deborah had foretold was not left unnamed; the song placed it upon Jael. Immediately before that blessing stands the curse upon Meroz for not coming to the help of the Lord against the mighty (Judges 5:23). One withheld help; the other acted. The placement weighs participation and refusal side by side. Being near the conflict was not the same as serving in the deliverance, and a convenient peace was not what decided the commendation. The song then turns to Sisera's mother, who waits for his return and supposes the delay is caused by the dividing of spoil (Judges 5:28-30). While his house imagines triumph, Jael has already ended his flight. The closing prayer asks that the Lord's enemies perish and that those who love him be as the sun going forth in strength (Judges 5:31). Jael's act belongs to that reversal: the terror of Israel is laid low, and the deliverance is celebrated.

name: Gideon
text: Throwing down the altar of Baal in his father's house; going against Midian with three hundred, as the Lord said. Threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites, the least in his father's house was called a mighty man of valour. He cut down Baal's altar by night, sent home thirty-one thousand seven hundred men because the Lord said the army was too big, and broke the Midianites with pitchers, lamps and trumpets. Before the Lord sent a deliverer, he sent a prophet. Midian had destroyed Israel's increase until the people hid in dens and caves, but the prophet named the cause: the Lord had brought them out of Egypt, and they had not obeyed his voice (Judges 6:1-10). Gideon's question—where were the miracles their fathers had told them of?—stood within that answer (Judges 6:13). The Lord had not lost his power. Israel had departed from him. The angel called Gideon a mighty man of valour while he threshed wheat in a winepress to hide it. Gideon answered with his family's poverty and his own low place, but the Lord answered with his presence (Judges 6:11-16). First Corinthians 1:26-29 shows the same order: God chooses what the world counts weak so that flesh will not glory before him. The commission was not founded upon Gideon's standing among men. His first commanded work was at home. He threw down his father's altar of Baal, cut down the grove, and built an altar to the Lord. Fear made him work by night, but he still did what was commanded (Judges 6:25-27). When the men of the city demanded his death, Joash answered that Baal should plead for himself if he were a god (Judges 6:28-32). An idol whose worshippers must defend it cannot be the deliverer of those worshippers. Before Gideon confronted Midian, he confronted the false worship in his own household. The Lord then reduced the army from thirty-two thousand to ten thousand, and from ten thousand to three hundred (Judges 7:2-7). Gideon had to release men he might naturally have wanted to keep. The reason was given: Israel must not boast that its own hand had saved it. Deuteronomy 8:14-18 had warned against that very pride. Obedience required trusting the Lord's choice even when it made the army look weaker. The Lord strengthened Gideon before the attack by sending him with Phurah to hear the enemy's dream and its interpretation. Gideon heard that Midian had been delivered into his hand, worshipped, and returned ready to act (Judges 7:9-15). The one who had asked for assurance was prepared for the work, not excused from it. Three companies sounded trumpets, broke their pitchers, held their lamps, and stood every man in his place. The Lord set the enemy's swords against one another (Judges 7:16-22). Numbers 10:9 connects the alarm of trumpets in war with being remembered before the Lord and saved from the oppressor. The trumpets were joined to that covenant remembrance; victory did not come from noise apart from the God who heard it. Other Israelites joined the pursuit, and Ephraim took Oreb and Zeeb. When Ephraim complained, Gideon answered by acknowledging what God had delivered into their hands, and their anger abated (Judges 7:23-25; 8:1-3). He had to lead brethren as well as defeat an enemy. Midian was subdued and the country rested forty years (Judges 8:28). The victory was the Lord's from the calling of the least man to the scattering of the great host.

name: The men of Succoth and Penuel
text: Refusing bread to the Lord's army in pursuit, and taunting them with it. Gideon and his three hundred came to Jordan faint, yet pursuing, and asked loaves of bread. Succoth and Penuel both answered with a sneer: are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thine army? He told them what he would do when he came back, and he came back. Gideon's three hundred crossed Jordan faint, yet pursuing. They had not abandoned the work, but their bodies needed bread. Gideon asked Succoth for loaves because he was pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian (Judges 8:4-5). This was an opportunity to sustain brethren in the deliverance of Israel, not a demand that the city invent a victory of its own. The princes answered by asking whether the kings were already in his hand. Penuel answered in the same manner (Judges 8:6-8). They made help depend on an outcome already secured: capture the kings first, and then speak of bread. Their answer sought safety from involvement while other men carried the danger. Exhaustion became an occasion for taunting rather than mercy. This refusal belongs beside Meroz, cursed for not coming to help against the mighty (Judges 5:23). A man can withhold the service within his reach without ever joining the enemy's army. The three hundred needed support in an unfinished pursuit; to wait until there was no risk was to withhold what was needed when it mattered. The law of loving one's neighbour required more than acknowledging him after his success (Leviticus 19:18).

name: Gideon's ephod
text: Making an ephod from the spoil; Israel whoring after it. Gideon refused the crown and said the Lord should rule, then asked for the golden earrings of the spoil and made an ephod of them and put it in Ophrah. All Israel went a whoring after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his house. After Midian's defeat, Israel offered Gideon rule for himself, his son, and his son's son. He refused and said the Lord should rule over them (Judges 8:22-23). Those were right words, but the test did not end when he refused the crown. He next asked for the golden earrings from the spoil, and the people willingly spread a garment and cast them into it (Judges 8:24-25). The earrings weighed seventeen hundred shekels of gold, besides other royal ornaments and apparel. Gideon made an ephod and placed it in Ophrah, and all Israel went there a whoring after it (Judges 8:26-27). Spoil taken in the Lord's deliverance was turned into a snare against the Lord's worship. The willingness of the donors did not make the use of their gifts righteous. Gideon had begun by throwing down his father's altar of Baal. Now an object he made drew Israel away (Judges 6:25-27; 8:27). A former act of obedience did not make every later act safe. First Timothy 6:10 warns that the love of money causes men to err from the faith and pierce themselves through with sorrows. The danger of the spoil was what the heart and hands did with it after the battle was won. The ephod became a snare to Gideon and his house (Judges 8:27). The man who had refused to replace the Lord as ruler had nevertheless furnished the people with an occasion of unfaithfulness. The judgment is already present in that word, snare: what appeared valuable and honourable caught the household that possessed it. Midian remained subdued and the land rested forty years in Gideon's days (Judges 8:28). Peace did not prove that the ephod was acceptable. Israel could enjoy the fruit of the earlier deliverance while another departure grew among them. A successful past is no measure by which to excuse a present offense. After Gideon's death, Israel returned to Baalim, made Baal-berith their god, forgot the Lord who had delivered them, and showed no kindness to Gideon's house (Judges 8:33-35). Forgetting the Lord and forgetting the service of his deliverer stood together. The history proceeds from a household snare into a national return to false worship. Right words about the Lord's rule must be followed by conduct that keeps the people under that rule.

name: Abimelech son of Gideon
text: Murder of seventy brothers on one stone; usurping a crown. Gideon's son by a Shechemite concubine hired vain and light persons with silver from the house of Baal-berith, killed his seventy brothers on one stone, and had himself made king at Shechem. Only Jotham escaped, and his parable from Mount Gerizim pronounced the sentence. Abimelech appealed to his mother's brethren in Shechem and asked whether they preferred seventy sons of Jerubbaal to rule them or one man who was their own bone and flesh (Judges 9:1-2). They promoted him because he was their brother. Kinship took the place of judgment, and money from the house of Baal-berith financed the choice: seventy pieces of silver paid the vain and light men who followed him (Judges 9:3-4). He went to his father's house at Ophrah and slew his brethren upon one stone; Jotham escaped by hiding. Shechem then made the killer king (Judges 9:5-6). Their part was not confined to approving him afterward. They supplied the means by which he established his rule. The blood would be laid upon the man who killed and upon the men who strengthened his hands (Judges 9:24). Jotham spoke from Mount Gerizim. In his parable, the olive, fig, and vine would not forsake their fruitfulness to reign over the trees, but the bramble offered its shadow and threatened fire (Judges 9:7-15). He applied it to the ingratitude shown his father's house: Gideon had risked his life to deliver them, and they had answered by destroying his sons. If their choice was not true and sincere, Abimelech and Shechem would consume one another (Judges 9:16-20). Three years passed before the alliance broke. God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem so that the blood of Gideon's sons would be requited upon both parties (Judges 9:22-24). The interval had not erased the murder. Numbers 32:23 warns that sin will find the offender out; a season of apparent success is not acquittal. Shechem dealt treacherously, trusted Gaal, and cursed Abimelech; Abimelech returned with ambush and slaughter. He destroyed the city and burned the stronghold where about a thousand men and women had taken refuge (Judges 9:26-49). The man they had called their brother brought the fire Jotham had pronounced. The god whose treasury financed his rise could not shelter those who fled into its house. At Thebez, Abimelech approached another tower to burn it, but a woman cast a piece of millstone upon his head and crushed his skull.
