He ordered his armour-bearer to kill him so that men would not say a woman slew him (Judges 9:50-54). Even at death he sought control of his reputation. The history still records the woman and the stone. God rendered Abimelech's wickedness upon him and Shechem's evil upon its own head; Jotham's curse came upon them (Judges 9:56-57). The killer and his backers did not cancel one another's guilt by becoming enemies. Their conflict became the means by which both were repaid.

name: Jephthah's vow
text: A rash vow, and its performance on his daughter. Before battle with Ammon, Jephthah vowed that what came from his doors to meet him would be the Lord's. His only daughter came out with timbrels and dances. She accepted the dedication, mourned her virginity, and remained unmarried as her father fulfilled his vow. The vow itself was the sin: sworn thoughtlessly with the lips, as Leviticus describes, binding himself to a thing God never asked and, on the plain reading, forbade. Ecclesiastes: suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin. The text records that she bewailed her virginity and knew no man; readers have long divided over whether the sacrifice was literal or a life devoted, and the text does not settle it. He lost his only child and his line ended with him. The daughters of Israel kept a yearly lament for her. Jephthah is nonetheless counted among the faithful in Hebrews 11, which is the record's own tension.

name: Manoah and his wife
text: Asking how shall we order the child, and doing all that was commanded them. The angel of the Lord appeared to a barren woman of Zorah and told her she would bear a son who was to be a Nazarite from the womb, and gave her a rule for herself as well. She told her husband. He entreated the Lord that the man of God might come again and teach them what they should do unto the child, and the angel came again to the woman in the field, and she ran for her husband. They offered a kid on a rock and the angel ascended in the flame. Israel had again done evil and had been delivered into the Philistines' hand for forty years when the angel appeared to Manoah's barren wife (Judges 13:1-3). The promise of a son was also the beginning of an answer to the nation's affliction. The child would begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines, and his dedication would start in the womb (Judges 13:5). The mother was commanded to drink no wine or strong drink and eat no unclean thing. No razor was to come upon the child's head (Judges 13:4-7). Numbers 6:1-5 gives the separation of the Nazarite: abstinence from the vine and uncut hair during the vow. Nazarite describes consecration, not residence in Nazareth. The instructions were particular, and the promise did not release the household from observing them. Manoah prayed for the messenger to return and teach them how to order the child. When the angel came again, he repeated what had already been commanded to the woman (Judges 13:8-14). Their task was not to invent a manner of upbringing because the child was extraordinary. They were to receive and keep the instruction given. The Lord's purpose for a child lays responsibility upon those raising him. When Manoah offered hospitality, the angel directed any burnt offering to the Lord, not to himself (Judges 13:15-16). Colossians 2:18 warns against worshipping angels, and the angel before John likewise commanded him to worship God (Revelation 22:8-9). Honour toward a heavenly messenger must not become the worship that belongs to the one who sent him. Manoah offered the kid and meat offering to the Lord upon a rock. The angel ascended in the flame, and the husband and wife fell upon their faces (Judges 13:19-20). They had received a heavenly visitation, but they had not seen the Most High himself. The messenger's appearance and departure made clear that the promise was no ordinary man's assurance. Manoah feared they would die. His wife answered from what the Lord had done: he had accepted their offering, shown them these things, and announced what was to come (Judges 13:21-23). She weighed the fear against the received promise. The Lord had instructed them concerning a child's life, not prepared them for their own immediate destruction. She bore Samson; he grew, the Lord blessed him, and the Spirit began to move him (Judges 13:24-25). Psalms 113:9 speaks of the barren woman made a joyful mother. Here the blessing reached beyond the household: the promised child would begin the deliverance of an afflicted people. The parents' part was to honour the giver by obeying what he had commanded.

name: Samson
text: Marrying a Philistine; going in to a harlot; betraying his Nazarite vow to Delilah. A Nazarite from the womb who repeatedly went down to the Philistines for women: a wife at Timnath against his parents' counsel, a harlot at Gaza, and Delilah in Sorek, to whom he told all his heart. He woke from her lap shaven, and the Lord had departed from him. Samson's parents questioned his desire for a Philistine wife, but he insisted upon the woman who pleased him. At the same time, the Lord sought an occasion against the Philistines who ruled Israel (Judges 14:1-4). His purpose worked through Samson's weakness without making that weakness a rule of obedience. Isaiah 55:8-9 places the Lord's thoughts above man's, and Proverbs 21:30 declares that no counsel stands against him. At Timnath, the Philistines threatened the woman and her father's house to obtain the answer to Samson's riddle. She pressed him until he told her, then gave the answer to her people (Judges 14:15-18). Samson's strength did not keep him from yielding to pressure. The quarrel spread through the loss of his wife, the burning of the Philistines' crops, and further bloodshed (Judges 14:19-20; 15:1-8). The Lord was bringing an occasion against the oppressor through the very entanglement Samson had pursued. At Gaza he went in to a harlot and escaped an ambush by carrying away the city gates. Afterward he loved Delilah, and the Philistine lords offered her silver to discover how to bind him (Judges 16:1-5). She asked for the means of his affliction, tried what he told her, and repeatedly called the enemy upon him. The warning was not hidden. He remained after the withs, the new ropes, and the weaving of his locks had each been used against him (Judges 16:6-14). Daily pressure overcame his discretion, and he told her all his heart: he had been a Nazarite from his mother's womb, and no razor had come upon his head (Judges 16:15-17). Micah 7:5 commands a guard upon the mouth even toward one who lies in the bosom. Samson treated attachment as security after Delilah had shown what she would do with his words. She called the lords, received their money, and caused his locks to be shaved while he slept (Judges 16:18-19). He awoke expecting to escape as before, not knowing that the Lord had departed from him. The Philistines put out his eyes, bound him in brass, and made him grind in prison (Judges 16:20-21). Past escapes had become presumption. The strength that broke cords and carried gates was the Lord's gift, not a possession Samson could command while disregarding his consecration. The Philistines credited Dagon with delivering him into their hands and brought him out for sport (Judges 16:23-25). Yet Dagon had not overcome the Lord. Samson's fall had followed the Lord's departure, and his last strength would come by calling upon the Lord again. At Lehi, the man who slew a thousand had needed God even for water to revive him (Judges 15:14-19). Dependence had always been the truth beneath his great strength. Between the pillars he prayed to be remembered and strengthened once more. He bowed with all his might, the house fell, and he slew more at his death than in his life (Judges 16:26-30). The Lord's occasion against the Philistines reached their lords in the place where they honoured Dagon. Samson died with them and was buried by his father's house (Judges 16:31). His history warns against playing with a known snare, and shows that the oppressor's triumph did not overturn the Most High's purpose.

name: Micah's idols and the tribe of Dan
text: A house of gods, a hired Levite, and a tribe that stole both. Micah of Ephraim stole silver from his mother, returned it, and she had it made into a graven and molten image. He set up a house of gods, consecrated his own son, then hired a wandering Levite as priest. The Danites, migrating north, took the priest and the idols for themselves. Micah stole eleven hundred shekels of silver from his mother and restored them after hearing her curse. She answered with a blessing in the Lord's name, then devoted silver to a graven and molten image (Judges 17:1-4). Restitution of the theft was followed by another offense. Calling the gift dedicated to the Lord did not make an image lawful (Exodus 20:4-5). Micah established a house of gods, made an ephod and teraphim, and appointed one of his sons as priest. When a travelling Levite arrived, he offered him ten shekels a year, clothing, and food to become his priest (Judges 17:5-10). The Levite accepted, and Micah concluded that the Lord would do him good because he now had a Levite (Judges 17:11-13). He trusted the man's tribe and title while disregarding what the man had agreed to serve. Religious office cannot sanctify disobedience. Dan's five spies lodged there, obtained the priest's favourable answer concerning their journey, and saw the images. When six hundred armed Danites returned, the spies took the objects. The priest objected until they offered him a whole tribe instead of one household. His heart was glad, and he went with them (Judges 18:14-20). The service purchased by Micah's silver was transferred for a larger place. A change in patron did not change the corruption. Micah pursued and cried that they had taken the gods he had made and his priest. He asked what he had left (Judges 18:22-24). The question exposed the emptiness of his confidence: his gods depended on his hands to make them and his strength to recover them. The Danites threatened his household, and he turned back because they were stronger (Judges 18:25-26). Neither his images nor his hired priest delivered him. Dan smote Laish, a quiet and secure people far from Zidon with no deliverer, rebuilt the city, and named it Dan. There they established the image and its priesthood while the house of God was in Shiloh (Judges 18:27-31). A successful conquest did not cleanse what they carried into it. One man's false worship became an institution maintained among a tribe. That course reaches forward to Jeroboam's calf at Dan and to Amos's word against those who swear by its god (1 Kings 12:28-30; Amos 8:14). Judges records the priesthood continuing until the captivity of the land (Judges 18:30). The refrain that every man did right in his own eyes explains the beginning: private invention, a purchased ministry, theft, and public establishment followed one another where the Lord's command should have governed all (Judges 17:6).

name: The men of Gibeah, and Benjamin
text: Sodomy, gang rape and murder of a stranger's concubine; a tribe that shielded the guilty. The men of Gibeah surrounded the house where a Levite lodged, demanding him; they were given his concubine and abused her all night until she died on the threshold. He cut her into twelve pieces and sent them through Israel. Benjamin refused to surrender the guilty, and Israel went to war. The Levite passed by Jebus because he would not lodge in a city of strangers and chose Gibeah, a city of Benjamin. Yet no man there first received him, and an old man from Mount Ephraim brought the travellers into his house (Judges 19:10-21). The guest expected safety among brethren; the city's conduct betrayed that expectation. Men surrounded the house and demanded the male guest, as the men of Sodom had demanded Lot's visitors (Judges 19:22; Genesis 19:4-9). The woman was brought out to them, and they raped and abused her through the night. She fell at the door with her hands upon the threshold and gave no answer when her husband spoke (Judges 19:25-28). This was violence against her, not consent. Deuteronomy 22:25-26 places the guilt of forced intercourse upon the attacker and compares the assault to a man rising against his neighbour to slay him. The Levite sent the evidence throughout Israel, and the congregation assembled as one man. They demanded that Benjamin surrender the perpetrators so that evil could be put away (Judges 19:29-30; 20:1-13). Benjamin refused and gathered to fight its brethren (Judges 20:14). The tribe made itself the defence of the guilty. Loyalty to one's own becomes transgression when it shields the crime instead of submitting the offenders to judgment.

name: Ruth and Boaz
text: Ruth: cleaving to Naomi and to Naomi's God. Boaz: the law of gleaning, and the law of the kinsman, done to the letter. A Moabite widow left her people for a mother in law with nothing, and said, thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God. A man of Bethlehem let her glean, ordered handfuls dropped on purpose, and then went to the gate and settled the redemption and marriage before ten elders. Their son was Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David. Ruth: Intreat me not to leave thee; whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God. Boaz to Ruth: It hath fully been shewed me, all that thou hast done unto thy mother in law since the death of thine husband. Boaz to his reapers: Let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her. At the gate: The day thou buyest the field of the hand of Naomi, thou must buy it also of Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of the dead, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance. And the near kinsman drew off his shoe. The Lord recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the Lord God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust. The Lord make the woman that is come into thine house like Rachel and like Leah, which two did build the house of Israel. So Boaz took Ruth, and she was his wife; and the Lord gave her conception, and she bare a son. Blessed be the Lord, which hath not left thee this day without a kinsman, that his name may be famous in Israel. They called his name Obed: he is the father of Jesse, the father of David.

name: Hannah
text: Praying in bitterness of soul, vowing a son to the Lord, and giving him when she had him. Barren, provoked yearly by her rival, mistaken for a drunkard by the high priest, she poured out her soul before the Lord and vowed that if he gave her a son she would give him back for all his days. He did, and she did: she brought Samuel to Shiloh as soon as he was weaned. The Lord gave her five more. Hannah's barrenness was made bitter by repeated provocation. Year by year, when the household went up to worship, her adversary vexed her until she wept and would not eat (1 Samuel 1:4-7). She brought that sorrow before the Lord and vowed that, if he gave her a son, she would give him to the Lord all his days, with no razor upon his head (1 Samuel 1:9-11). The words joined her petition to the separation described in Numbers 6:5. Eli saw her moving lips without hearing her voice and thought her drunk. She answered that she had poured out her soul before the Lord, and he sent her away in peace. She then ate, and her countenance was no more sad (1 Samuel 1:12-18). Her faith was shown before the birth, when she went from prayer able to receive food again. Being misunderstood by the priest did not turn her from the one to whom she had prayed. First John 5:14-15 joins confidence in prayer to asking according to the Lord's will; First John 3:22 joins receiving to keeping his commandments and doing what pleases him. Hannah's answer came in the Lord's time. Prayer did not put the timing of the gift under her control. She entrusted the petition to him and afterward named her son in remembrance of what she had asked (1 Samuel 1:19-20). When Samuel was weaned, she brought him to Shiloh with the offerings and presented him to Eli. The child she had wanted was the child she now gave for lifelong service (1 Samuel 1:24-28). Ecclesiastes 5:4-6 commands the payment of a vow instead of dismissing it as an error. Hannah did not treat answered prayer as the end of her obligation. She performed the promise when its fulfilment required parting with the son she loved. Samuel ministered before the Lord, and Hannah brought him a little coat each year. Her dedication did not become forgetfulness; she continued to supply the care she could give (1 Samuel 2:18-19). Eli blessed the household, and the Lord visited her with three sons and two daughters (1 Samuel 2:20-21). The one son was not withheld, and her house received five more. Her song declares that the Lord is a God of knowledge and that actions are weighed by him (1 Samuel 2:3). Her own conduct had joined prayer, promise, and performance. Christ's question—why call him Lord and not do what he says—reaches the same distinction between profession and obedience (Luke 6:46). The words spoken before God are to be followed by the life promised to him. The song passes from her household to the Lord's rule over strength, riches, life, and death. He brings low and lifts up; by strength no man prevails; he gives strength to his king and exalts his anointed (1 Samuel 2:4-10). Hannah's joy therefore ends in the Lord's salvation, not her own victory over the woman who provoked her. The gift was his, the service was his, and the glory remained his.

name: Eli and his sons
text: Corrupt priesthood; a father who would not restrain it. Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas treated the Lord's offering with contempt and lay with the women at the tabernacle door. Eli rebuked them weakly but did not remove them. The house fell together. Hophni and Phinehas held priestly office, yet knew not the Lord (1 Samuel 2:12). They served where Israel brought offerings, but their conduct contradicted the service. Before the fat was burned, their servant demanded raw flesh for the priest and threatened to take it by force if the worshipper resisted (1 Samuel 2:13-16). They put appetite ahead of the Lord's portion. The law reserved the fat to him; priestly provision did not permit them to seize whatever they wanted whenever they wanted it (Leviticus 3:16-17). Their sin made men abhor the Lord's offering. They also lay with the women who assembled at the tabernacle door, and Eli told them that they made the Lord's people transgress (1 Samuel 2:17, 22-24). The damage was not confined to private misconduct. Men entrusted with holy service were teaching contempt by example and attaching the people's experience of worship to their own corruption. Eli knew and spoke, but did not restrain them (1 Samuel 3:13). His rebuke stopped short of the action his office required. The man of God therefore charged him with honouring his sons above the Lord and making himself fat with the chief of the offerings (1 Samuel 2:27-29). It was not enough to disapprove in speech while the abuse continued under his authority. Abraham's household supplies the contrast: the Lord knew he would command his children to keep the way of the Lord and do justice and judgment (Genesis 18:19). Joshua likewise declared that he and his house would serve the Lord (Joshua 24:15). Family affection does not remove the duty of government. Eli's sons could not be permitted to make their father's office a shelter from correction. The Lord declared that those who honour him would be honoured and those who despise him lightly esteemed. Eli's house would lose its strength, its increase would die in the flower of age, and both sons would die in one day as a sign (1 Samuel 2:30-34). The family that seized offerings would be brought to seeking a piece of silver and a morsel of bread (1 Samuel 2:36). The privilege they abused became the provision they lost. The warning against a corrupt household is not a licence for a son to continue his father's evil. Ezekiel 18:10-17 distinguishes the violent son who commits abominations from the son who considers his father's sins and refuses them. The former bears his own guilt; the latter shall live. The way out of an evil example is to turn from it, not to claim the family's office while keeping the family's transgression. Through Samuel the Lord confirmed that the iniquity of Eli's house would not be purged with sacrifice or offering (1 Samuel 3:11-14). The very institution they had abused would not annul the sentence. Samuel told Eli the whole word, though he feared to deliver it (1 Samuel 3:15-18). A faithful servant had to speak what the compromised household would not correct. Hophni and Phinehas died when the ark was captured. At the mention of the ark, Eli fell backward, broke his neck, and died; Phinehas' wife died in childbirth after naming the child Ichabod (1 Samuel 4:11-22). The later removal of Abiathar from the priesthood fulfilled the word spoken against Eli's house in Shiloh (1 Kings 2:27). Neither office, ancestry, nor a verbal rebuke preserved the house that refused restraint.

name: The Philistines and the captured ark
text: Setting the ark of God in the house of Dagon, and keeping it seven months. The Philistines took the ark in battle and set it beside Dagon as a trophy. Dagon fell on his face before it twice, the second time without head or hands, and the men of Ashdod, Gath and Ekron were smitten with emerods until they sent it home on a new cart with golden offerings. After Israel's first defeat, the elders asked why the Lord had smitten them, but answered their trouble by fetching the ark. They expected it to save them, and the camp shouted when it arrived (1 Samuel 4:2-5). The ark contained the tables of the covenant (Deuteronomy 10:1-5). Bringing the commandments into camp was not the same as keeping them. Hophni and Phinehas came with it while the judgment upon their corruption still stood. The Philistines feared when they heard that the ark had come, remembering the plagues upon Egypt, but they fought and defeated Israel again. Thirty thousand footmen fell, the priests died, and the ark was taken (1 Samuel 4:6-11). Israel's confidence in possession had not replaced obedience. Samuel would later require the nation to put away its strange gods and serve the Lord only (1 Samuel 7:3-4). The victors made a corresponding error: they brought the ark into Dagon's house at Ashdod and set it beside their idol (1 Samuel 5:1-2). Capturing it did not make them masters of the God of Israel. The Lord had judged his people; he had not surrendered his power to the Philistines' god. Samson's last act had already brought destruction upon a gathering that glorified Dagon (Judges 16:23-30). Dagon fell upon his face before the ark. They set him up again, but the following morning his head and the palms of his hands lay cut off upon the threshold (1 Samuel 5:3-4). The worshippers could restore the statue to its place but could not preserve its head or hands. The supposed victor had to be lifted by the very men who trusted it. The Lord's hand was heavy upon Ashdod with destruction and emerods. Moving the ark to Gath brought affliction there, and Ekron cried out when it was sent onward (1 Samuel 5:6-12). A change of city did not change whose hand was against them. Seven months later their priests counselled a trespass offering and warned them not to harden their hearts as Pharaoh had done (1 Samuel 6:1-6). The captured object was to be returned with an acknowledgment of offense. They placed it upon a new cart drawn by two cows that had never borne a yoke, shut up their calves at home, and watched whether they went toward Beth-shemesh. If they did, the Philistines would know that the Lord had sent the affliction. The cows took the straight way, lowing as they went, and did not turn aside (1 Samuel 6:7-12). Their own test answered the claim that the destruction had happened by chance.

name: The men of Beth-shemesh
text: Looking into the ark of the Lord. When the Philistines returned the ark on a cart, the men of Beth-shemesh rejoiced, offered the kine, and looked into the ark. The Lord smote them with a great slaughter, and they asked, who is able to stand before this holy Lord God? The people of Beth-shemesh were reaping wheat when they saw the returning ark and rejoiced. The cart came into the field of Joshua the Beth-shemite and stood by a great stone; the Levites took down the ark and the coffer, and offerings were made to the Lord (1 Samuel 6:13-15). The return was a cause for thanksgiving. The Philistines had not kept what they took, and the Lord had shown his hand in bringing it back. But the men looked into the ark, and the Lord smote them for that act (1 Samuel 6:19). Joy did not grant unrestricted access to holy things. The law had distinguished the service appointed to the Levites from what they were forbidden to touch or see. Even the bearers were not to touch the holy things, and Numbers 4:20 forbade the prohibited looking upon them (Numbers 4:15, 20). Appointment to one duty was not permission for every approach. The boundary applied among Israel as surely as the Lord's power had applied among the Philistines. The people could not receive the ark with reverence and then treat its holiness as open to their curiosity. Obedience governs the eyes as well as the hands. What is near, available, or greatly desired to be seen is not therefore given to a man to examine.

name: Samuel
text: Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth; and an accounting no man could contradict: whose ox have I taken?. Dedicated to the Lord and brought to Shiloh as a child, Samuel received a word of judgment against Eli's house and delivered it without concealment. He judged Israel throughout his life, anointed Saul and David, and stood before the people to give an account of his conduct. They testified that he had neither oppressed them nor taken anything from them. Samuel's service began before he understood the voice that called him. He ministered before Eli, but the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him. When Eli perceived who was calling, he taught Samuel to answer as a servant ready to hear (1 Samuel 3:1-10). Growing up beside holy things was preparation for service; receiving the word required his own response. The first message placed him under a difficult obligation. The Lord pronounced judgment upon the house that had raised him because Eli knew his sons' iniquity and did not restrain them. Samuel feared to tell the vision, yet told Eli everything and hid nothing (1 Samuel 3:11-18). Affection for the hearer could not become permission to alter the judgment. Faithful teaching begins with being faithful to what was given to teach. When Israel demanded a king, Samuel submitted his own administration to examination. Before the Lord and the new king, he asked whose property he had taken, whom he had defrauded or oppressed, and whose bribe had blinded his eyes. The people testified that he had taken nothing (1 Samuel 12:1-5). Exodus 23:8 forbids the gift that blinds judgment. Samuel's authority was supported by an account the people themselves could verify. He then rebuked their demand without abandoning them. He rehearsed the Lord's deliverances, warned both people and king to obey, and declared that he would sin against the Lord if he ceased praying for them (1 Samuel 12:6-25). Correction and intercession belonged together. Their refusal of his counsel did not release him from teaching the good and right way. The Lord was with Samuel and let none of his words fall to the ground. Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew him to be an established prophet (1 Samuel 3:19-21). His standing came through the fulfilment of the Lord's word, not through a title taken to himself. At Mizpeh the Lord heard his prayer and thundered against the Philistines; he continued his circuit of judgment through Bethel, Gilgal, Mizpeh, and Ramah (1 Samuel 7:9-17). He anointed Saul, mourned Saul's rejection, and obeyed the command to anoint David (1 Samuel 10:1; 15:35; 16:1-13). The work continued even when its history grieved him. All Israel lamented him at his death (1 Samuel 25:1). Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 46:13-17 remembers his faithfulness in judging by the law and the prayer answered from heaven. His ministry joined an upright hand, an unaltered word, and continuing care for the nation.

name: Joel and Abiah, the sons of Samuel
text: Turning aside after lucre, taking bribes, and perverting judgment in the seat of the judge. Samuel made his sons judges over Israel, and they walked not in his ways. They took bribes and perverted judgment, and the elders of Israel used it as the reason to ask for a king. The sentence recorded falls on the nation that asked, not on the two men who gave them the excuse. Samuel appointed Joel and Abiah as judges in Beersheba, but they did not walk in his ways. They turned aside after gain, received bribes, and perverted judgment (1 Samuel 8:1-3). Their father's upright administration did not pass to them merely because his office did. The contrast was public: the people could testify that Samuel had taken nothing, while the sons made the seat of judgment serve their own increase (1 Samuel 12:3-5). The law names the corruption precisely. Judges were to judge with just judgment, without respecting persons or taking a gift that blinded the wise and perverted righteous words (Deuteronomy 16:18-20). Exodus 23:8 gives the same warning. A bribe does more than enrich an official. It bends what he is entrusted to see and say, placing those who seek justice at the mercy of those who can buy an answer. The elders brought the sons' conduct before Samuel when they asked for a king (1 Samuel 8:4-5). Corruption in an office that should protect the people gave force to their complaint. A father's reputation could not excuse his sons, and the people's knowledge of their wrongdoing could not be dismissed as a rejection of order. The judges themselves had violated the order established by the Lord. The recorded consequence reaches the nation: the elders used the sons' departure as their reason to demand a king like the nations. The Lord identified that demand as a rejection of his reign and instructed Samuel to warn them what the king would take (1 Samuel 8:6-18). Their grievance against corrupt judges was real; the remedy they insisted upon brought obligations and burdens of its own. No personal penalty upon Joel or Abiah is recorded in this chapter. Their offense remains named without an account of their later punishment. Ecclesiastes 5:8 warns the observer of perverted judgment that one higher than the official regards the matter. Silence about the sons' end does not turn their bribery into righteousness. Their place in the history is the damage caused when inherited authority is exercised without the character required to govern.

name: Israel asking for a king
text: Rejecting the Lord's rule to be like the nations. The elders came to Samuel and demanded a king to judge them like all the nations. The Lord told Samuel: they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me. Warned what a king would take from them, they said, nay, but we will have a king over us. Israel's elders named Samuel's age and his sons' corruption, then demanded a king to judge them like the nations (1 Samuel 8:4-5). The law had already provided for a king whom the Lord would choose, a brother who would remain under the commandments (Deuteronomy 17:14-20). The offense was not the existence of every king. It was the rejection of the Lord's reign in favour of the security Israel imagined the nations possessed. Samuel prayed, and the Lord told him that the people had rejected him, not merely his prophet. Their request continued the course of forsaking him and serving other gods since Egypt (1 Samuel 8:6-9). Joshua's congregation had promised to serve the Lord and obey his voice (Joshua 24:21-24). Now the people insisted upon a visible ruler to go before them and fight their battles, though the Lord had repeatedly delivered them through the judges (1 Samuel 8:19-20; 12:6-12).

name: King Saul
text: Unlawful sacrifice; sparing what was devoted; consulting a medium. A king undone by a pattern of partial obedience. He offered a sacrifice that was not his to offer, spared Agag and the best of the spoil against a direct command, and at the end sought a medium the law condemned. Saul's fall began with a command displaced by pressure. At Gilgal he saw the people scattering and the Philistines gathering. Samuel had instructed him to wait, but Saul offered the burnt offering and defended himself by naming the circumstances that frightened him (1 Samuel 10:8; 13:8-12). He had not been given authority to change the command because waiting became difficult. The trial exposed whose word governed him when the people grew afraid. The kingdom was torn from him and given to another. 'To obey is better than sacrifice.' He died by his own hand on Gilboa the next day, his sons with him.

name: David
text: A man after the Lord's own heart; keeping his commandments and following him with all his heart, save only in the matter of Uriah. Shepherd, giant-killer, hunted man who twice had Saul in his hand and would not touch the Lord's anointed, king who danced before the ark and would not build a house until told he could. The Lord made a covenant with his house that has a Son sitting on it for ever. His one great fall is its own case; this is the rest. David was taken from keeping sheep to feed Israel. Samuel first looked upon Jesse's older son, but the Lord corrected the measure: man looks upon appearance; the Lord looks upon the heart (1 Samuel 16:6-13). Psalms 78:70-72 joins David's shepherding of the flock to the integrity and skill with which he fed the nation. The calling required the same care on a greater charge. Before he held the throne, he served the king who would come to hate him. He played for Saul's relief, went where Saul sent him, and behaved wisely while Saul's envy grew (1 Samuel 16:21-23; 18:5-16). Twice Saul was placed within his reach, and twice David refused to kill him. Even cutting the skirt of Saul's robe troubled his heart (1 Samuel 24:4-7; 26:8-12). He would not use a promised kingdom to justify taking the life of the Lord's anointed.

name: Saul's rash oath, and the people at the blood
text: A rash oath that snared the army; the people eating flesh with the blood; the son who unknowingly broke the oath. Saul adjured the people to eat nothing until evening, and the army fainted in the pursuit. Jonathan, who had not heard, ate honey; the people, famished, fell on the spoil and ate with the blood; and when the lot fell on Jonathan the people would not let the king kill the man who had wrought the day's salvation. Jonathan went against the Philistine garrison trusting that the Lord could save by many or by few. The attack was followed by trembling throughout the host and the enemy turning its swords against itself (1 Samuel 14:6-23). In the midst of that deliverance, Saul placed the army under a curse against eating until evening, so that he might be avenged upon his enemies (1 Samuel 14:24). His added command deprived the pursuing men of strength. Honey lay within reach, but the people feared the oath. Jonathan, who had not heard it, tasted honey and was refreshed. When told, he said his father had troubled the land and that the army could have done more had it eaten (1 Samuel 14:25-30). The distinction matters: he had not knowingly broken a charge he heard. Saul's command had nonetheless brought the deliverer himself within the danger of the curse. The famished people fell upon the spoil and ate with the blood (1 Samuel 14:31-33). Their hunger did not repeal the commandment. Leviticus 17:10-14 forbids eating blood because the life of the flesh is in it. A ruler's imprudent burden and the people's unlawful response both belong to the history; correcting the one did not make the other righteous.

name: Agag king of the Amalekites
text: The sword that made women childless. The Lord had sworn war with Amalek from generation to generation for what they did to Israel on the way out of Egypt. Saul was sent to finish it and spared Agag. Samuel did not: as thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women. The command against Amalek reached back to its assault upon Israel in the wilderness. Amalek struck the hindmost, the feeble, and the weary, without fear of God; Israel was commanded to remember and blot out that memory when the Lord gave rest (Deuteronomy 25:17-19). Exodus 17:14-16 placed the matter before succeeding generations. The passage of time had not discharged the word. Samuel said, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites, and hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal. The sentence pronounced at Rephidim was carried out by a prophet's hand when the king's hand failed.

name: Goliath of Gath
text: Defying the armies of the living God, morning and evening, forty days. Six cubits and a span, with a spear like a weaver's beam, Goliath stood in the valley of Elah and reproached Israel for forty days. A shepherd boy came in the name of the Lord of hosts and took his head with his own sword. Goliath stood before Israel morning and evening for forty days. His height, armour, spear, and shield-bearer made his challenge formidable, but his words defined the offense: he defied the armies of Israel and demanded a man to fight him (1 Samuel 17:4-16). Saul and the people answered the spectacle with fear. They measured the champion while forgetting whose army they were. David heard the same challenge and called it reproach against the armies of the living God (1 Samuel 17:26, 36). Deuteronomy 20:1-4 commanded Israel not to fear a greater host when the Lord went with them. David's answer was therefore not confidence that youth was stronger than experience. It was confidence that the enemy's equipment did not determine the Lord's power. Eliab accused him, and Saul questioned his ability, but David rehearsed the deliverance from the lion and bear. The Lord who preserved him with the sheep could preserve him in the valley (1 Samuel 17:28-37). When Goliath saw him, he despised him, cursed him by his gods, and promised his body to the birds and beasts (1 Samuel 17:41-44). Contempt for the messenger did not answer the God in whose name he came. David rejected armour he had not proved and went with his staff, sling, and stones. He declared that the battle belonged to the Lord, who would make the earth know there was a God in Israel and the assembly know that he saved without sword and spear (1 Samuel 17:38-47). Zechariah 4:6 places the work in the Lord's Spirit rather than man's might. The weapon was in David's hand; the deliverance was not confined to the weapon. David ran to meet Goliath, struck him in the forehead with a stone, and brought him down. He then took the champion's sword and cut off his head (1 Samuel 17:48-51). The very sword that had helped present Goliath as invincible was used at his death.

name: Jonathan
text: Stripping himself of his robe for the man whom the Lord would make king; and thou shalt be king, and I shall be next unto thee. The king's son and heir made a covenant with the shepherd who had just killed Goliath, and gave him his robe, his garments, his sword, his bow and his girdle. He warned him of his father's intent, spoke for him and was nearly killed for it, and met him in the wood at Ziph to strengthen his hand in God. He said outright that David would be king and he himself would be next. He died with his father on Gilboa. Jonathan's confidence in the Lord preceded his covenant with David. At the Philistine garrison he declared that no restraint could keep the Lord from saving by many or by few, and went forward with his armour-bearer (1 Samuel 14:6-14). He had already risked his life for Israel when David came into the history as its champion. Their bond joined men who had acted upon the same trust. Jonathan loved David as his own soul, made a covenant with him, and gave him his robe, garments, sword, bow, and girdle (1 Samuel 18:1-4). His conduct was the opposite of Saul's envy. As David's honour increased, Jonathan did not treat another servant's calling as an injury to himself. Colossians 2:2 speaks of hearts knit together in love; shared faith strengthens service instead of dividing it by rivalry. When Saul ordered David killed, Jonathan warned him and argued his innocence before the king. David had risked his life and done Saul good; killing him without cause would shed innocent blood (1 Samuel 19:1-7). Later Saul explicitly connected David's survival to Jonathan's loss of the kingdom and threw a javelin at his own son (1 Samuel 20:30-33). Jonathan would not purchase a throne through the murder of his friend. He met David in the wood and strengthened his hand in God, acknowledging that David would be king (1 Samuel 23:16-18). The threatened man needed more than information about Saul's movements. He needed a brother who would stand with the Lord's purpose when doing so cost him advantage. Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 6:14 calls a faithful friend a strong defence; Jonathan supplied that defence in counsel, warning, and covenant.

name: Saul and Doeg at Nob
text: Slaughter of the priests of the Lord on an informer's report. Doeg the Edomite, Saul's chief herdsman, told the king that Ahimelech had given David bread and Goliath's sword. Saul summoned the priests, condemned them unheard, and when his own guard refused to strike them, Doeg killed eighty-five men in linen ephods and then the whole city of Nob. Doeg reported to Saul that Ahimelech had received David at Nob, enquired for him, given him food, and supplied Goliath's sword (1 Samuel 22:9-10). Saul treated help given to David as conspiracy against himself. Ahimelech answered that David was the king's faithful servant and son in law and that he knew nothing of a plot (1 Samuel 22:11-15). His defence was heard but rejected. The king's suspicion had taken the place of a righteous judgment. Saul ordered the priests killed. His servants refused to stretch out their hands against the priests of the Lord, but Doeg obeyed, killing eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod. He then smote Nob, including its households and animals (1 Samuel 22:16-19). The refusal of the guard shows that the king's order did not remove the responsibility of those commanded. Doeg did what others would not do. Exodus 23:1 forbids joining a false report or becoming an unrighteous witness; verse 7 forbids slaying the innocent and righteous. Psalms 52 names the malicious tongue that loves evil rather than good. Speech and violence worked together at Nob: the report furnished an occasion, the king supplied the order, and the willing hand carried it through.

name: Nabal
text: Churlish refusal of hospitality; railing on the Lord's anointed. David's men had guarded Nabal's shepherds all season. At sheep-shearing David asked for provision; Nabal, churlish and evil in his doings, answered, who is David? and sent them away. Abigail's wisdom stopped David's sword. The Lord did not stop his own. Nabal possessed three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. At sheep-shearing David sent a peaceful request for provision, reminding him that his shepherds and goods had been safe among David's men (1 Samuel 25:2-9). Nabal's own servant confirmed their conduct: they had been a wall by night and day, and nothing had gone missing (1 Samuel 25:14-16). The benefit was known within the household before the request arrived. Nabal answered with contempt, asking who David was and comparing him to a servant breaking away from his master. He would not give his bread, water, and meat to these men (1 Samuel 25:10-11). His repeated claim upon his possessions ignored the protection through which he had enjoyed them. Wealth had become the reason to close his hand rather than the means to supply a need. His servant described him as a man who could not be reasoned with (1 Samuel 25:17). That spirit made correction difficult before the danger arrived. Deuteronomy 15:7-11 forbids hardening the heart and shutting the hand against a needy brother. Nabal joined refusal to railing, repaying good with evil while his household prepared to feast.

name: Abigail
text: Keeping David from shedding blood and avenging himself with his own hand. Her husband Nabal railed on David's men; David strapped on his sword to kill every male of the house by morning. Abigail met him on the road with two hundred loaves and a speech that is one of the wisest in scripture, and turned him back. Ten days later the Lord smote Nabal, and David sent for her. Abigail heard from a servant what Nabal had done and what David's men had done for the household. The men had protected the shepherds; Nabal had railed upon their messengers; now destruction threatened the house (1 Samuel 25:14-17). She did not make loyalty to her husband mean agreement with his folly. She acted to preserve the household he had placed in danger. She prepared substantial provision and went to meet David without first telling Nabal. David had already armed his men and sworn to leave no male of the house alive (1 Samuel 25:18-22). Her haste addressed a danger that could not wait for the husband described as unwilling to hear reason. The food answered the need; her speech addressed the wrath. She humbled herself, took the burden of pleading upon herself, and named Nabal's folly without disguising it. Then she directed David toward the future the Lord had promised him. When he ruled Israel, he should not carry the grief of causeless bloodshed or self-avenging violence (1 Samuel 25:23-31). She appealed to his calling against the conduct his anger was about to produce. Wise counsel did not flatter the armed man; it stopped him. Proverbs 14:1 says that a wise woman builds her house. Abigail's conduct protected more than its possessions. It preserved lives and called the approaching king back to the fear of the Lord. She neither approved Nabal's railing nor answered it by delivering him to David's sword. David blessed the Lord who sent her, blessed her advice, and acknowledged that she had kept him from shedding blood and avenging himself. He accepted the provision and sent her home in peace (1 Samuel 25:32-35). Her counsel succeeded because he received correction while there was still time to turn from the act. At home she again governed the moment of speaking. Nabal was drunk, so she waited until morning. After he heard what had happened, he became as a stone, and about ten days later the Lord smote him (1 Samuel 25:36-38). The household was spared David's intended slaughter; Nabal's own judgment remained with the Lord. David then sought Abigail as his wife, and she answered with the same humility that had marked her appeal (1 Samuel 25:39-42). The blessing follows a woman of understanding who brought provision, spoke truth, and preserved another from sin. Her wisdom was not merely knowledge of what was right. It was the ability to bring that knowledge to bear before blood was shed.

name: Saul and the witch of Endor
text: Seeking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, after cutting them off out of the land himself. With the Philistines encamped and the Lord not answering him by dreams, by Urim, or by prophets, Saul disguised himself, went by night to a woman at Endor, and asked her to bring up Samuel. He had himself put the mediums out of the land. He was told he and his sons would be with Samuel the next day, fell on the earth, and died on Gilboa. Chronicles names this as a cause of his death. Saul had removed those with familiar spirits and wizards from the land. When the Philistine host frightened him and the Lord answered neither by dreams, Urim, nor prophets, he sought a woman with a familiar spirit himself (1 Samuel 28:3-7). He knew the prohibition because he had enforced it. The silence he encountered did not give him permission to seek an answer by a forbidden means. He disguised himself and went by night. The woman feared a trap because of Saul's own earlier action, but he swore by the Lord that no punishment would come upon her for the deed (1 Samuel 28:8-10). The name of the Lord was invoked to reassure someone in the performance of what his law condemned. An oath cannot make disobedience holy. Leviticus 19:31 forbids seeking familiar spirits; Deuteronomy 18:10-12 forbids the necromancer and places these practices among the abominations Israel was to reject. Saul sought counsel while continuing the course for which counsel had condemned him. His need was not another voice agreeing to direct him, but obedience to the word already received.

name: The Amalekite who claimed to kill Saul
text: Claiming to have slain the Lord's anointed. A young Amalekite came to David at Ziklag with Saul's crown and bracelet and said he had killed the wounded king at his own request. The earlier chapter says Saul fell on his own sword. Either way, his mouth condemned him. The messenger arrived with torn clothes and earth upon his head, bringing news that Saul and Jonathan were dead. David required him to explain how he knew. He said he had found Saul in anguish upon Gilboa, had killed him at his request, and had taken the crown and bracelet to bring to David (2 Samuel 1:1-10). The ornaments were presented as the tokens of a deed from which he expected advantage. David did not receive the report as the happy removal of a rival. He and his men mourned, wept, and fasted for Saul, Jonathan, and the fallen of Israel (2 Samuel 1:11-12). The throne's opening did not make the nation's loss a cause for celebration. The man who had refused to kill Saul in the cave and camp was not about to reward another for claiming the act (1 Samuel 24:6; 26:9-11). David asked why the messenger had not feared to stretch forth his hand against the Lord's anointed (2 Samuel 1:13-14). The man's appeal to Saul's request and approaching death did not persuade him that killing the king was a service. He had offered his own account as evidence, and the judgment was returned upon that testimony.

name: Joab
text: Murder of Abner and Amasa in time of peace. David's general killed Abner in the gate of Hebron under cover of a private word, avenging Asahel's death in battle, and years later killed Amasa with a kiss and a hidden sword. David laid both on Solomon's charge. Abner killed Asahel in battle after repeatedly warning him to turn aside. Later Abner came to David to bring Israel under his rule, and the king sent him away in peace (2 Samuel 2:19-23; 3:12-21). Joab recalled him without David's knowledge, took him aside as if to speak privately, and killed him for Asahel's blood (2 Samuel 3:26-30). He turned a peaceful meeting into revenge. David declared himself and his kingdom guiltless of Abner's blood, mourned openly, and said the Lord would reward the evildoer according to his wickedness (2 Samuel 3:28-39). Joab's military importance did not change what he had done. The man who served the throne had acted against the peace the king had given. He later killed Amasa, the captain appointed in his place. He greeted him as a brother, took him by the beard as if to kiss him, and struck him with the sword (2 Samuel 19:13; 20:8-10). The greeting concealed the blow. David's final charge gathered Abner and Amasa together: Joab had shed the blood of war in peace (1 Kings 2:5-6). Experience in battle did not authorize treachery outside it.

name: Mephibosheth
text: Answering the king, What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am; and let him take all. Lame on both feet from the day his nurse dropped him fleeing the news of Gilboa, the last of Saul's line was fetched from Lodebar and given all the land of his grandfather and a place at the king's table continually. When David fled from Absalom his servant slandered him and took the property. When David returned, Mephibosheth met him unwashed and unshaven since the day the king departed, and when the land was divided said, let him take all, forasmuch as my lord the king is come again in peace. Mephibosheth was five when the news of Saul and Jonathan's deaths caused his nurse to flee with him. He fell in her haste and became lame (2 Samuel 4:4). Years later he was summoned from Lodebar to the king who now ruled in his grandfather's place. He came with reverence and fear, but David's purpose was kindness for Jonathan's sake (2 Samuel 9:1-7). His standing rested upon the covenant between his father and David, not his ability to serve in battle or strengthen the king politically. He received the kindness humbly (2 Samuel 9:8). The promise had reached a member of the former royal house who could offer little power in return. David's care made remembrance of Jonathan a continuing work rather than a passing expression of grief. During Absalom's rebellion Ziba accused Mephibosheth of remaining in Jerusalem to recover Saul's kingdom. When David returned, Mephibosheth came with his neglected feet, beard, and clothes bearing the marks of mourning. He explained that Ziba had deceived and slandered him (2 Samuel 16:1-4; 19:24-28). His answer to the king's order to divide the land was that Ziba could have it all, since David had returned safely (2 Samuel 19:29-30). His joy in the king's preservation stood above the disputed estate. David restored Saul's land and appointed Ziba's household to cultivate it, while Mephibosheth ate continually at the king's table as one of his sons (2 Samuel 9:9-13). Provision included both the inheritance's produce and an honoured place in the household. His disability did not exclude him from the kindness pledged to his father. When the Gibeonites required seven of Saul's house, David spared Jonathan's son because of the Lord's oath between David and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:7). The broken covenant that brought judgment upon Saul's house was met by a kept covenant preserving Mephibosheth. The king did not allow the pressure of one obligation to make him forget another.

name: Baanah and Rechab
text: Murder of Ish-bosheth in his bed. Two captains of Saul's son entered his house at noon under pretense of fetching wheat, killed him as he lay on his bed, cut off his head, and carried it all night to David at Hebron expecting a reward. After Abner's death, Ishbosheth's hands were feeble and Israel was troubled. Rechab and Baanah, captains from his own company, entered his house in the heat of the day as though fetching wheat and killed him upon his bed (2 Samuel 4:1-7). Their access became the means of betrayal. They did not meet him in an open contest but took advantage of his rest within his own house. They carried his head through the night to David and called the killing the Lord's vengeance upon Saul and his seed (2 Samuel 4:8). The claim attempted to make murder into religious service. David's rise did not mean that any deed removing a rival had been commanded by God. The promise of the kingdom was not permission to put innocent blood beneath it. David answered by naming the Lord who had redeemed his soul from adversity (2 Samuel 4:9). His deliverance did not depend upon these men. He had already put to death the messenger who expected favour for reporting Saul's death; he would not now reward men who brought proof of a killing in a bedroom (2 Samuel 4:10-11). David called Ishbosheth a righteous person slain by wicked men and required his blood from their hands (2 Samuel 4:11). The judgment distinguished a political opponent from a person whom it was lawful to murder. The king would not receive the brothers' account of divine vengeance as an answer to what they had done. He ordered their execution. Their hands and feet were cut off, and their bodies were hung over the pool in Hebron; Ishbosheth's head was buried in Abner's sepulchre (2 Samuel 4:12). The murderers were publicly judged, while the remains they had carried as a reward-bearing token were given burial. The same distinction later governed David's charge against Joab: blood shed through treachery in peace did not become lawful because the killer served the king (1 Kings 2:5-6). Rechab and Baanah misjudged both David and the Lord whose name they used. Advantage offered to a ruler did not remove the ruler's obligation to judge the act.

name: Uzzah and the ark
text: Touching the ark, transported unlawfully. The ark had been taken by the Philistines in the days of the judges and had rested in the house of Abinadab. David gathered thirty thousand chosen men to bring it up, and they set it upon a new cart driven by Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab. At Nachon's threshingfloor the oxen shook the cart, Uzzah put forth his hand and took hold of the ark, and God smote him there for his error, and he died by the ark. David and the congregation agreed to bring the ark up from the house of Abinadab. They placed it upon a new cart, and music and rejoicing accompanied the journey (2 Samuel 6:1-5). The purpose was welcome to the people, but the manner of carrying the ark had already been commanded. Approval by an assembly did not replace the Lord's due order. Numbers 4:15 required the holy things to be covered before the appointed bearers approached and forbade them to touch them lest they die. The ark's staves were to remain in their rings (Exodus 25:14-15). The Philistines had returned it upon a cart, but Israel was responsible for the instruction given to Israel. A new vehicle was not an improvement upon obedience. At the threshingfloor the oxen shook it, and Uzzah put out his hand to hold the ark (2 Samuel 6:6). His reach answered an immediate danger, but it crossed a boundary the law had not left to personal judgment. Even Aaron was forbidden to enter the holy place at all times, a warning given after the deaths of his sons (Leviticus 16:1-2). Nearness to holy service required greater care, not freedom from its limits. The Lord's anger was kindled against Uzzah, and he died there beside the ark. David was displeased at the breach and afraid, asking how the ark could come to him (2 Samuel 6:7-9). The celebration was stopped by a judgment that made the neglected command impossible to dismiss. Psalms 119:120 joins trembling in the flesh to fear of the Lord's judgments. The ark remained three months in Obed-edom's house. When David returned to bring it up, he did not merely try the same journey with more confidence. He declared that none but the Levites ought to carry it, called them to sanctify themselves, and acknowledged that the first breach came because they had not sought the Lord after the due order (1 Chronicles 15:2, 12-13). The failure was confessed as theirs, not assigned to Uzzah alone. The Levites then bore the ark upon their shoulders with the staves as Moses had commanded (1 Chronicles 15:14-15). Rejoicing continued, but now the service followed the word. The distinction between the journeys was not whether David wanted to honour the Lord. It was whether that honour was offered in the manner the Lord had appointed.

name: Obed-edom the Gittite
text: Keeping the ark of God in his house three months, after it had killed Uzzah. Uzzah had just died for touching the ark, and David was afraid to bring it into the city. It went instead into the house of Obed-edom of Gath, and stayed three months. The Lord blessed him and all his household so visibly that David heard of it and came back for the ark with sacrifices and dancing. After the breach upon Uzzah, David would not bring the ark into the city of David. He carried it aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, where it remained three months (2 Samuel 6:10-11). The same ark before which judgment had interrupted the procession now stood within a household. The Lord's holiness had not changed; neither had his power to bless. Obed-edom's house received what David had become afraid to bring nearer. Yet the blessing was not a licence to handle the ark however a man pleased. When the journey resumed, the Levites sanctified themselves and carried it upon their shoulders according to the commandment (1 Chronicles 15:12-15). Receiving holy things and observing the order of their service belonged together.

name: Michal
text: Despising the king in her heart for dancing before the ark. As the ark came into the city of David with shouting and trumpets, Michal, Saul's daughter, watched from a window and despised David in her heart for leaping and dancing. She met him with contempt: how glorious was the king of Israel to day. Michal had once warned David of Saul's attempt upon his life and helped him escape through a window (1 Samuel 19:11-17). But when she saw him leaping and dancing before the Lord as the ark entered the city, she despised him in her heart (2 Samuel 6:16). An earlier act of loyalty did not prevent contempt from taking root later. David had laid aside the display of royal greatness for the service of that day. Chronicles describes him clothed in a robe of fine linen and wearing an ephod of linen (1 Chronicles 15:27). Michal's rebuke treated his public rejoicing as a disgrace before the handmaids. Her concern was how the king appeared in the eyes of servants, while David answered concerning the Lord before whom he rejoiced. David did not attribute the throne to his own dignity. He said that the Lord had chosen him before her father and his house, appointing him ruler over Israel (2 Samuel 6:21). The office was a gift, not a reason to consider himself too great to rejoice before its giver. The king's answer exposed the difference between honouring the Lord and guarding an image of personal importance. David declared that he would yet be more vile and base in his own sight, and that the maidservants Michal had mentioned would honour him (2 Samuel 6:22). Her scorn did not govern his worship. He would not make royal appearance the measure of what was fitting before God. The account closes with Michal having no child unto the day of her death (2 Samuel 6:23). Her place as Saul's daughter and David's wife did not turn the contempt into a small matter. The final word upon the encounter was not the preservation of her dignity, but the absence of children. The ark's arrival had brought sacrifices, gifts of food to the people, and David's return to bless his household. Michal met that return with reproach. The contrast is within the house itself: David came to bless, while she condemned the humility with which he had honoured the Lord.

name: David and Bathsheba
text: Adultery and the arranged death of Uriah. The king took another man's wife, and when she conceived, engineered her husband's death to cover it. The prophet Nathan exposed it with a parable, and David confessed, but the consequences ran through his house for years. At the season when kings went forth to battle, David remained in Jerusalem. He saw Bathsheba, inquired after her, and was told that she was Uriah's wife before he sent messengers and took her (2 Samuel 11:1-4). Knowledge of the marriage stood before the act. The king's power to summon did not give him a right to another man's wife. When Bathsheba sent word that she was with child, David recalled Uriah from the war. Questions about Joab, the people, and the battle covered the purpose of bringing him home. Uriah would not go to his house while the ark, Israel, Judah, and his lord's servants remained in tents and the open fields (2 Samuel 11:6-11). His faithfulness frustrated the concealment. David then made him drunk, but Uriah still did not go home. The king turned from arranging an appearance to arranging a death. Uriah carried the letter ordering Joab to place him in the hottest battle and retire from him. Other servants fell with him, and David answered the report by saying that the sword devoured one as well as another (2 Samuel 11:13-25). The language of ordinary losses concealed a deliberately ordered killing. After mourning, Bathsheba became David's wife and bore a son. The matter appeared settled within the king's house, but it displeased the Lord (2 Samuel 11:26-27). Adultery had been followed by deceit and bloodshed. Deuteronomy 27:24 pronounces a curse upon the man who secretly smites his neighbour; a command carried through another man's hands did not remove David's responsibility. Nathan brought the case of a rich man who took a poor man's only lamb. David burned with anger and pronounced judgment before Nathan answered, “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:1-7). The king who could see the cruelty in a parable had concealed the same disregard in his own house. The Lord named what he had given David and what David had despised. Uriah's death was charged to David even though the sword was the sword of the children of Ammon (2 Samuel 12:7-9). Neither the battlefield nor Joab's obedience could stand between the king and the deed he had ordered. The sword would not depart from his house. Evil would arise within it, and his wives would be taken openly, answering what he had done secretly (2 Samuel 12:10-12). David confessed his sin without charging the people or the circumstances. Nathan declared that the Lord had put away his sin and that David would not die, yet the child would die because the deed had given occasion to the Lord's enemies to blaspheme (2 Samuel 12:13-14). Forgiveness and the removal of every consequence were not the same thing. David fasted and pleaded while the child lived. When the child died, he arose, washed, worshipped, and ate, acknowledging that he could not bring him back (2 Samuel 12:15-23). The judgment had not ceased to be the Lord's judgment because David had wept beneath it. Solomon was afterward born, and the Lord loved him (2 Samuel 12:24-25). Mercy continued in the house, but Amnon's death, Absalom's rebellion, and the taking of the concubines before Israel showed that Nathan's word had not fallen. The king was restored to life and service without being permitted to call the offense harmless.

name: Uriah the Hittite
text: Refusing the comfort of his own house while the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents. Recalled from the siege of Rabbah so that the king's crime could be covered, he would not go down to his house. He slept at the door of the king's house with the servants. Asked why, he said the ark and Israel and Judah abide in tents, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are encamped in the open fields; shall I then go into mine house? He was made drunk and still would not go, and was sent back carrying the letter that ordered his death. Uriah the Hittite is numbered among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:39). When recalled from the war, he would not receive the comforts of his own house while the ark, Israel, Judah, Joab, and the servants remained in tents and the open fields. He answered David with an oath that he would not do such a thing (2 Samuel 11:11). David's invitation would have been convenient to accept. Uriah had the king's permission to go home, and the king sent a mess of meat after him. Yet he slept at the door of the king's house with the servants (2 Samuel 11:8-9). His concern reached beyond what he was personally allowed to enjoy. He remembered the men still bearing the burden from which he had briefly been recalled. Even when David made him drunk, Uriah did not return to his wife (2 Samuel 11:13). The purpose concealed behind the hospitality failed. The servant maintained his course while the king employed his authority to hide a transgression. David then entrusted him with the letter that ordered his death. Uriah carried it to Joab and returned to the fighting (2 Samuel 11:14-17). The loyalty by which he served his king was used against him. His death did not expose a failure of courage or duty; it exposed the treachery of the command placed over him. Nathan's charge did not let Uriah disappear into the unnamed losses of battle. The Lord declared that David had killed Uriah with the sword and taken his wife (2 Samuel 12:9). The man whom the king had sought to conceal remained named in the judgment against the king. The later summary of David's reign again singled out the matter of Uriah the Hittite (1 Kings 15:5). Matthew also identifies Solomon's mother as her who had been the wife of Urias (Matthew 1:6). The record of the royal line did not erase the marriage that David had violated. Uriah was not delivered from the fatal order. His fidelity must not be measured by whether he escaped suffering. The account honours the servant's conduct while condemning the ruler who exploited it. The throne could command his movements, but it could not make the blood innocent of accusation.

name: Amnon
text: Rape of his sister Tamar. David's firstborn feigned sickness to get his half-sister alone, and when she pleaded that such a thing should not be done in Israel, forced her, then hated her more than he had loved her and had her thrown out. David was very wroth and did nothing. Amnon desired Tamar, his sister, and received Jonadab's counsel to feign sickness and ask that she prepare food before him. David sent her without knowing the purpose of the request. Once she had brought the food, Amnon dismissed the others and drew her into the chamber (2 Samuel 13:1-10). A household duty became the means by which he isolated her. Tamar refused him plainly. She named the act folly in Israel and spoke of the shame it would bring upon her and the wickedness it would attach to him. He would not hearken, but overpowered and forced her (2 Samuel 13:11-14). Her words were not a hesitation to be overcome; they were a refusal that he chose to disregard. The law forbade uncovering a sister's nakedness (Leviticus 18:9). Tamar's appeal to speak to the king did not repeal that command. Nor could Amnon's desire make the violence a mutual offense. Deuteronomy 22:25-26 distinguishes the man who forces a woman from the woman against whom he acts, comparing the assault to a man rising against his neighbour and slaying him. Afterward Amnon hated her more than he had loved her and ordered her out. When she protested that this added evil to the first, he would not listen. His servant put her out and bolted the door (2 Samuel 13:15-18). The appetite that had called itself love would neither protect her nor hear her distress once it had obtained its object. Tamar rent her garment, put ashes upon her head, and went away crying. She remained desolate in Absalom's house. David heard and was very wroth, but the account records no judicial sentence imposed by him upon Amnon (2 Samuel 13:19-22). Anger within the palace did not repair what had been done to Tamar. Absalom concealed his hatred for two full years. At his sheep-shearing feast he instructed his servants to strike Amnon when his heart was merry with wine, and they killed him (2 Samuel 13:23-29). The death answered a brother's revenge, not an orderly hearing under the law. Amnon's guilt did not make every act against him righteous. The king's sons fled, David mourned, and Absalom escaped to Geshur. The sword Nathan had announced was working within David's own house (2 Samuel 12:10; 13:30-39). The calamity was larger than the death of the offender: Tamar remained desolate, the brothers were scattered, and the father was left to mourn a household he had not kept from violence.

name: Absalom
text: Murder of Amnon; conspiracy and rebellion against the king his father; lying with his father's concubines. David's son killed his brother, fled, was restored, then stole the hearts of Israel at the gate with flattery, raised a rebellion from Hebron, drove his father from Jerusalem, and lay with David's concubines on the roof before all Israel by Ahithophel's counsel. Absalom received Tamar into his house after Amnon forced her. He held his hatred silently for two years, then arranged Amnon's death at a feast and fled to Geshur (2 Samuel 13:20-38). His sister's injury was real, but he answered it through a concealed command to kill, not through a lawful hearing. Joab afterward used the woman of Tekoah to persuade David to bring him home. Absalom returned to Jerusalem but was not admitted to the king's face for two years. When Joab would not answer his summons, he ordered Joab's field set on fire to compel a meeting (2 Samuel 14:23-33). Even the recovery of access to his father proceeded through pressure upon another man's property. Once restored, Absalom prepared chariots, horses, and fifty men to run before him. He stood by the gate, met those coming for judgment, and affirmed their matters while telling them that the king had appointed no man to hear them. He wished aloud that he were judge, took men by the hand, and kissed them (2 Samuel 15:1-6). He offered a favourable answer before a dispute had been heard. Affection and the promise of justice became instruments for stealing the people's hearts. He then asked leave to fulfil a vow in Hebron. Beneath that religious purpose he sent messengers to announce his kingship. Two hundred men went with him in simplicity, knowing nothing of the conspiracy, while Ahithophel joined it knowingly (2 Samuel 15:7-12). The company around a rebellion did not all bear the same knowledge, but Absalom used them together to give it strength. After David fled, Absalom accepted Ahithophel's counsel and went in to his father's concubines upon the roof before all Israel (2 Samuel 16:20-22). The act publicly severed reconciliation and transgressed the prohibition concerning a father's wife (Leviticus 18:8). What Nathan had declared against David's house was fulfilled through a son who remained answerable for his own wickedness. David prayed that Ahithophel's counsel would be turned into foolishness. Hushai countered the proposed immediate pursuit with a plan to gather all Israel and have Absalom go in person. The Lord appointed the defeat of Ahithophel's good counsel to bring evil upon Absalom (2 Samuel 15:31; 17:1-14). What appeared the stronger plan gave David time to cross Jordan and prepare. Before the battle, David charged his commanders to deal gently with the young man for his sake. During the fighting, Absalom's head caught in a great oak and his mule went from under him (2 Samuel 18:5-9). The display of princely strength ended with him suspended and unable to free himself. The soldier who found him refused to strike him even for a thousand shekels, remembering the king's command. Joab disregarded that restraint, thrust three darts through Absalom's heart, and his armourbearers finished the killing (2 Samuel 18:10-15). Absalom's rebellion was judged, but Joab's disregard of the command was not thereby made obedience. His body was cast into a pit in the wood and covered with a great heap of stones. The record sets that burial beside the pillar he had raised to preserve his own name (2 Samuel 18:17-18). He had sought a monument and a kingdom; his rebellion ended away from both, while David wept that he would have died in his son's place. A throne seized from a father had brought grief to that father instead of honour to the son.

name: Ahithophel
text: Treason against David; counsel of incest; suicide. David's counselor, whose word was as if a man had inquired at the oracle of God, joined Absalom, advised him to take his father's concubines publicly, and asked for twelve thousand men to kill David that night. When Hushai's counsel was preferred, he went home, set his house in order, and hanged himself. Ahithophel's counsel was esteemed as though a man had inquired at the oracle of God. That reputation was shared in the days of David and Absalom (2 Samuel 16:23). Yet the weight men gave his advice did not make every purpose he served righteous. He left David and joined the conspiracy at Hebron (2 Samuel 15:12). His first recorded counsel in Jerusalem was for Absalom to go in to his father's concubines. It would make the breach with David unmistakable and strengthen those who had joined the rebellion (2 Samuel 16:20-22). The advice was politically calculated and morally corrupt. The prohibition concerning a father's wife did not change because violating it could secure a faction (Leviticus 18:8). He next proposed taking twelve thousand men to pursue David that night, strike the weary king, and bring the people back. He described peace for the multitude through the death of one man (2 Samuel 17:1-4). The promised settlement depended upon killing the king whom he had served. Skill in choosing a moment did not cleanse the betrayal at the centre of the plan. David had prayed that Ahithophel's counsel would become foolishness. Hushai did not deny David's danger; he spoke of David's experience in war and urged a larger gathering with Absalom himself at its head. Absalom and the men of Israel preferred Hushai's answer (2 Samuel 17:5-14). The account gives the cause beyond the debate: the Lord had appointed the defeat of Ahithophel's good counsel to bring evil upon Absalom. “Good” described its effectiveness for the pursuit, not the righteousness of the enterprise. The counsel most likely to serve the rebellion was prevented from carrying it to its intended end.

name: Ittai the Gittite
text: As the Lord liveth, in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be. David offered Ittai the Gittite, whom he called a stranger and an exile, leave to return instead of sharing his uncertain flight. Ittai swore to remain with the king in death or life and crossed with his men and their little ones. David later placed a third of the army under his command. When David fled Jerusalem, Ittai the Gittite went with him. David called him a stranger and an exile, spoke of his recent arrival, and released him from following a king who did not know where he would go (2 Samuel 15:19-20). The choice was not presented as a command to preserve Ittai's position. David gave him leave to return with his brethren. Ittai answered with an oath by the Lord and by the life of the king: wherever David should be, in death or life, there his servant would be also (2 Samuel 15:21). He accepted uncertainty when a safer course had been offered. His word did not depend upon the king first proving that he could recover Jerusalem. David told him to pass over, and Ittai crossed with his men and the little ones who were with him (2 Samuel 15:22). This was more than a favourable statement at the roadside. His company entered the journey with the displaced king while the country wept and Absalom advanced toward the city. The contrast with Absalom was sharp. David's own son sought his throne, while the man whom David had offered to release bound himself to share his danger. Nearness by household did not guarantee faithfulness, and the absence of long-standing advantage did not prevent it. When David ordered the army for battle, he placed a third under Joab, a third under Abishai, and a third under Ittai (2 Samuel 18:2). The man who had pledged to remain with him was entrusted with a substantial command. Fidelity in flight was followed by responsibility in the defence of the kingdom. Ittai's promise had included death as well as life. It was therefore not a bargain made upon a guaranteed reward. The honour recorded afterward shows David's trust in him without changing the conditions under which he first gave his word. His place in the account preserves the value of loyalty when loyalty costs something. The throne's favour could attract many servants in Jerusalem; the road out of Jerusalem disclosed who would remain when that favour no longer promised immediate security.

name: Shimei son of Gera
