text: Cursing the king and casting stones at him. As David fled Jerusalem, Shimei of Saul's house came out cursing and throwing stones and dust: come out, thou bloody man, thou man of Belial. David forbade Abishai to kill him and later swore he would not put him to death. Solomon inherited the case. As David fled from Absalom, Shimei came out cursing, casting stones, and calling him a bloody man. He claimed that the Lord had returned the blood of Saul's house upon David (2 Samuel 16:5-8). David had repeatedly refused to kill Saul and had judged men who expected reward for deaths within Saul's house. Shimei used David's present distress as proof of an accusation the record did not sustain. Abishai asked leave to take his head, but David restrained him. With his own son seeking his life, David would not make Shimei's abuse the occasion for another immediate killing. He left room for the Lord to look upon his affliction and return good for the cursing (2 Samuel 16:9-12). The restraint belonged to David; it did not turn the curse into lawful speech. Exodus 22:28 forbids cursing the ruler of the people.

name: Barzillai the Gileadite
text: Bringing beds, wheat, and honey to the king and his hungry men in the wilderness at Mahanaim. When David fled from Absalom, an old man of Rogelim brought provision for the king and the people with him, saying, The people is hungry, and weary, and thirsty, in the wilderness. David wanted to keep him at court for life. Barzillai was eighty and asked only to die in his own city; David took his son instead, and charged Solomon on his deathbed to remember the house. When David came to Mahanaim during Absalom's rebellion, Barzillai joined Shobi and Machir in bringing beds, vessels, grain, pulses, honey, butter, sheep, and cheese for the people. They considered the people hungry, weary, and thirsty in the wilderness (2 Samuel 17:27-29). Their service answered the actual condition of those who had fled. Barzillai was very aged and a very great man, and he sustained the king while David lay at Mahanaim (2 Samuel 19:32). Wealth became provision at a moment when the kingdom's outcome was not settled. He assisted the displaced king before the victory made that assistance safe or fashionable. After the rebellion, he came down to conduct David over Jordan. David offered to take him to Jerusalem and feed him there. Barzillai, eighty years old, answered concerning the limits of his age and asked to return to his own city near the burial place of his father and mother (2 Samuel 19:31-37). His service had not been a concealed demand for life at court.

name: Sheba son of Bichri
text: Insurrection: we have no part in David. On the heels of Absalom's rebellion, Sheba the Benjamite blew a trumpet and cried, every man to his tents, O Israel, and all Israel went up after him. David judged him more dangerous than Absalom. He was besieged in Abel of Beth-maachah. The return of David was followed by strife between the men of Judah and the men of Israel over their share in bringing the king back (2 Samuel 19:41-43). Into that contention Sheba the son of Bichri blew a trumpet and declared that Israel had no part in David or inheritance in the son of Jesse. The men of Israel went up after him, while Judah clave to the king (2 Samuel 20:1-2). The rebellion drew strength from a quarrel that should not have governed the people's allegiance. Sheba offered separation as the answer to wounded tribal honour. The kingdom had scarcely emerged from Absalom's conspiracy when another man turned contention into a summons to depart. David saw that Sheba could do greater hurt if he gained fenced cities. The pursuit brought Joab's army to Abel of Beth-maachah, where it raised a bank and battered the wall (2 Samuel 20:6, 14-15). One man's cause now placed a whole city's life and inheritance beneath the danger of a siege. A wise woman called to Joab from the city and asked why he would swallow up the inheritance of the Lord. She identified herself with those who were peaceable and faithful in Israel (2 Samuel 20:16-19). Her appeal distinguished the city's people from the rebellion of the man within it. Joab answered that he did not seek to destroy the city. Sheba had lifted his hand against David; if the city delivered him alone, the army would depart (2 Samuel 20:20-21). The demand narrowed the matter to the rebel instead of treating everyone behind the wall as equally guilty.

name: Rizpah
text: Spreading sackcloth on the rock and suffering neither the birds by day nor the beasts by night to touch the bodies. Seven of Saul's sons were given to the Gibeonites and hanged in the hill before the Lord in the beginning of barley harvest. Two of them were hers. She took sackcloth and spread it on the rock and stayed from the beginning of harvest until water dropped on them out of heaven, keeping the birds off by day and the beasts off by night. It was told David, and he took the bones of Saul and Jonathan and of those seven and buried them in the sepulchre of Kish. Two of Rizpah's sons were among the seven delivered to the Gibeonites in the judgment concerning Saul's bloody house. From the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon the bodies from heaven, she spread sackcloth upon the rock and kept the birds away by day and the beasts by night (2 Samuel 21:8-10). She could not restore her sons to life, but she would not abandon their bodies to be consumed. Her watch extended beyond an hour of mourning. Day and night brought different threats, and she remained attentive to both. The account records her action without placing a speech in her mouth. Her perseverance itself made the condition of the dead known. The law required care even for the body of a man put to death and hanged, forbidding it to remain upon the tree overnight and defile the land (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). The exposure in this account was prolonged; Rizpah's vigil did not substitute for burial. It preserved the bodies until the matter reached the king and burial followed. David was told what Rizpah had done. He went to gather the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead and gathered the bones of those who had been hanged (2 Samuel 21:11-13). The response reached beyond her two sons to the earlier dead of Saul's house. The bones of Saul and Jonathan were buried in the sepulchre of Kish, and all that the king commanded was performed. Afterward God was entreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:14). The account closes not with the bodies exposed upon the hill, but with burial and the land's relief. Rizpah's sons were not returned to her. The good that followed her endurance was the care given to the dead and the completion of a matter affecting the whole land. Her vigil stands within the record of judgment as an act of steadfast attention to those who could no longer speak for themselves.

name: Saul's house and the Gibeonites
text: Breaking Israel's sworn covenant by slaying the Gibeonites. Three years of famine in David's reign were traced by inquiry of the Lord to Saul and his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites in his zeal for Israel, against the oath Joshua had sworn. David asked the Gibeonites what atonement they required. There was famine for three successive years, and David inquired of the Lord. The answer named Saul and his bloody house because he had slain the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:1). The land's distress had a cause beyond the conditions of a single harvest. The Gibeonites were a remnant of the Amorites with whom the children of Israel had sworn an oath. Joshua and the princes had made a league to let them live, and the princes refused to violate it after the deception by which it was obtained became known (Joshua 9:15-20). Israel's oath in the Lord's name remained binding when it became inconvenient. Saul nevertheless sought to slay them in his zeal for the children of Israel and Judah (2 Samuel 21:2). Zeal for one's people did not authorize breaking the word by which those people were bound. A purpose presented as national benefit could still bring bloodguilt upon the nation. When David asked what should be done, the Gibeonites refused silver and gold and did not demand an indiscriminate killing in Israel. They asked for seven men of Saul's sons from the house that had sought their destruction (2 Samuel 21:3-6). The injury could not be treated as an ordinary debt to be settled by wealth. Numbers 35:33 declares that blood pollutes the land. David delivered seven men but spared Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, because of the Lord's oath between David and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:7-9). The same matter that exposed a broken national oath also recorded the keeping of a personal one. Judgment did not permit the king to forget every other obligation. The seven were hanged together at the beginning of barley harvest. Rizpah guarded the bodies until rain came, and her conduct was reported to David. He then gathered the remains of Saul, Jonathan, and those who had been hanged, and ordered burial (2 Samuel 21:9-14). After the king's command was carried out, God was entreated for the land. The resolution included reckoning with bloodshed, remembering the oath, and caring for the remains; the story does not stop at the execution itself. Saul had acted in a zeal that disregarded an obligation sworn before the Lord. His death did not make that breach disappear from the land. The king who followed him had to inquire into the cause and address what remained unresolved beneath the years of famine.

name: David's numbering of the people
text: Numbering Israel in pride; a plague on the nation. David commanded Joab to number Israel and Judah. Joab objected; the king's word prevailed. When the count came in, David's heart smote him: I have sinned greatly. Gad offered three judgments, and David chose to fall into the hand of the Lord. The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and David was moved to number the people; Chronicles names Satan as the one who stood up against Israel and provoked him (2 Samuel 24:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1). The provocation did not make David an unwilling bystander. He gave the command and pressed it against objection. Joab wished that the Lord would multiply the people a hundredfold and asked why David delighted in this thing. Chronicles records his warning that the act would bring trespass upon Israel (1 Chronicles 21:3). The king's word prevailed, and the officers went through the land (2 Samuel 24:2-8). Authority could compel the count without making the purpose acceptable. Numbering itself was not absent from the law. Exodus 30:12 required a ransom for each man when Israel was numbered, that there be no plague among them. The people were the Lord's, not a measure of strength for a ruler to possess independently of him. Joab's protest and the prescribed warning both stood against treating the census as a harmless exercise of royal pleasure. Afterward David's heart smote him. He confessed that he had sinned greatly and done very foolishly (2 Samuel 24:10). He did not place the guilt upon the officers who had obeyed him. The recognition came after the command had already carried its work through the kingdom.

name: Adonijah
text: Exalting himself to be king; asking for the king's concubine. David's fourth son exalted himself, saying, I will be king, and gathered chariots, horsemen, Joab, and Abiathar for a coronation feast at En-rogel while David lay dying. Solomon was anointed the same day. Pardoned once, Adonijah then asked for Abishag the Shunammite. Adonijah exalted himself, saying that he would be king, and prepared chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. David had not displeased him by asking why he acted so (1 Kings 1:5-6). The display of succession grew without the father's correction, but display was not appointment. Joab and Abiathar supported him. He made a sacrificial feast and invited the king's sons and servants while leaving out Solomon, Nathan, Benaiah, and the mighty men (1 Kings 1:7-10). The invitations divided the house according to the claim he intended to establish. Religious sacrifice accompanied a decision made without the king's declaration. Nathan and Bathsheba brought the matter before David, who confirmed his oath that Solomon would reign. Solomon was placed upon the king's mule and anointed at Gihon by Zadok and Nathan (1 Kings 1:28-40). David also declared that the Lord had chosen Solomon to sit upon the throne (1 Chronicles 28:5). Adonijah's seniority among the surviving sons did not overrule that choice. When the news reached his feast, the guests rose in fear and departed. Adonijah caught hold of the horns of the altar and sought assurance that Solomon would not kill him (1 Kings 1:41-51). The man who had announced himself king now depended upon the king's mercy.

name: Solomon at Gibeon
text: Asking for an understanding heart to judge the people, and not for long life, riches, or the life of his enemies. Offered anything he wanted, the young king asked for wisdom to judge a great people. The speech pleased the Lord, who gave him the wisdom and added the riches and honour he had not asked. The kingdom he built on it was the greatest Israel ever had. What he did with his wives afterward is another case. Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad: for who is able to judge this thy so great a people? And the speech pleased the Lord, that Solomon had asked this thing. In Wisdom: I called upon God, and the spirit of wisdom came to me; I preferred her before sceptres and thrones, and esteemed riches nothing in comparison of her. Because thou hast asked this thing, and hast not asked for thyself long life; neither hast asked riches for thyself, nor hast asked the life of thine enemies; but hast asked for thyself understanding to discern judgment; behold, I have done according to thy words: lo, I have given thee a wise and an understanding heart; so that there was none like thee before thee, neither after thee shall any arise like unto thee. And I have also given thee that which thou hast not asked, both riches, and honour. All the earth sought to Solomon, to hear his wisdom, which God had put in his heart.

name: The two women before Solomon
text: Conflicting claims to a living child. Two women brought competing claims to a living infant before Solomon. One alleged that the other had exchanged their children after her own child died. Solomon tested their responses to a proposed division of the child and identified his mother. The account first presents the exchange of the children as one woman's testimony. Both women claimed the surviving child. The narrator identifies the mother through her compassion: she preferred to surrender the child rather than see him killed. Solomon ordered that the living child be given to his mother and not killed. Israel recognized the wisdom of God in his judgment. The custody decision is explicit; no punishment of the false claimant is recorded. The unrecorded classification refers only to that punishment, not to an absence of a judicial decision.

name: King Solomon
text: Multiplying foreign wives; building high places to their gods. The wisest king loved many strange women, seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, from the very nations the Lord had said, ye shall not go in to them. When he was old they turned his heart, and he built high places for Chemosh and Molech in the hill before Jerusalem. Solomon received wisdom, riches, honour, and the work of building the Lord's house. Yet he loved many strange women of the nations concerning whom the Lord had warned Israel, and he clave to them in love. In his old age his wives turned his heart after other gods (1 Kings 11:1-4). The warning concerned the very influence he allowed nearest his heart. The law for a king had forbidden multiplying horses, wives, silver, and gold, and required him to read the law all the days of his life so that his heart would not be lifted above his brethren (Deuteronomy 17:16-20). Royal greatness was to remain under instruction. Solomon's abundance did not place him beyond the dangers the command had named in advance. He went after Ashtoreth and Milcom and built high places for Chemosh and Molech. He did likewise for his strange wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods (1 Kings 11:5-8). The man who had built the temple in Jerusalem also established places of forbidden worship. Providing for the practice of those around him made the compromise part of the kingdom's life. The Lord had appeared to him twice and commanded him concerning this very matter (1 Kings 11:9-10). His failure was not a lack of access to wisdom. Nehemiah later remembered that even Solomon, beloved of God and made king over all Israel, was caused to sin by such marriages (Nehemiah 13:26). The greatness of the beginning deepened the warning of the end.

name: Rehoboam
text: Forsaking the counsel of the old men; forsaking the law of the Lord. Solomon's son rejected the elders' advice to serve the people and took his young companions' line: my little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins. Ten tribes left him that day. Later, when the kingdom was established, he forsook the law of the Lord and all Israel with him. The people came to Rehoboam at Shechem asking that he lighten the grievous service and heavy yoke laid upon them under Solomon. They offered to serve him if he would hear their burden (1 Kings 12:1-5). The new king asked for three days before answering. Taking time for counsel was sound; the failure came in choosing which counsel would govern him. The elders who had stood before Solomon told him to serve the people that day and answer with good words. His companions told him to announce a heavier yoke and scorpions in place of whips (1 Kings 12:6-11). One answer sought an enduring bond through service. The other treated the people's distress as an opportunity to display superiority. Proverbs 15:1 sets a soft answer against grievous words that stir up anger. Rehoboam chose the rough answer. Possession of the throne had not given him the understanding by which it could be held. Later, after he established and strengthened the kingdom, he forsook the law, and the people followed him (2 Chronicles 12:1). The repeated failure was a heart that had not prepared itself to seek the Lord (2 Chronicles 12:14). Neither inherited position nor strengthened cities supplied that preparation. The northern tribes rejected the house of David, stoned Adoram, and made Jeroboam king. Rehoboam fled to Jerusalem (1 Kings 12:16-20). His answer fulfilled the division already declared through Ahijah, yet the prophecy did not make his pride wise. The Lord accomplished his word through a king responsible for the answer he chose. When Rehoboam assembled Judah and Benjamin to recover the kingdom, Shemaiah forbade them to fight their brethren because the division was from the Lord. They obeyed and returned (1 Kings 12:21-24). He could still hearken to correction after refusing sound counsel at Shechem. Shishak afterward took Judah's fortified cities and threatened Jerusalem. Shemaiah named the cause: because they had forsaken the Lord, he had left them in Shishak's hand. The king and princes humbled themselves and confessed that the Lord was righteous (2 Chronicles 12:2-6). The Lord granted some deliverance, but they would serve Shishak and learn the difference between his service and the service of earthly kingdoms (2 Chronicles 12:7-8). Egypt carried away the treasures and Solomon's golden shields; Rehoboam replaced the gold with brass. Humbling preserved him from utter destruction without restoring everything his departure had cost.

name: Jeroboam son of Nebat
text: Two golden calves; priests of the lowest of the people; a feast devised of his own heart. Given ten tribes by the Lord, Jeroboam feared the people would return to Jerusalem to worship, so he set calves in Bethel and Dan, saying, behold thy gods, O Israel, made priests of any who were not Levites, and moved the feast to a month of his own choosing. His sin became a recurring measure of the kings who followed him. The Lord gave Jeroboam ten tribes and promised an established house if he would hearken, walk in his ways, and keep his commandments (1 Kings 11:37-38). The kingdom came with a charge to obey, not permission to construct a religion suited to its preservation. Jeroboam reasoned that worship at Jerusalem would turn the people's hearts toward Rehoboam and lead to his own death. Instead of trusting the promise, he made two golden calves, set them at Bethel and Dan, and told Israel that going to Jerusalem was too much for them (1 Kings 12:26-30). Convenience offered to the people concealed the king's fear for himself. The words announcing their gods repeated the language of the calf in the wilderness (Exodus 32:4). He also made priests who were not sons of Levi and appointed a feast in the eighth month, a month devised from his own heart (1 Kings 12:31-33). He altered the objects, ministers, place, and time of worship to secure his rule. The priests and Levites who would not serve his arrangement left their possessions and came to Judah; others from the tribes followed to seek the Lord at Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 11:13-17). A man of God cried against the altar at Bethel. Jeroboam's hand dried up when he reached to seize him, and the altar was rent. The king asked for his hand to be restored, and it was healed (1 Kings 13:1-6). Yet relief from the immediate judgment did not produce a turning from the system that had occasioned it. After these things Jeroboam continued making priests for the high places. This became sin to his house, to cut it off from the earth (1 Kings 13:33-34). The warning, sign, and restoration of his hand left him without cause to treat the matter as unknown. When his son Abijah fell sick, Jeroboam sent his wife in disguise to Ahijah. The blind prophet was told who was coming and addressed her before the disguise could serve its purpose (1 Kings 14:1-6). Concealment from men's eyes could not conceal the household from the Lord.

name: Amaziah the priest of Bethel
text: Forbidding Amos to prophesy at the king's chapel; accusing him to Jeroboam of conspiracy. A priest of the calf at Bethel sent word to Jeroboam that Amos had conspired against him, then told the prophet to go earn his bread in Judah. Amos answered that he was no prophet's son but a herdman the Lord had taken from the flock, and gave Amaziah a sentence for his wife, his children, his land and himself. Amos had pleaded for Jacob when shown judgments of grasshoppers and fire. The Lord then showed him a plumbline set in the midst of Israel and declared the coming desolation of its high places and sanctuaries (Amos 7:1-9). The prophet who announced judgment had first interceded for the people; rebuke was not proof that he wished their destruction. Amaziah sent word to Jeroboam that Amos had conspired against him and that the land could not bear his words. He then told Amos to flee to Judah, eat bread there, and prophesy no more at Bethel because it was the king's chapel and court (Amos 7:10-13). The priest treated the royal sanctuary as a place where the king's interests could set the limits of the Lord's speech. Amos answered that he had been a herdman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit. The Lord had taken him from following the flock and sent him to prophesy to Israel (Amos 7:14-15). His commission was not employment that Amaziah could transfer to another country. The question was not where he might earn bread, but to whom the Lord had sent him. Amos turned Amaziah's prohibition back upon him: because he said not to prophesy against Israel, a word now came concerning his own house. His wife would be a harlot in the city, his sons and daughters would fall by the sword, his land would be divided, and he would die in a polluted land. Israel would surely go into captivity (Amos 7:16-17). The sentence reached the things his royal protection could not secure: household, children, inheritance, and burial land. Silence imposed upon the messenger would not silence the judgment or preserve the place from which he was expelled. The king named here was Jeroboam in the days of Amos, not Jeroboam son of Nebat who first established the calves. Generations had passed, yet Bethel's service still joined royal power to resistance against the Lord's word. The priest defended the sanctuary's standing while refusing the correction that exposed its condition.

name: The man of God from Judah
text: Turning back to eat and drink at Bethel against the word of the Lord. Sent to cry against Jeroboam's altar, the prophet was charged to eat no bread, drink no water, and not return the way he came. An old prophet of Bethel lied to him, claiming an angel had said otherwise; he went back and ate. A lion met him on the road. The man of God came to Bethel by the word of the Lord and cried against Jeroboam's altar. He named Josiah and foretold the burning of men's bones upon it. The altar was rent, and the king's outstretched hand dried up (1 Kings 13:1-5). His commission was confirmed before the king and the people. When Jeroboam offered food and reward, he refused even half the king's house. He had been charged to eat no bread, drink no water, and return by another way (1 Kings 13:7-10). He knew the command distinctly and had already kept it under the pressure of royal favour.

name: The old prophet of Beth-el
text: Lying in the name of the Lord, and claiming an angel's word to turn a prophet from his charge. An old prophet in Beth-el heard what the man of God had done, rode after him, and brought him home to eat by claiming an angel had told him to. The text states it flatly: but he lied unto him. The lie killed the man who believed it, and then the same mouth pronounced his sentence over the table. The old prophet heard from his sons what had happened at Bethel and went after the man of God. He found him beneath an oak and invited him home. The man told him the precise command that prevented his acceptance (1 Kings 13:11-17). The old prophet therefore knew that his invitation stood against an instruction the guest believed he had received from the Lord. He answered by claiming equal prophetic standing and a newer message from an angel. The account states that he lied (1 Kings 13:18). This was not an innocent misunderstanding between two men. He supplied a false divine authorization for the very act the man had been forbidden to perform.

name: Baasha
text: Walking in the way of Jeroboam after being raised up to destroy Jeroboam's house. Baasha killed Nadab and every soul of the house of Jeroboam, exactly as Ahijah had prophesied. Then he reigned twenty-four years in the same sins, and the same prophecy was spoken over his own house by Jehu the son of Hanani. Baasha conspired against Nadab while Israel besieged Gibbethon, killed him, and took his throne. He destroyed the house of Jeroboam according to Ahijah's word (1 Kings 15:25-30). He saw at close hand what became of a royal house that made Israel sin. Nevertheless he walked in Jeroboam's way throughout his own reign (1 Kings 15:33-34). Removing the family did not remove its worship. The man who profited from another king's fall repeated the offense that had brought the fall about. Through Jehu son of Hanani, the Lord reminded Baasha that he had raised him from the dust and made him prince over Israel. The charge was not merely that Baasha had failed to improve the kingdom, but that he had made the people sin and provoked the Lord by the work of his hands (1 Kings 16:1-2, 7). His authority had become another means of perpetuating the corruption he had inherited. The word also charged him concerning the killing of Jeroboam's house (1 Kings 16:7). The fulfilment of a declared judgment did not make every purpose and act of its human instrument obedient. Baasha could not take the outcome as proof that his own conduct stood beyond examination. The Lord declared that Baasha's house would become like Jeroboam's. Those dying in the city would be eaten by dogs and those in the field by birds (1 Kings 16:3-4). The comparison made his own history a witness against him: he knew the destruction named because he had carried it out upon another house. Baasha himself died and was buried in Tirzah, and Elah succeeded him (1 Kings 16:6). The destruction of the dynasty followed in Elah's days, when Zimri killed the king and cut off the house, its kinsfolk, and its friends (1 Kings 16:8-13). Baasha's personal burial must be distinguished from the sentence upon his succession.

name: Zimri
text: Conspiring against his master Elah as he drank himself drunk; slaying all the house of Baasha. Captain of half the chariots, Zimri killed his king in a steward's house and took the throne. Seven days later the army chose Omri, Tirzah was taken, and Zimri burned the king's house over his own head. His name became a byword: Had Zimri peace, who slew his master? Zimri commanded half of Elah's chariots. While the king drank himself drunk in the house of his steward Arza, Zimri conspired, struck him, and reigned in his stead (1 Kings 16:8-10). Military office gave him access that he turned against his master. He then destroyed Baasha's house, sparing neither kinsfolk nor friends. The overthrow fulfilled the word spoken through Jehu against Baasha and Elah, but Zimri also walked in Jeroboam's sin (1 Kings 16:11-13, 19). His success in removing the old house did not establish a righteous one. The change was in the man holding the palace, not in the kingdom's obedience. Baasha had repeated Jeroboam's course after destroying his descendants; Zimri repeated it after destroying Baasha's. The accumulated examples of judgment did not persuade the next claimant to forsake the sin beneath them. The army encamped against Gibbethon heard that Zimri had conspired and slain the king. It made Omri, captain of the host, king that day. Omri and Israel went up from the camp and besieged Tirzah (1 Kings 16:15-17). Holding the palace did not mean holding the allegiance of the army. When Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the palace, burned the king's house over himself, and died. His reign lasted seven days (1 Kings 16:15, 18). The place seized as the seat of his advancement became the place of his death. The account names his sins and treason, not merely Omri's greater force (1 Kings 16:19-20). Years later Jezebel invoked his name against Jehu: had Zimri peace, who slew his master (2 Kings 9:31)? His short reign remained a warning that the killing of a king did not secure the killer's future. The advantage gained through conspiracy was consumed before it could become an enduring house.

name: Omri
text: Doing worse than all that were before him; walking in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin. After Zimri burned the palace over himself, Israel divided: half followed Tibni and half followed Omri. Omri prevailed, reigned twelve years, bought the hill Samaria, and built the city that became the northern kingdom’s capital. He wrought evil in the eyes of the Lord and did worse than all that were before him. After Zimri’s death the people of Israel divided into two parts: half followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king, and half followed Omri. The people that followed Omri prevailed, Tibni died, and Omri reigned (1 Kings 16:21–22). The throne was gained through civil struggle, and the cost of the division left no visible impression on the rule that followed. Omri reigned twelve years over Israel, six of them in Tirzah. He bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver, built on it, and named the city after the owner of the hill (1 Kings 16:23–24). Samaria became the seat of the northern kingdom and the symbol of its departure from the Lord. Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the Lord and did worse than all that were before him. He walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin, to provoke the Lord God of Israel to anger with their vanities (1 Kings 16:25–26). Each king surpassed his predecessor, yet the standard of comparison was always the original departure: the sin of Jeroboam. Omri slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and Ahab his son reigned in his stead (1 Kings 16:28). His son then exceeded him, as if walking in Jeroboam’s sins were a light thing (1 Kings 16:31). The house Omri built became the house through which Baal worship entered Israel, and the prophet Micah later named the accumulated corruption as the statutes of Omri (Micah 6:16).

name: Ahab
text: Marrying Jezebel; serving Baal; sparing Ben-hadad whom the Lord appointed to destruction. Ahab did more to provoke the Lord than all the kings before him: he married a Zidonian, built Baal a house in Samaria, and made a grove. He spared the king of Syria for a trade deal after the Lord gave him the victory, and sold himself to work wickedness in Naboth's vineyard. Ahab treated walking in Jeroboam's sins as a light thing and added service to Baal. He married Jezebel, built a house and altar for Baal in Samaria, and made a grove, provoking the Lord above the kings before him (1 Kings 16:30-33). The inherited corruption became the foundation for further departure rather than a warning to turn back. During the famine he called Elijah the troubler of Israel. Elijah returned the charge to Ahab and his father's house for forsaking the commandments and following Baalim (1 Kings 18:17-18). The king blamed the bearer of the warning for the distress produced by his own course. Killing the messenger or silencing him could not restore the rain. The Lord afterward delivered the Syrians into his hand, declaring that Israel would know him as the Lord. Ahab received Ben-hadad as a brother and released him under a covenant promising restored cities and trading streets (1 Kings 20:28-34). The prophet answered that Ahab had let go a man appointed to destruction; his life would answer for that life (1 Kings 20:42). A useful agreement did not authorize setting aside the judgment. When Naboth refused his vineyard, Ahab withdrew in displeasure. Jezebel arranged false witnesses and Naboth's death, and Ahab went down to take possession (1 Kings 21:1-16). Elijah met him there and joined the acts in one charge: killing and taking possession. Ahab's benefit from the murder was not separated from its guilt because another person organized it. Elijah pronounced the cutting off of Ahab's house and the consuming of its dead by dogs and birds. Ahab rent his clothes, fasted, wore sackcloth, and went softly. The Lord regarded his humbling and deferred the evil upon his house to his son's days (1 Kings 21:20-29). Mercy was shown within the judgment, without declaring his earlier deeds acceptable. At Ramoth-gilead, Micaiah warned that Israel would be scattered as sheep without a shepherd. Ahab imprisoned him and went to battle in disguise (1 Kings 22:17, 26-30). He sought safety through changing his appearance while refusing to change the course against which the word had spoken. An archer drawing at a venture struck him between the joints of his armour. He died that evening, and dogs licked his blood when the chariot was washed at Samaria (1 Kings 22:34-38). Neither a royal army nor a disguise could keep the sentence from finding him. His house continued for a time, but the king himself did not return in the peace he had demanded from his prophets.

name: Jezebel
text: Killing the prophets of the Lord; promoting Baal; witchcrafts. Ahab's Zidonian queen cut off the prophets of the Lord, fed four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal at her table, swore to kill Elijah, and stirred up her husband to every evil. Jehu named her whoredoms and witchcrafts as the reason there could be no peace. Jezebel used the place she held beside Ahab to sustain false worship and attack the Lord's servants. While she cut off the prophets, Obadiah hid a hundred in caves and fed them with bread and water (1 Kings 18:4). Within the same royal household, one person's resources supported persecution while another's service preserved its intended victims. Elijah summoned the prophets of Baal and the prophets of the groves who ate at Jezebel's table (1 Kings 18:19). Royal provision helped maintain the worship that opposed the Lord. After Carmel, Jezebel answered the report of the prophets' deaths with an oath to kill Elijah (1 Kings 19:1-2). The public judgment did not bring her to submission; it brought a renewed threat against the man who had declared it. Her conduct toward Naboth showed the same use of authority. She wrote in Ahab's name, sealed the letters with his seal, and instructed the elders to proclaim a fast, install false witnesses, and stone an innocent man (1 Kings 21:8-14). Forms belonging to religion and judgment were used to obtain a coveted vineyard. A fast did not sanctify the lie, and the king's seal did not make murder lawful. Revelation 2:20 uses her name for a woman who claims prophetic standing while seducing the servants into fornication and idolatrous eating. The danger is not confined to an open enemy: corrupt teaching seeks a place within the company it turns aside. Elijah declared that dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel (1 Kings 21:23). When Jehu was anointed, the charge against Ahab's house expressly included avenging the blood of the prophets and servants shed at her hand (2 Kings 9:7-10). The victims she had attempted to remove remained named before the Lord. As Jehu entered Jezreel, she looked from a window and challenged him with Zimri's fate. Jehu called for those on his side, and two or three eunuchs looked out. At his command they threw her down (2 Kings 9:30-33). The household from which she had exercised power no longer preserved her against the judgment. When men went to bury her, only the skull, feet, and palms of her hands remained. Jehu recalled Elijah's word concerning the dogs and the loss of an identifiable grave (2 Kings 9:34-37). Her rank as a king's daughter could not restore the body or overturn the sentence. The woman who had ordered others removed from the land could not secure her own remembrance within it.

name: Hiel the Bethelite
text: Rebuilding Jericho under the oath Joshua swore before the Lord. When Jericho fell, Joshua adjured Israel: cursed be the man that riseth up and buildeth this city; he shall lay the foundation in his firstborn and set up the gates in his youngest son. Generations later, in the days of Ahab, Hiel rebuilt it at the cost of Abiram his firstborn and Segub his youngest son. After Jericho fell, Joshua pronounced a curse before the Lord upon the man who would rise to rebuild it: he would lay the foundation in his firstborn and set up the gates in his youngest son (Joshua 6:26). The destroyed city stood under a word that placed a limit upon a future builder's ambition. In Ahab's days Hiel of Bethel rebuilt it (1 Kings 16:34). The account places the undertaking beside Ahab's establishment of Baal worship and his exceeding provocation of the Lord. The kingdom's departure was visible not only at an altar but also in a building work that crossed a boundary spoken generations earlier. The passage of years did not make Joshua's word an empty saying. A man might see walls to be raised and gates to be fitted while overlooking the charge that governed the place. The land could not be measured only by what could be built upon it. Its history included the Lord's judgment as well as the builder's opportunity. Hiel laid the foundation in Abiram his firstborn and set up the gates in Segub his youngest son, according to the word the Lord had spoken by Joshua (1 Kings 16:34). The two ends of the undertaking answered the two parts of the curse. The names of the sons preserve the cost beside the report that the city was built. The judgment was not cancelled by the successful completion of the structure. Gates could stand while the household mourned. Outward accomplishment was therefore no proof that the work had been undertaken with the Lord's approval. Joshua 23:14 declares that not one good thing spoken by the Lord had failed. Hiel's history shows that the word of warning was no less certain. The generation that heard Joshua had passed, but the Lord who spoke through him had not forgotten the boundary. What was old to the builder remained binding before God.

name: Elijah
text: Standing alone against the prophets of Baal, and running before the king in the power of the Lord. Elijah announced the drought to Ahab, received provision at Cherith and Zarephath, and called Israel back to the Lord at Carmel. After Jezebel threatened him, the Lord sustained him in the wilderness and gave him further work, a successor, and assurance that seven thousand had not bowed to Baal. He was later taken up by a whirlwind, and Elisha received his mantle. Elijah stood before Ahab and declared that there would be neither dew nor rain except according to his word. His authority was expressed in the confession that he stood before the Lord God of Israel (1 Kings 17:1). He did not stand before the king to obtain permission to speak. The king himself was beneath the word he brought. The same word that sent him to announce the drought directed his preservation within it. He went to Cherith, where ravens brought bread and flesh and he drank from the brook. When the brook dried, he went to Zarephath as commanded (1 Kings 17:2-9). Obedience did not keep the brook from drying; it kept him ready to follow the next instruction. The Lord's provision was not confined to one place or one means. When he returned to Ahab, he refused the accusation that he troubled Israel. The trouble arose from forsaking the commandments and following Baalim (1 Kings 18:17-18). At Carmel he called the people to cease halting between two opinions. Their silence could not remain an answer when the question was whom they would serve. He repaired the Lord's altar with twelve stones according to the tribes of Israel, laid the sacrifice in order, and had water poured over it three times. His prayer asked that the people know the Lord was God, that he was the Lord's servant, and that he had done these things at his word (1 Kings 18:30-37). The sign was not sought to establish an independent greatness for the prophet. It was sought to turn the people's hearts back.

name: The widow of Zarephath
text: Making the prophet's cake first, out of the last handful of meal. A Gentile widow gathering two sticks to cook a last meal for herself and her son was asked by a stranger to feed him first from it, on a promise from the God of Israel. She did. The barrel of meal did not waste and the cruse of oil did not fail until the rain came, and when her son died the prophet raised him. As the Lord thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die. Elijah said, Fear not; go and do as thou hast said: but make me thereof a little cake first, and bring it unto me, and after make for thee and for thy son. And she went and did according to the saying of Elijah. Christ named her against Nazareth: unto none of the widows of Israel was Elias sent, save unto Sarepta. For thus saith the Lord God of Israel, The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the Lord sendeth rain upon the earth. And she, and he, and her house, did eat many days. When her son fell sick and there was no breath left in him, Elijah stretched himself upon the child three times and cried unto the Lord, and the Lord heard the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived. The woman said, Now by this I know that thou art a man of God, and that the word of the Lord in thy mouth is truth.

name: Obadiah, who hid the prophets
text: Taking a hundred prophets and hiding them by fifty in a cave, and feeding them with bread and water, while serving in Ahab's house. The governor of Ahab's house feared the Lord greatly. When Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord he took a hundred of them, hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water through a famine. Sent out by the king to look for grass, he met Elijah, and was afraid to carry the message that would summon Ahab, in case the Spirit carried the prophet away and he was killed for it. Elijah swore he would shew himself, and he went. Obadiah governed Ahab's house and feared the Lord greatly. When Jezebel cut off the Lord's prophets, he hid a hundred of them, fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water (1 Kings 18:3-4). Service within the royal household did not require him to join its persecution. The fear of the Lord governed what he would do with the position he held. The famine made this sustained care costly. Ahab himself went out seeking grass to preserve horses and mules, dividing the search with Obadiah (1 Kings 18:5-6). While the kingdom struggled to find provision, Obadiah maintained people the queen intended to destroy. His service was measured in lives sheltered and food supplied, not merely in a private refusal to approve her deeds. When Elijah met him and sent him to announce his presence to Ahab, Obadiah named his fear. Ahab had searched kingdoms and nations for the prophet. If Obadiah reported that Elijah was there and the Spirit carried him away before Ahab arrived, the king would kill the messenger (1 Kings 18:7-12). His concern was not imaginary, nor did he conceal it beneath a claim of fearlessness. He reminded Elijah that he had feared the Lord from his youth and had hidden the prophets. Elijah swore that he would show himself to Ahab that day. Obadiah then went to meet the king and told him (1 Kings 18:12-16). He received the assurance and performed the errand. Courage was seen in his obedience with the danger understood. A hundred prophets had been preserved when Jezebel sought to cut them off. Obadiah's provision kept their hiding places from becoming places of starvation. His fear of God bore fruit in the continuing lives of other servants, even while he occupied a post beneath a king who had forsaken the commandments. His message also brought Ahab to Elijah, preparing the meeting from which the summons to Carmel followed (1 Kings 18:16-19). The hidden work of feeding and sheltering was followed by an errand that served a public confrontation. Different duties required the same fidelity. Hebrews 6:10 declares that God does not forget work and labour of love shown in ministering to the saints. Obadiah's account does not conclude with a new title or an estate bestowed upon him. The good already accomplished was substantial: servants were alive, and the required message was delivered. Elijah would later speak of being left alone, but the Lord's work in Israel had never been limited to what one prophet could see (1 Kings 19:10, 18). Obadiah's caves belonged to that larger history of preservation. A man inside Ahab's house had feared the Lord more than he agreed with the house's evil.

name: The prophets of Baal at Carmel
text: Prophesying in the name of other gods. Four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal cried from morning to noon and cut themselves with knives until the blood gushed out, and there was neither voice nor any to answer. Elijah's bullock, drenched three times, was consumed by fire from heaven with the water and the stones. At Carmel Elijah asked Israel how long they would halt between two opinions. If the Lord was God, they were to follow him; if Baal, then Baal. The people answered nothing (1 Kings 18:21). The contest exposed a divided service that could not be made right by refusing to decide. Four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal stood against Elijah. They chose a bullock, dressed it, and called upon Baal from morning until noon. There was no voice and no answer. They leaped upon the altar and, after Elijah challenged them, cried aloud and cut themselves with knives and lancets until the blood flowed (1 Kings 18:22-28). Increasing noise and injury did not give their god power to answer. The law forbade a prophet to speak in the name of other gods (Deuteronomy 18:20). Deuteronomy 13:1-5 also required Israel to reject a teacher who led them after other gods, even if a sign accompanied his words. Here no answer came at all, yet the servants of Baal continued until the time of the evening sacrifice (1 Kings 18:29). Zeal for the practice could not make the practice obedience. Elijah repaired the Lord's altar, drenched the offering, and prayed that the people know the Lord and turn back to him (1 Kings 18:30-37). The difference was not merely between two methods of conducting worship. It was between calling upon the living God according to his word and persisting in a service he had forbidden. The Lord's fire consumed the offering, wood, stones, dust, and water. The people fell upon their faces and confessed that the Lord was God (1 Kings 18:38-39). The answer left the assembly no reason to maintain its earlier silence. What the prophets of Baal could not obtain through hours of crying was accomplished when the Lord answered his servant. Elijah commanded that none of the prophets of Baal escape. They were taken to the brook Kishon and slain (1 Kings 18:40). The sentence belonged to the covenant law against leading Israel into the service of other gods; the crowd's earlier acceptance and the worship's royal standing did not remove that charge. Rain followed after Elijah prayed upon Carmel (1 Kings 18:41-45). The drought had not been ended by Baal's servants, their multitude, their cries, or their wounds. The return of rain confirmed the same distinction as the fire: the Lord who had withheld it was the one who could send it again.

name: Elisha
text: Asking a double portion of the spirit; leaving the oxen and following, and refusing Naaman's reward. Called from ploughing, Elisha fed the people and followed Elijah. He asked a double portion of his spirit and continued the ministry after his master was taken. He supplied households, restored the Shunammite’s son, refused Naaman’s reward, and fed the Syrians delivered into Samaria. After his death, a man revived upon touching his bones. Elisha was ploughing when Elijah cast his mantle upon him. He left the oxen, asked to kiss his father and mother, and returned to prepare a farewell meal. He slew a yoke of oxen, boiled the flesh with their instruments, fed the people, and arose to minister to Elijah (1 Kings 19:19-21). The call was answered by a change of service, not merely an expression of admiration for the prophet. When Elijah's departure approached, Elisha would not leave him at Gilgal, Bethel, or Jericho. He crossed Jordan with him and asked for a double portion of his spirit. Elijah called it a hard thing and gave the condition that Elisha see him taken (2 Kings 2:1-10). The request concerned the power required to continue the work, not wealth or a place at the king's table. After Naaman's cleansing, Elisha refused the gift pressed upon him, swearing by the Lord before whom he stood that he would receive none (2 Kings 5:15-16). Gehazi afterward pursued what his master refused. The same opportunity distinguished service from covetousness. The healing was not to be turned into a private bargain by a servant who had not supplied its power. At Dothan, surrounded by the Syrian host, Elisha answered his servant's fear by praying that his eyes be opened. The mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:15-17). Elisha did not deny the surrounding army; he knew it was not the only host present. He sought that his servant see the protection already there. Elisha saw Elijah taken and received the mantle that fell. Returning to Jordan, he struck the water and called upon the Lord God of Elijah. The waters divided, and the sons of the prophets recognised that Elijah's spirit rested upon him (2 Kings 2:11-15). The departed master was not the source exhausted by his departure. The Lord remained with the servant appointed to continue. His ministry supplied households and preserved life: the widow's oil paid her debt, the Shunammite received her son alive, harmful pottage was made safe, and a hundred men ate from twenty barley loaves and left food remaining (2 Kings 4:1-7, 32-44). The wonders were not detached displays. They answered debt, bereavement, hunger, and danger among the people. When the Syrians sent to seize him were led into Samaria, the king asked whether to kill them. Elisha commanded that food and water be set before them and that they return to their master. They ate and departed (2 Kings 6:18-23). Power to deliver an enemy into the city did not require that power to be used for slaughter. The prophet who announced judgments also directed mercy where the Lord had given that charge. Elisha eventually became sick and died, but the Lord's power was not buried with him. A dead man cast into his sepulchre touched his bones, revived, and stood upon his feet (2 Kings 13:20-21). Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 48:12-14 remembers both the wonders of his life and the marvel after his death. His strength had never resided in possessions gathered from those he helped, but in the Lord whose word he served.

name: Ben-hadad and the Syrians at Aphek
text: Saying the Lord is a god of the hills and not of the valleys. Beaten at Samaria, the Syrians told their king the God of Israel was a hill god and would lose on level ground. The Lord heard it. A prophet told Ahab the outcome before the battle: that ye may know that I am the Lord. After defeat before Samaria, the Syrian servants attributed Israel's strength to the hills. They proposed replacing the kings with captains and fighting on the plain, where they supposed Israel's God could not give the same victory (1 Kings 20:23-25). They changed the ground without changing the presumption beneath the war. Ben-hadad gathered another host at Aphek. Israel appeared like two little flocks while the Syrians filled the country (1 Kings 20:26-27). The visible imbalance encouraged confidence in numbers, but the Lord's answer addressed the claim about his power. He would deliver the multitude so Israel would know that he was the Lord (1 Kings 20:28). Neither terrain nor a larger army marked the limit of his dominion. After seven days facing one another, Israel struck a hundred thousand Syrian footmen in one day. The survivors fled into Aphek, where a wall fell upon twenty-seven thousand; Ben-hadad hid in an inner chamber (1 Kings 20:29-30). The place chosen to reverse the first defeat became the place of a greater overthrow. Ahab afterward received Ben-hadad and released him under a covenant. That release was charged against Ahab: he had let go a man appointed to destruction (1 Kings 20:31-42). The Syrian king's escape did not prove his claim about the Lord or make the agreement righteous. Victory given to Israel still required obedience from Israel's king.

name: The man who refused the prophetic command
text: Refusing a command delivered in the word of the Lord. A man of the sons of the prophets asked his neighbour to strike him in the word of the Lord. The neighbour refused. The prophet announced that a lion would kill him, and the stated judgment followed. A son of the prophets commanded his neighbour, in the word of the Lord, to smite him. The man refused (1 Kings 20:35). The command belonged to the prophetic action by which Ahab would be confronted, and the prophet expressly identified the refusal as not obeying the Lord's voice (1 Kings 20:36). The act must be understood within that commission. The prophet needed to appear wounded before the king and present the case of a prisoner allowed to escape. The neighbour was asked to participate in a particular sign, not to decide whether the message against Ahab should proceed. His refusal did not cancel the work the Lord had appointed.

name: Jezebel and Naboth's vineyard
text: Judicial murder to seize an inheritance. Ahab coveted Naboth's vineyard; Naboth would not sell his fathers' inheritance. Jezebel arranged false witnesses to accuse him of blaspheming God and the king, had him stoned, and handed the land to Ahab. Naboth refused to sell or exchange his vineyard because it was the inheritance of his fathers (1 Kings 21:1-3). Ahab's desire for a garden did not extinguish the obligation by which Naboth held the land. The king withdrew in displeasure, and Jezebel promised to obtain what he had been refused. She wrote in Ahab's name, sealed the letters with his seal, and ordered a fast, an accusation by two false witnesses, and Naboth's execution (1 Kings 21:8-14). The elders obeyed. The outward form of judgment was made to serve a conclusion already chosen. Exodus 23:7 forbids slaying the innocent and righteous; the number of witnesses could not cleanse testimony known to be false. Ahab went down to take possession, and Elijah met him there with the question joining the crimes: had he killed and also taken possession (1 Kings 21:16-19)? The benefit of the murder stood beside the murder itself. Jezebel's management of the plot did not remove the king's responsibility for receiving its fruit. The Lord pronounced judgment upon Ahab, Jezebel, and their house. Ahab's humbling delayed the destruction of his house, but did not restore Naboth or approve the seizure (1 Kings 21:20-29). Later Joram's body was cast into Naboth's portion, and Jehu recalled the blood of Naboth and his sons (2 Kings 9:25-26). The stolen inheritance remained a witness against the royal house.

name: Micaiah the son of Imlah
text: What the Lord saith unto me, that will I speak; against four hundred prophets and two kings. Two kings sat in their robes at the gate of Samaria and four hundred prophets told them to go up and prosper. Jehoshaphat asked whether there was not one more. There was one, whom Ahab hated because he never prophesied good. The messenger who fetched him coached him to agree. He said he would speak what the Lord said, told them the truth, was struck on the face and sent to prison on bread and water until the king came back in peace. The king did not come back. Four hundred prophets encouraged the expedition to Ramoth-gilead, and the messenger sent for Micaiah urged him to agree. His answer was settled before he entered the court: what the Lord said, he would speak (1 Kings 22:6, 13-14). Agreement with a multitude was not his commission. Before the enthroned kings he declared that Israel would be scattered like sheep without a shepherd. He also disclosed the vision of the lying spirit sent to persuade Ahab through his prophets (1 Kings 22:17-23). The warning reached the king before the battle. Ahab was not left without testimony against the pleasant answer he preferred.

name: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah, and the four hundred prophets
text: Prophesying victory at Ramoth-gilead by a lying spirit; smiting Micaiah on the cheek. Four hundred prophets told Ahab to go up and prosper. One, Micaiah, saw the Lord on his throne and a lying spirit sent into the mouths of the rest. Zedekiah struck him for it and asked which way the Spirit had gone. The battle answered for Ahab; scripture leaves Zedekiah hiding in an inner chamber. Zedekiah made horns of iron and announced, in the Lord's name, that Ahab would push the Syrians until he consumed them. The other prophets agreed (1 Kings 22:11-12). The visible sign and united approval presented certainty without establishing that the Lord had sent the word. When Micaiah exposed the contrary purpose, Zedekiah struck him and demanded how the Spirit had passed from himself to Micaiah (1 Kings 22:24). He treated his own standing as proof against correction. The blow defended a claim of authority; it supplied no answer to the prophecy. Micaiah told him he would see when he went into an inner chamber to hide (1 Kings 22:25). The confidence displayed before the kings was set against an approaching need for concealment. Ahab died at Ramoth-gilead rather than consuming the Syrians as promised. Deuteronomy 18:22 identifies the unfulfilled word as one the Lord has not spoken. The failure of Zedekiah's promise exposed his presumption, although no subsequent account of his personal punishment is given. Iron horns, agreement, and violence could not make a false assurance stand against the Lord's judgment.

name: Ahaziah of Israel
text: Inquiring of Baal-zebub the god of Ekron. Ahab's son fell through a lattice in Samaria and sent messengers to ask Baal-zebub whether he would recover. Elijah met them on the road: is it not because there is not a God in Israel that ye go to inquire of Baal-zebub? Two captains of fifty sent to arrest the prophet were consumed by fire. After falling through a lattice and becoming sick, Ahaziah sent to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron. Elijah intercepted the messengers with the question whether there was no God in Israel that the king sought this answer elsewhere (2 Kings 1:2-4). The inquiry exposed whom he trusted when his own life became uncertain. Recognising Elijah from the messengers' description, Ahaziah sent soldiers to summon him. Two captains addressed the man of God with the king's demand, and fire consumed their companies (2 Kings 1:9-12). Royal force did not give the king command over the word already pronounced against him. The third captain knelt and pleaded that his life and his men's lives be precious. The angel told Elijah to go with him and not fear (2 Kings 1:13-15). The change from command to humble petition distinguished this company from those before it. Before Ahaziah, Elijah repeated the sentence: because he had sent to Ekron, he would not come down from his bed but would die. He died according to the word, and Jehoram succeeded him because he had no son (2 Kings 1:16-17). Bringing the prophet before the throne had not brought the judgment under the throne's control.

name: The young mockers of Bethel
text: Mocking the prophet of the Lord. As Elisha went up to Bethel, the seat of Jeroboam's calf, a company came out of the city mocking him: go up, thou bald head. He cursed them in the name of the Lord, and two she-bears came out of the wood and tore forty-two of them. As Elisha went toward Bethel, a group came out of the city and mocked him, repeatedly calling him bald and telling him to go up (2 Kings 2:23). Their common voice turned the prophet's passage into an occasion of public contempt. The encounter follows the recognition that Elijah's spirit rested upon Elisha and the healing of Jericho's waters (2 Kings 2:15, 19-22). One community brought its need before the man of God; these mockers met him with derision. The difference lay not in the prophet's appearance, but in how his presence was received. Elisha turned, looked upon them, and cursed them in the name of the Lord. Two she-bears came from the wood and tore forty-two of the group (2 Kings 2:24). The sentence interrupted the mockery with a calamity far beyond what the speakers had reckoned upon. Leviticus 26:21-22 warns Israel of wild beasts among the judgments of resisting the Lord. At Bethel, the injury is recorded plainly without a count of deaths. Elisha continued to Carmel and Samaria (2 Kings 2:25). The company that presumed to dismiss him could not prevent his ministry from going forward, and its contempt did not remain without consequence.

name: The prophet's widow, and the pot of oil
text: Borrowing not a few vessels, as the prophet said, and shutting the door. A widow of the sons of the prophets had a creditor coming to take her two sons for bondmen and one pot of oil in the house. Elisha told her to borrow empty vessels, not a few, shut the door, and pour. The oil stopped when the vessels did. She paid the debt and lived on the rest. A widow appealed to Elisha because her creditor was coming to take her two sons as bondmen. Her husband had feared the Lord, but his death had left an obligation her household could not meet. She possessed only a pot of oil (2 Kings 4:1-2). The need was both immediate and practical: the debt threatened the family that remained. Elisha told her to borrow empty vessels from her neighbours, not a few, and shut the door upon herself and her sons. She was to pour into the vessels and set aside those filled (2 Kings 4:3-4). Her preparation answered the word before the supply had multiplied. The sons whose removal she feared now helped bring the vessels to her. She poured until every available vessel was full. When her son said there was no vessel more, the oil stayed (2 Kings 4:5-6). The account connects the extent of the filling with the vessels brought, without making the widow's poverty a limit upon the Lord's provision. Elisha directed her to sell the oil, pay the debt, and live with her children upon the rest (2 Kings 4:7). Deliverance did not mean pretending the debt had never existed. It supplied the means to discharge it and sustain the household afterward. The blessing reached the creditor's claim and the family's continuing need together, preserving the sons without exchanging one unresolved burden for another.

name: The Shunammite woman
text: Constraining the man of God to eat bread; building him a little chamber on the wall, with a bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick. A great woman of Shunem noticed that a holy man of God passed by continually and made him a room. She asked nothing. She was given a son; when he died on her knees she laid him on the prophet's bed, saddled the ass, and said, It is well. He was raised. Years later, back from a famine, she got her whole house and land restored by the king in one morning. She said unto her husband, Behold now, I perceive that this is an holy man of God, which passeth by us continually. Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick. Asked what could be done for her, she answered, I dwell among mine own people. When the child was dead she said to her husband and to Gehazi, It is well, and did not stop until she caught the prophet by the feet. About this season, according to the time of life, thou shalt embrace a son. And the woman conceived, and bare a son at that season. The child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes; and Elisha said, Take up thy son. Then she went in, and fell at his feet, and bowed herself to the ground, and took up her son. After seven years' famine she came to cry to the king for her house and land at the very moment Gehazi was telling him how Elisha had restored a dead body to life; and the king appointed an officer: Restore all that was hers, and all the fruits of the field since the day that she left the land, even until now.

name: Naaman the Syrian
text: Going down and dipping himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God, after his anger. Captain of the host of Syria, a mighty man of valour, and a leper. He came with horses and chariots and a letter from his king, and was sent to wash in Jordan by a messenger who did not come to the door. He went away in a rage, was talked round by his servants, obeyed, and came up with the flesh of a little child. He went home with two mules' burden of earth and a vow to sacrifice to no other god. Naaman had rank, victories, and honour, but he was a leper. The witness that directed him toward help came from a captive maid serving his wife (2 Kings 5:1-4). A great commander had to receive useful counsel from one with little power in his house. He arrived with wealth and a royal letter, but the king of Israel could not heal him. Elisha sent a messenger requiring him to wash seven times in Jordan. Naaman became angry because he expected the prophet to appear and perform the healing in the manner he had imagined (2 Kings 5:5-12). His objection was not that the command was impossible, but that it did not honour his expectation. His servants reasoned that he would have attempted a great thing if commanded; how much more should he wash and be clean. He hearkened and dipped seven times according to the word (2 Kings 5:13-14). Humility made room for the obedience his first anger had refused. His flesh became like a child's, and he returned with his company confessing that there was no God in all the earth but in Israel (2 Kings 5:14-15). Cleansing was followed by an acknowledgment beyond the cure itself. Elisha refused payment. Naaman declared that he would no longer offer sacrifice to other gods and asked pardon concerning his attendance upon his master in Rimmon's house (2 Kings 5:16-19). The exchange turned from purchasing a remedy to ordering future worship. Christ later named Naaman when warning hearers who would not receive a prophet among their own people (Luke 4:27). The man who first resisted a simple command became a witness to what followed when he finally obeyed it.

name: Gehazi
text: Greed and lying to a prophet. Elisha refused payment from the healed Syrian Naaman. His servant Gehazi ran after Naaman, invented a story to collect silver and garments, then lied to Elisha's face about where he had been. Elisha refused Naaman's gift after his cleansing, but Gehazi resolved to run after the departing company and take something. He claimed that his master had sent him because two young men of the prophets had arrived in need (2 Kings 5:20-22). Covetousness borrowed both Elisha's authority and the appearance of care for others. Naaman gave silver and garments, and Gehazi concealed the goods before returning to his master. Asked where he had been, he said he had gone nowhere (2 Kings 5:23-25). One lie acquired the property; another attempted to preserve it. His nearness to prophetic service had not kept his heart from trading upon its reputation. Elisha disclosed his knowledge of the encounter and asked whether this was a time to receive money, garments, and the possessions they could purchase (2 Kings 5:26). The question returned Gehazi to the discernment expressed in the refusal he had disregarded. Naaman's leprosy was pronounced upon Gehazi and his seed, and he went out a leper (2 Kings 5:27). The servant had pursued the healed man's wealth and received the affliction from which that man had been delivered. Hidden goods could not conceal a deed known to the Lord, and an appeal to his master's name could not make private gain faithful ministry.

name: The lord on whose hand the king leaned
text: Scoffing at the word of the Lord by Elisha in the famine of Samaria. In a siege so hard that women ate their children, Elisha said that by the next day fine flour would sell for a shekel in the gate. The king's officer answered that it could not happen if the Lord opened windows in heaven. He saw it, and was trampled in the gate by the crowd rushing to buy. Samaria's famine had reached extremity when Elisha declared that flour and barley would be sold cheaply at the gate the next day. The officer upon whose hand the king leaned answered by asking whether such a thing could happen even if the Lord made windows in heaven (2 Kings 7:1-2). Present scarcity became his measure of what the Lord could provide. The promise did not require him to explain the means before believing the word. His answer treated the announcement as impossible at the moment it was expressly given in the Lord's name. A trusted position beside the king did not supply understanding of a deliverance neither man had arranged. Elisha told him that he would see the abundance but not eat it. The Lord caused the Syrians to hear a host approaching, and they fled, leaving their provisions behind. Four leprous men discovered the empty camp and reported it (2 Kings 7:3-11). Relief came through a means the officer had not included in his objection. The people spoiled the camp, and the prices fell as announced. Appointed to oversee the gate, the officer was trampled there and died (2 Kings 7:16-20). The place where the promised provision became publicly available was the place where his exclusion was fulfilled. He witnessed the answer his unbelief had dismissed, but did not share its food.

name: Hazael king of Syria
text: Smothering his master to take the throne, and doing to Israel the evil Elisha wept over. Elisha looked at Hazael and wept, and told him why: he knew the evil he would do to the children of Israel. Hazael said, Is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing? He went home, lied to his master about the prophet's word, and smothered him with a wet cloth the next morning. Ben-hadad sent Hazael to ask Elisha whether he would recover. Elisha spoke of recovery yet disclosed that the Lord had shown him the king would surely die. He then wept over the violence Hazael would bring upon Israel (2 Kings 8:7-12). Knowledge of an approaching reign did not turn its cruelties into good deeds. Hazael returned with the assurance of recovery but withheld the disclosure of death. The next day he spread a water-soaked cloth over the king's face, killed him, and reigned in his place (2 Kings 8:14-15). The messenger's access to a sick master became the means of taking his throne. Hazael afterward struck Israel and reduced its territory (2 Kings 10:32-33). The Lord used Syrian power in chastening Israel, but that use did not place Syria beyond judgment for its violence. Elisha's tears had already distinguished the coming suffering from something to celebrate. Amos charged Damascus with threshing Gilead with iron instruments and pronounced fire upon the house of Hazael and the palaces of Ben-hadad, with Syria carried to Kir (Amos 1:3-5). The house that made others suffer was itself named for overthrow. Being an instrument in another people's punishment did not give its ruler ownership of their lives or immunity from the Lord's reckoning.

name: Jehu
text: Executing the house of Ahab, then keeping the calves of Jeroboam. Anointed to cut off the house of Ahab, Jehu killed Joram, Ahaziah, Jezebel, seventy sons of Ahab, and every worshipper of Baal in Samaria, and destroyed Baal out of Israel. But from the golden calves at Bethel and Dan Jehu departed not. Jehu executed the judgment against Ahab's house and destroyed Baal's worship in Israel. Yet he did not depart from Jeroboam's calves at Bethel and Dan (2 Kings 10:28-29). His zeal removed one established evil while leaving another standing. He invited Jehonadab to see his zeal, but the final measure was whether he took heed to walk in the law with all his heart (2 Kings 10:16, 31). A public work of judgment was not a substitute for continuing obedience. The destruction of a rival house did not release the new king from the same commandments. The Lord acknowledged what Jehu had done rightly against Ahab and promised that his sons would sit upon Israel's throne to the fourth generation (2 Kings 10:30). The record preserves that reward beside the charge against the calves. Approval of one deed was not blanket approval of the reign. In those days Hazael began cutting Israel short. Jehu's line continued as promised, ending with Zechariah, who was murdered after six months (2 Kings 15:8-12). Hosea also pronounced the visiting of Jezreel's blood upon Jehu's house (Hosea 1:4). The dynasty's promised duration and its eventual reckoning stand together: a commission carried out did not make the house permanent or its bloodshed beyond examination.

name: Athaliah
text: Destroying the seed royal of Judah; usurping the throne. Ahab's daughter, married into Judah's line, saw her son Ahaziah dead at Jehu's hand and murdered all the seed royal to reign herself. One infant, Joash, was hidden in the house of the Lord for six years. In the seventh, Jehoiada the priest brought him out. When Ahaziah died, Athaliah rose against the royal seed and seized the kingdom. Jehosheba rescued Joash and hid him with his nurse, preserving a child from the destruction (2 Kings 11:1-3). Athaliah's possession of the throne rested upon violence against the house she should have protected. Her reign also belonged to the corruption of worship. Her sons had broken up God's house and devoted its things to Baalim (2 Chronicles 24:7). The seizure of the kingdom and misuse of holy possessions joined the same disregard for what had been entrusted to the royal house. In the seventh year Jehoiada revealed the king's son, arranged his protection, and crowned him with the testimony. Athaliah heard the rejoicing and cried treason when she saw him standing in his place (2 Kings 11:4-14). The cry came from the ruler whose own position had been obtained by destroying the succession. Jehoiada ordered her taken outside rather than killed within the Lord's house. She was slain by the way leading to the king's house, and the people broke down Baal's house (2 Kings 11:15-18). The covenant was renewed, the people rejoiced, and the city was quiet. The hidden child outlasted the reign that had sought to erase him.

name: Jeroboam the son of Joash
text: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord; not departing from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat. Jeroboam the son of Joash reigned forty-one years over Israel and restored the coast from Hamath to the sea of the plain, as the Lord had spoken by Jonah the prophet. The Lord saw that Israel’s affliction was bitter and saved them by his hand, yet Jeroboam did evil and departed not from Jeroboam’s sins. Jeroboam the son of Joash began to reign in the fifteenth year of Amaziah and reigned forty-one years in Samaria. He did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord: he departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin (2 Kings 14:23–24). The longest reign of any northern king carried no reform with it. He restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, according to the word of the Lord spoken by the hand of his servant Jonah the son of Amittai (2 Kings 14:25). The restoration was accomplished through him, yet it was the Lord’s doing, because the Lord saw the affliction of Israel, that it was very bitter: there was not any shut up, nor any left, nor any helper for Israel (2 Kings 14:26). The Lord said not that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven but saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash (2 Kings 14:27). The deliverance was not because of Jeroboam’s righteousness but because of the Lord’s mercy toward His afflicted people. Jeroboam slept with his fathers, and Zechariah his son reigned in his stead (2 Kings 14:29). The prosperity of his reign did not secure his house: Zechariah was slain after six months, fulfilling the word that Jehu’s house would sit on the throne unto the fourth generation (2 Kings 15:12). The kingdom was saved through an evil king and then taken from his descendants according to a limit already spoken.

name: Hosea the prophet
text: Obeying the Lord’s command to take a wife of whoredoms as a sign; prophesying Israel’s scattering and restoration. The word of the Lord came to Hosea in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, and of Jeroboam the son of Joash. He was commanded to marry Gomer, a wife of whoredoms, as a living sign of how Israel committed spiritual fornication against the Lord. Three children bore prophetic names—Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah, Lo-ammi—yet the promise followed: the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea. The Lord told Hosea to go take a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms, for the land had committed great whoredom, departing from the Lord. So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim (Hosea 1:2–3). The prophet’s own household became the picture of the nation’s unfaithfulness.
