Three children were born, each named by the Lord’s word. Jezreel: the Lord would avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu and cause to cease the kingdom of Israel (Hosea 1:4). Lo-ruhamah: the Lord would no more have mercy upon the house of Israel but utterly take them away (Hosea 1:6). Lo-ammi: ye are not my people and I will not be your God (Hosea 1:9). The names declared scattering, the withdrawal of mercy, and the severing of the covenant. Yet the promise followed: the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered, and in the place where it was said, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said, Ye are the sons of the living God (Hosea 1:10). They would be gathered under one head (Hosea 1:11). The Lord commanded Hosea again to love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the Lord toward the children of Israel. He bought her for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley and told her to abide many days (Hosea 3:1–3). For the children of Israel shall abide many days without a king, without a prince, without a sacrifice, without an image, without an ephod, and without teraphim. Afterward shall the children of Israel return and seek the Lord their God, and David their king, and shall fear the Lord and his goodness in the latter days (Hosea 3:4–5). The long dispersion would end in a return.

name: Menahem king of Israel
text: Ripping up the women with child at Tiphsah, and buying Assyria with money exacted from Israel. Menahem came up from Tirzah, killed Shallum, and took the throne. When Tiphsah would not open to him he smote it and ripped up all the women therein that were with child. He then paid Pul a thousand talents of silver, exacted from the wealthy of Israel, to confirm the kingdom in his hand — and died in his bed. Menahem struck Tiphsah because it would not open to him and ripped up its pregnant women (2 Kings 15:16). The refusal of entry became an occasion for cruelty against those least able to resist. His rise did not bring a departure from Jeroboam's sins; he continued in them throughout his reign (2 Kings 15:17-18). When Pul of Assyria came, Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver to confirm the kingdom in his hand. He exacted the money from Israel's wealthy men (2 Kings 15:19-20). The people paid for the foreign support by which their ruler sought to secure his own position. Assyria withdrew, and Menahem died after a ten-year reign, with Pekahiah succeeding him (2 Kings 15:20-22). No separate personal penalty is recorded against him. The successful payment must not be mistaken for a judgment declaring his cruelty righteous. His son's reign lasted two years before Pekah killed him. Further Assyrian conquest and deportation followed in Pekah's days (2 Kings 15:23-29). The support purchased for Menahem did not establish lasting security for the house or nation. He had obtained time on the throne without addressing the sin that left Israel exposed to further overthrow.

name: Hoshea, last king of Israel
text: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord; conspiring with Egypt against Assyria. Hoshea the son of Elah, last king of the northern kingdom, did evil though not as the kings before him. He became tributary to Assyria, then conspired with So king of Egypt and withheld tribute. Shalmaneser shut him in prison, besieged Samaria three years, and carried Israel away to Assyria. Hoshea the son of Elah began to reign in the twelfth year of Ahaz and reigned nine years in Samaria. He did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, but not as the kings of Israel that were before him (2 Kings 17:1–2). The qualification does not excuse his reign; it measures how far the standard had fallen when the best that could be said of a king was that he was less evil than his predecessors. Shalmaneser king of Assyria came against him, and Hoshea became his servant and paid tribute. But the king of Assyria found conspiracy in Hoshea, for he had sent messengers to So king of Egypt and brought no present as he had done year by year (2 Kings 17:3–4). Instead of turning to the Lord, Hoshea turned to Egypt, the very nation from which the Lord had brought Israel out. The king of Assyria shut Hoshea up and bound him in prison. He came up throughout all the land and besieged Samaria three years. In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria took Samaria and carried Israel away, placing them in Halah, in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:4–6). The northern kingdom ceased to exist. The Lord removed Israel out of His sight, as He had said by all His servants the prophets (2 Kings 17:23). Every warning through every prophet sent to the northern kingdom was fulfilled in a single removal. The accumulated sin from Jeroboam through Hoshea was answered in captivity, and the tribes were scattered among the nations.

name: The captivity of Israel (the northern kingdom)
text: Two centuries of the sins of Jeroboam; secret sins; idols, high places, and children through the fire. Second Kings 17 is the indictment of a nation: they feared other gods, walked in the statutes of the heathen and of the kings of Israel, built high places in every city, served idols the Lord had said they should not, made their sons and daughters pass through the fire, used divination and enchantments, and sold themselves to do evil. Hoshea's conspiracy and withheld tribute occasioned Assyria's siege, but the account gives a deeper cause for Israel's removal: they sinned against the Lord who brought them out of Egypt and feared other gods (2 Kings 17:3-8). Political events carried a judgment rooted in the covenant they had forsaken. The Lord repeatedly sent prophets and seers to call them back to his statutes. They refused, hardened their necks, followed vanity, and continued the calves, Baal worship, divination, and the burning of their children (2 Kings 17:13-17). Repetition of warning was evidence of mercy; repetition of refusal made the guilt no less deliberate. Samaria fell after a three-year siege. Israel was carried to Halah, Habor, and the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:5-6). The land from which their fathers had driven other worships no longer protected them while they practised those same departures. Assyria brought other peoples to dwell in the cities. Their mixture of reverence for the Lord and service to their own images did not fulfil the command to serve him alone (2 Kings 17:24-41). The account also warns that Judah had failed to keep the commandments (2 Kings 17:19). The northern kingdom's fall was not permission for the southern kingdom to presume upon its own continued place.

name: Hezekiah
text: Trusting in the Lord God of Israel; cleaving to him and keeping his commandments; breaking the brasen serpent; keeping the passover; spreading Sennacherib's letter before the Lord. He opened the doors of the house of the Lord in the first month of his first year, kept a passover Jerusalem had not seen since Solomon, broke the brasen serpent of Moses because Israel burned incense to it, and prayed his way through Sennacherib and through a sentence of death. The one pride of his heart is its own case. This is the rest. Hezekiah opened and repaired the temple doors in his first year, gathered the priests and Levites, and required them to sanctify themselves and remove the uncleanness left by earlier rulers (2 Chronicles 29:3-11). Reform began with restoring the service that had been neglected, not merely with denouncing the past. He also broke the brazen serpent because Israel burned incense to it (2 Kings 18:4). An object associated with Moses could not be preserved as an idol on account of its history. Faithfulness distinguished the Lord's former use of a thing from the people's present misuse of it. He invited Israel to Passover, provided for priestly service, and arranged faithful distribution of the people's offerings (2 Chronicles 30:1-5; 31:11-21). Prayer accompanied that order: when some ate without the required cleansing, he besought pardon for those who prepared their hearts to seek God, and the Lord heard (2 Chronicles 30:18-20).

name: Shebna the treasurer
text: Hewing himself a sepulchre on high; a shame to his lord's house. Over the house of the king in Hezekiah's day, Shebna cut himself a tomb in the rock as if Jerusalem were his to be buried in on high. Isaiah was sent to him with a sentence: the Lord would toss him like a ball into a large country and give his office to Eliakim. Shebna, who was over the house, prepared himself a sepulchre on high. Isaiah challenged what right he had to establish that memorial there (Isaiah 22:15-16). The officer entrusted with a household's affairs had directed his concern toward the permanence of his own name. The surrounding prophecy describes a city attending to walls and water while failing to look to its Maker (Isaiah 22:9-11). Shebna's monument belonged to that misplaced confidence. A carved habitation in the rock could not secure the future of the man who built it.

name: Sennacherib and Rabshakeh
text: Reproaching the living God; setting him among the gods of the nations that could not save. Rabshakeh stood by the conduit of the upper pool and told Jerusalem in the Jews' language that no god of any nation had ever delivered a land from the king of Assyria. Hezekiah spread the letter before the Lord. That night an angel slew a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib went home to be murdered by his sons in the house of his god. Rabshakeh addressed Jerusalem's people in their own language to shake their confidence. He promised provision if they surrendered and compared the Lord with the gods of cities Assyria had already taken (2 Kings 18:28-35). Past victories were used as evidence that no power could now deliver Judah. Sennacherib's letters repeated the railing. The offense was not merely confidence in his army, but the claim that the God of Israel could be measured by defeated idols (2 Chronicles 32:17-19). Assyria's strength was real; the conclusion drawn from it was false. Hezekiah brought the letter before the Lord. Through Isaiah the answer identified the one they had reproached: the Holy One of Israel. The Lord knew Sennacherib's rage and would turn him back by the way he came (2 Kings 19:14-28). An angel struck a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib returned to Nineveh and was later killed by his sons while worshipping in the house of Nisroch (2 Kings 19:35-37). The commander who said no god could save Jerusalem could not be preserved in his own god's house. His return and death answered the word; Jerusalem's deliverance did not depend upon matching the host he had displayed.

name: Hezekiah and the ambassadors of Babylon
text: Showing all his treasures to Babylon in the pride of his heart. Healed of a mortal sickness and given fifteen years, Hezekiah received envoys from Babylon and showed them the house of his precious things, the silver, the gold, the armor, everything. Isaiah asked what they had seen. Nothing hidden, said the king. After receiving healing and a sign, Hezekiah did not render according to the benefit done to him, because his heart was lifted up (2 Chronicles 32:24-25). Mercy received became an occasion for self-regard instead of gratitude. The Babylonian envoys came with letters and a present, and he showed them his treasures, armour, and all that was in his dominion (2 Kings 20:12-15). Chronicles says that God left him to try him and disclose what was in his heart (2 Chronicles 32:31). The trial came through honour and interest, not only through an enemy's threat. The king who had sought the Lord under siege also had to remember him amid admiration. Isaiah declared that the treasures would be carried to Babylon and that descendants of the king would serve in its palace (2 Kings 20:16-18). What he displayed as the strength of his house was named as another kingdom's future spoil. Hezekiah and Jerusalem humbled themselves, and the wrath did not come in his days (2 Chronicles 32:26). The delay was mercy within the sentence. The lesson reached beyond whether the king could survive an immediate danger: the blessings entrusted to him required humility after the danger had passed, and the future of his house could not be measured only by peace during his own remaining years.

name: Isaiah
text: Answering the Lord’s call; prophesying judgment and redemption through persecution and rejection. In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up upon a throne, with seraphim crying Holy, holy, holy. His unclean lips were cleansed with a coal from the altar, and he answered, Here am I; send me. He walked naked and barefoot three years as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia, counseled Hezekiah against Sennacherib, and prophesied the angel that smote 185,000 Assyrians in one night. In the year that King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple. Above it stood the seraphims, each with six wings, crying one to another, Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory. The posts of the door moved at the voice, and the house was filled with smoke (Isaiah 6:1–4). Isaiah cried, Woe is me, for I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips, for mine eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts. A seraphim flew with a live coal from the altar and laid it upon his mouth, saying his iniquity was taken away and his sin purged (Isaiah 6:5–7). He heard the voice of the Lord saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? And he answered, Here am I; send me (Isaiah 6:8). He was sent to a people whose hearts were made fat, whose ears were heavy, whose eyes were shut, lest they see, hear, understand, convert, and be healed. The blindness was decreed until the cities be wasted and the land utterly desolate (Isaiah 6:9–11). At the Lord’s command, Isaiah walked naked and barefoot three years as a sign and wonder upon Egypt and Ethiopia, that the king of Assyria would lead them away captive, young and old, naked and barefoot, to the shame of Egypt (Isaiah 20:2–4). The prophet’s body became the sign, and the sign endured for three years.

name: Manasseh
text: Rebuilding the high places; altars to the host of heaven in the temple; passing his sons through the fire; witchcraft; filling Jerusalem with innocent blood. Hezekiah's son undid everything his father had done and more: altars for Baal, a grove, worship of all the host of heaven in both courts of the Lord's house, his children through the fire, observing times, enchantments, familiar spirits, wizards. He shed innocent blood until Jerusalem was filled from one end to another. Manasseh rebuilt the high places Hezekiah had removed, established idolatrous altars even in the Lord's house, practised forbidden divination, and caused his children to pass through the fire (2 Chronicles 33:1-7). He reversed a reform whose work was visible before him. He also shed innocent blood until Jerusalem was filled from end to end, and led Judah into greater evil than the nations expelled before Israel (2 Kings 21:9, 16). The Lord spoke to him and his people, but they would not hear (2 Chronicles 33:10). Authority amplified his departure by making it the nation's course.

name: Amon
text: Serving his father's idols and refusing his father's repentance. Manasseh's son reigned two years, sacrificed to all the carved images his father had made, and humbled not himself before the Lord as Manasseh had humbled himself, but trespassed more and more. Amon served the images Manasseh had made and forsook the Lord. Chronicles expressly contrasts him with his father: he did not humble himself, but trespassed more and more (2 Chronicles 33:21-23). Within one preceding reign he could see both apostasy and repentance; he continued the former. His succession supplied an office, not the character required to govern it. The Lord's mercy toward Manasseh was no promise that a son might repeat the sin while refusing the humbling. The history he inherited should have instructed him concerning both judgment and return. After two years his servants conspired and killed him in his own house. The people then killed the conspirators and made Josiah king (2 Chronicles 33:24-25). Amon's evil did not make the assassins immune from judgment for their own deed. The short reign ended without the repentance recorded of his father. The throne passed to a child who would seek the Lord while young. The contrast was not settled by age or proximity to power, but by whether the ruler prepared his heart to receive instruction and turn from evil.

name: Josiah
text: A tender heart at the reading of the book; turning to the Lord with all his heart, soul, and might, according to all the law of Moses. Eight years old when crowned, sixteen when he began to seek the God of David, twenty when he began to purge Judah, twenty-six when the book of the law was found in the house and read to him. He rent his clothes, gathered the people, read it to them himself, and kept a passover like none since Samuel. He was promised he would be gathered to his grave in peace before the evil came. His death at Megiddo is its own case. Josiah began seeking the God of David while young, and his purge of idolatry began before the book of the law was found during the temple repairs (2 Chronicles 34:3-8). The discovery deepened an existing course of reform. It did not find him indifferent to the Lord until that day. When the book was read, he rent his clothes and sent to inquire because the fathers had not kept its words. Huldah answered concerning both the coming national judgment and his tender heart (2 Kings 22:11-20). He received the charge as something demanding a response, not an ancient record to be admired without obedience. He gathered the people, read the covenant, and bound himself to keep it with heart and soul. Idols and their places were removed, and Passover was ordered according to the word (2 Kings 23:1-24). Hearing produced public action reaching the temple, the countryside, and the nation's worship. The Lord acknowledged his humbling and promised that his eyes would not see the evil to come upon the place (2 Kings 22:18-20). The sentence upon Judah remained, but the king's response was not overlooked within it. No king before him had turned to the Lord with heart, soul, and might as he did according to Moses' law (2 Kings 23:25). The Passover likewise stood apart among the reigns (2 Chronicles 35:18). His later death at Megiddo was grievous and did not remove that testimony. The promise of being spared the approaching devastation and the record of his fatal battle must both be retained; the good of his reign did not make every later decision beyond correction.

name: Jehoahaz (Shallum) of Judah
text: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord according to all that his fathers had done. Josiah's son reigned three months. Pharaoh-necho put him in bands at Riblah, laid tribute on the land, and carried him to Egypt, where he died. Jeremiah told the people to weep not for the dead Josiah but for the son who would never see his native country again. Jehoahaz succeeded Josiah but did evil according to the former ways of Judah (2 Kings 23:31-32). The inheritance of a reforming father's throne did not ensure continuation of his obedience. His three months exposed how quickly the royal direction could change when the man who led the reform was gone. Jeremiah's charge to the royal house joined continued rule to doing justice, delivering the oppressed, and refusing innocent blood (Jeremiah 22:1-5). Succession did not place the new king outside those conditions. The office remained accountable to the covenant that had governed his father. Pharaoh-nechoh bound him at Riblah, imposed tribute on Judah, and installed his brother Eliakim, renaming him Jehoiakim. Jehoahaz was carried to Egypt and died there (2 Kings 23:33-34). Jeremiah told the people to weep for Shallum, the son of Josiah taken away, because he would not return to his native land (Jeremiah 22:10-12). The sorrow was not only a brief reign but permanent separation from the place he had expected to rule. His father's crown could not preserve the son who did not continue his father's course.

name: Jehoiachin (Coniah)
text: Doing evil as his father Jehoiakim had done; a signet plucked from the Lord's right hand. Eighteen years old and three months on the throne when Nebuchadnezzar came. Jeremiah's word over him is one of the hardest in the book: though Coniah were the signet on my right hand, yet would I pluck thee thence; write ye this man childless, for no man of his seed shall prosper sitting upon the throne of David. Jehoiachin followed his father Jehoiakim in doing evil, and his short reign stood within the judgment already gathering upon Jerusalem (2 Kings 24:8-9). The city possessed a temple and a royal line, but neither could be used as proof that the Lord would indefinitely overlook its bloodshed and covenant-breaking. I will give thee into the hand of them that seek thy life, and I will cast thee out, and thy mother that bare thee, into another country, where ye were not born; and there shall ye die. He went out to the king of Babylon with his mother, his servants, his princes and his officers, and was carried away with ten thousand captives and all the craftsmen and smiths. Thirty-seven years later Evil-merodach lifted up his head out of prison and set his throne above the kings that were with him in Babylon: a kindness, still in Babylon.

name: Asa in his first years
text: Taking away the strange altars and the high places; commanding Judah to seek the Lord and do the law; crying to the Lord against a million Ethiopians. Before the failure that is its own case, Asa did thirty-five years of what a king was for. He removed the idols, removed his own mother from being queen for her grove, made Judah swear to seek the Lord with all their heart, and when Zerah came against him with a million men he prayed one prayer and won. Asa removed the strange altars and images and commanded Judah to seek the Lord and do His law. He used the years of quiet to strengthen the cities, acknowledging that their rest came from seeking God. When Zerah came against him with an overwhelming army, Asa did not measure deliverance by numbers. He cried to the Lord, with whom it is nothing to help with many or with those who have no power. After the victory, Azariah called the king and people to continued faithfulness: the Lord would be with them while they were with Him. Asa took courage, renewed the altar, and gathered the people into a covenant to seek God with all their heart. He removed Maachah from being queen because of her idol, allowing neither family position nor royal privilege to shelter the abomination. The Lord defeated the Ethiopians before Asa, and Judah returned with spoil. Others gathered to Asa when they saw that the Lord was with him. The people rejoiced in the oath they had made, sought God with their whole desire, and found Him. He gave them rest round about. The strength of this beginning lay in dependence upon God, not simply in fortified walls or military success. The same word that encouraged Asa also warned him that forsaking the Lord would have consequences.

name: Asa in his latter years
text: Hiring the king of Syria against Israel; imprisoning the seer who reproved him; seeking to the physicians and not to the Lord. For thirty-five years Asa was one of Judah's best kings. Then Baasha fortified Ramah, and Asa emptied the temple treasury to buy Ben-hadad's help instead of relying on the Lord who had given him the Ethiopians. Rebuked, he put the seer in the stocks; diseased, he sought physicians; and he died in the forty-first year of his reign. When Baasha fortified Ramah, Asa took silver and gold from the house of the Lord and the king's house and hired Ben-hadad to break his agreement with Israel. The plan relieved the immediate pressure, but Asa had relied upon the king of Syria instead of the Lord who had delivered him from the Ethiopians. Hanani exposed the difference between a successful maneuver and a faithful heart. Asa answered the rebuke with anger, imprisoned the seer, and oppressed some of the people. Later, when disease afflicted his feet, he sought the physicians but not the Lord. The charge is his neglect of God; the passage does not make the use of physicians itself the offense. Hanani declared that the Syrian host had escaped Asa's hand and that he would have wars. Asa had purchased temporary relief while losing the greater deliverance that reliance upon God would have brought. His disease became exceedingly severe, and he died in the forty-first year of his reign. He received an honorable burial, but the honor shown at his death did not erase the rebuke recorded against his latter years. The king who once cried to God against an immense army resisted correction when his own policy was challenged.

name: Jehoshaphat
text: Seeking the Lord and walking in his commandments; sending Levites to teach the book of the law through all the cities of Judah; setting the battle in array with singers. He sent princes and Levites round Judah with the book of the law to teach it, and the fear of the Lord fell on the kingdoms round about. When Moab, Ammon and Edom came against him he proclaimed a fast, prayed in the congregation, and put the singers in front of the army. They came to the watchtower and found only dead bodies. His alliances with Ahab's house are their own case. Jehoshaphat sought the God of his father and sent princes, Levites, and priests through Judah with the book of the law. The people were to be taught what the Lord required, not merely governed by royal command. He appointed judges and charged them to judge for the Lord, without partiality or gifts. Their authority did not place them above the judgment they administered. When a great multitude came against Judah, Jehoshaphat feared, proclaimed a fast, and gathered the people to seek the Lord. His prayer rested upon God's rule, covenant, and sanctuary. He confessed that they had neither might against the company nor knowledge of what to do: their eyes were upon God. At Jahaziel's word, they went out, placing singers before the army to praise the beauty of holiness. The Lord established the kingdom, and the fear of God restrained surrounding kingdoms. In the wilderness battle, the enemies turned against one another. Judah found the multitude fallen and spent three days gathering spoil. On the fourth day they blessed the Lord in the valley of Berachah and returned to Jerusalem with joy. God gave Jehoshaphat rest round about. His victory joined prayer with obedience: the people stood where God directed and trusted the word He had sent before they saw the deliverance.

name: Jehoshaphat's alliances
text: Joining affinity with Ahab; going to Ramoth-gilead with him; joining with Ahaziah to make ships. A king who sought the Lord and taught the law through Judah kept making common cause with the house of Ahab. He nearly died at Ramoth-gilead in Ahab's place, was told by Jehu the seer that wrath was upon him for helping the ungodly, and later lost a whole fleet at Ezion-geber for the same fault. Jehoshaphat joined himself to Ahab by affinity and went with him to Ramoth-gilead. Though he asked for a prophet of the Lord, he still accompanied Ahab after Micaiah announced disaster. Seeking a true word did not excuse proceeding against it. The alliance placed a king who sought the Lord beside a king who hated the prophet's correction. Afterward Jehoshaphat joined Ahaziah in making ships. This partnership again joined his work to a wicked king. A profitable undertaking could not make the association acceptable to God. At Ramoth-gilead, Jehoshaphat was surrounded by the Syrian captains. He cried out, and the Lord helped him and moved them away. His rescue was mercy, not approval of the alliance. Jehu the son of Hanani met him with the question whether he should help the ungodly and love those who hated the Lord. Wrath was upon him, although God also acknowledged the good found in him. Eliezer later declared that because Jehoshaphat had joined Ahaziah, the Lord had broken his works. The ships were broken and could not go to Tarshish. Both accounts distinguish God's regard for the king's obedience from His rejection of particular choices.

name: Jehoram of Judah
text: Slaying all his brethren with the sword; walking in the way of the house of Ahab; making high places and compelling Judah to fornication. Jehoshaphat's eldest son married Ahab's daughter, killed his six brothers to secure the throne, and led Judah to the high places. A writing came to him from Elijah naming the sentence: a great plague on his people, his children and his wives, and a disease of the bowels that would take two years to kill him. Jehoram strengthened himself upon the throne and killed his brothers, together with princes of Israel. He walked in the ways of Ahab's house, made high places, and caused Judah to commit fornication. Royal power became an instrument for bloodshed and for leading the people away from God. Elijah's writing named both offenses: Jehoram had followed the corrupt kings of Israel and killed brothers better than himself. His marriage into Ahab's house did not diminish his responsibility for the course he chose. Edom and Libnah revolted. The Philistines and Arabians invaded, carried away the substance of the king's house, and took his sons and wives, leaving only his youngest son. The Lord then struck Jehoram with an incurable disease of the bowels. After two years he died in grievous suffering. The people made no burning for him as they had for his fathers, and he departed without being desired. He was buried in the city of David, but not in the sepulchres of the kings. Yet the Lord did not destroy David's house, because of His covenant. The preservation of that house displayed God's faithfulness, not Jehoram's innocence.

name: Ahaziah of Judah
text: Walking in the ways of the house of Ahab, his mother being his counsellor to do wickedly. Ahaziah followed the counsel of his mother and Ahab's house. He joined Joram in war and visited him at Jezreel. His coming to Joram brought him into the judgment executed by Jehu. He was killed, and those who buried him remembered the faithfulness of his forefather Jehoshaphat. Ahaziah followed the counsel of his mother and the house of Ahab. Those who should have guided the young king toward the Lord became his counselors to his destruction. He joined Joram of Israel in war against Hazael and afterward went to visit the wounded king at Jezreel. His connection to Jehoshaphat did not make his own conduct righteous. He chose the ways of Ahab's house and joined its cause when judgment was approaching it. Chronicles declares that Ahaziah's destruction was of God in coming to Joram. He went out with him against Jehu, whom the Lord had anointed to cut off Ahab's house. Jehu's men also killed the princes of Judah and Ahaziah's relatives who attended him. Ahaziah was sought out and killed. Those who buried him remembered Jehoshaphat, his forefather, who had sought the Lord with all his heart. That remembered faithfulness secured a measure of regard at his burial, but it had not sheltered Ahaziah from the consequences of his own alliance. His house was left without strength to retain the kingdom.

name: Jehoiada the priest
text: Hiding the king's son six years from Athaliah; making a covenant between the Lord, the king, and the people; doing good in Israel, both toward God and toward his house. When Athaliah killed the seed royal, Jehoiada's wife stole the baby Joash out of the slaughter and the priest hid him in the house of the Lord six years. In the seventh he armed the Levites, crowned the boy, had Athaliah taken out and slain, tore down the house of Baal, and set the temple in order. He was buried among the kings. While Athaliah destroyed the royal seed, Jehoshabeath rescued Joash and hid him in the house of God. Jehoiada guarded the child through the years of concealment. In the seventh year he gathered the captains, Levites, and fathers of Israel into a covenant and brought forth the king's son according to the Lord's promise concerning David. He ordered the guards, kept the holy place from unauthorized entry, and gave Joash the crown and testimony. He made a covenant that the king and people should be the Lord's people. The house of Baal was broken down, and the service of the Lord's house was restored according to its appointed order. Joash was established upon the throne, the people rejoiced, and the city was quiet after Athaliah was put to death outside the house of the Lord. Joash did right in the sight of the Lord during Jehoiada's lifetime. Jehoiada lived to be a hundred and thirty years old. He was buried among the kings because he had done good in Israel, toward God and His house. His honor was not founded on possessing the crown, but on faithfully preserving the king and restoring the people's covenant obligations.

name: Joash of Judah
text: Forsaking the Lord after Jehoiada's death; stoning Zechariah in the temple court. The boy king saved by the priest Jehoiada did right all the days of Jehoiada. When the priest died, the princes of Judah came and Joash hearkened to them, left the house of the Lord, and served groves and idols. Jehoiada's son Zechariah rebuked him by the Spirit; the king had him stoned in the court of the temple. Joash repaired the house of the Lord while Jehoiada lived. The collection and use of the money restored what had been damaged and returned the remaining funds to the service of the sanctuary. Yet after Jehoiada's death, the princes bowed before Joash and he listened to them. They left the Lord's house and served groves and idols. God sent prophets to bring them back, but they would not hear. When the Spirit of God came upon Zechariah, Jehoiada's son, he warned that forsaking the Lord had brought abandonment. Joash commanded that he be stoned in the court of the Lord's house. The king forgot the kindness Jehoiada had shown him and killed his son. Wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem. A small Syrian company defeated a very great host because Judah had forsaken the Lord. The invaders destroyed the princes and sent the spoil to Damascus. They left Joash severely wounded. His servants conspired against him because of the blood of Jehoiada's sons and killed him upon his bed. He was buried in the city of David, but not in the sepulchres of the kings. The king who had repaired the sanctuary afterward shed the blood of God's witness within its court.

name: Amaziah
text: Bringing home the gods of Seir and bowing to them. Having beaten Edom with the Lord's help, Amaziah brought back the gods of the children of Seir, set them up as his gods, and burned incense to them. A prophet asked why he sought gods that could not deliver their own people; the king told him to stop before he was smitten. Amaziah did right, but not with a perfect heart. He executed the servants who had murdered his father while sparing their children, according to the law that each should die for his own sin. He also obeyed the man of God who told him to dismiss the hired Israelite troops, accepting the loss of the hundred talents he had paid. After defeating Edom, however, Amaziah brought home its gods, bowed before them, and burned incense to them. When a prophet asked why he sought gods that could not deliver their own people, the king threatened him. Lifted up by victory, he then challenged Israel and refused the warning against provoking his own hurt. The prophet declared that God had determined to destroy Amaziah because he had done this and rejected counsel. Israel defeated Judah, captured Amaziah, broke down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall, and carried away treasure and hostages. Amaziah survived the defeat, but his turning away was followed by conspiracy. He fled to Lachish, where his pursuers killed him. Earlier acts of obedience did not authorize later idolatry. The gods he had carried home could neither preserve Edom nor secure the king who adopted them.

name: Uzziah
text: Entering the temple to burn incense, which belonged to the priests. A strong and prosperous king who sought God in the days of Zechariah. When he was strong his heart was lifted up, and he went into the temple with a censer. Eighty priests withstood him; while he raged at them, leprosy rose in his forehead. Uzziah sought God in the days of Zechariah and prospered while he sought Him. His victories, fortifications, husbandry, and military preparations made his name spread abroad. When he became strong, however, his heart was lifted up to his destruction. He entered the temple to burn incense upon the altar, taking to himself a service appointed to the sons of Aaron. Azariah and eighty priests withstood him and commanded him to leave. Uzziah answered with anger while holding the censer. The offense was not his success, but the pride that made him cross a boundary God had established and resist those charged to keep it.

name: Jotham
text: Preparing his ways before the Lord his God; not entering the temple as his father had. Uzziah's son had watched his father go into the temple to burn incense and come out a leper. Jotham did what was right, and stayed out of the priests' place. The chronicler gives the cause of his strength in one line: he prepared his ways before the Lord his God. Jotham did right in the sight of the Lord and did not repeat Uzziah's trespass in the temple. He built the high gate of the Lord's house, strengthened the wall of Ophel, and built cities, castles, and towers. His public work was joined to a deliberate ordering of his own conduct before God. The people still acted corruptly. Scripture does not conceal their condition in order to praise the king. Jotham's faithfulness is therefore distinguished from the conduct of those he governed; the one did not make the other disappear. Jotham prevailed against the Ammonites, who paid tribute for three years. He became mighty because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God. The explanation for his strength is given in the condition of his walk, not merely in the size of his building works. He reigned sixteen years and was buried in the city of David. His account sets the preparation of one's ways before God beside the danger shown in his father's latter years: strength must remain under obedience.

name: Ahaz
text: Burning his children in the fire; copying the altar of Damascus; sacrificing to the gods that smote him. Ahaz walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, made molten images for Baalim, burnt his children in the fire after the abominations of the heathen, and hired Assyria against Syria with the temple's silver. Defeated, he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus because they had helped his enemies. Ahaz made molten images for Baalim, burned his children in the fire, and sacrificed in the high places. In distress he became still more unfaithful. Seeing Damascus victorious, he reasoned that its gods would help him also and sacrificed to them. He mistook an enemy's success for proof that its worship was true. He stripped the Lord's house and the royal houses to purchase Assyrian help, cut up the vessels of God's house, shut its doors, and made altars throughout Jerusalem. His policy multiplied the very trespass that had brought Judah low. The Lord delivered Judah into the hands of Syria and Israel. Many were killed and many taken captive. Yet Israel's victory did not authorize its own cruelty: Oded rebuked the captors, and leaders of Ephraim required the captives to be released, clothed, fed, and brought to Jericho. The Philistines and Edomites also afflicted Judah. Assyria distressed Ahaz rather than strengthening him, despite the treasure he had paid. The gods he adopted became the ruin of him and of Israel. At death he was buried in Jerusalem, but not in the sepulchres of the kings of Israel.

name: Josiah at Megiddo
text: Going to battle against Necho without inquiring of the Lord. The reformer king, promised he would be gathered to his grave in peace, went out against Pharaoh Necho, who was marching to Carchemish and had no quarrel with Judah. Necho sent word that God had commanded him to make haste and that Josiah should not meddle with God, who was with him. Josiah disguised himself and fought anyway. After Josiah had prepared the temple, Pharaoh Necho came to fight at Carchemish. Josiah went out against him. Necho sent word that his quarrel was not with Judah and warned Josiah not to oppose the God who had commanded him to make haste. Josiah would not turn away. He disguised himself and entered the battle at Megiddo. Chronicles expressly says that he did not listen to the words of Necho from the mouth of God. The king's earlier reforms and devotion to the law did not make this later decision right.

name: Zedekiah
text: Breaking his oath to Nebuchadnezzar; stiffening his neck against the Lord's word by Jeremiah. Sworn by God to serve Babylon, Zedekiah rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar and would not humble himself before Jeremiah speaking from the mouth of the Lord. Warned to the last that surrender would save the city and his life, he feared the Jews who had defected more than he feared the word. Zedekiah did evil and would not humble himself before Jeremiah. He also rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God. Ezekiel exposed the broken covenant through the figure of the vine that turned toward another eagle, seeking Egyptian help. The oath was not made harmless by the fact that it had been sworn to a foreign king. Jeremiah told Zedekiah that surrender would preserve his life and prevent the city from being burned. Zedekiah feared that the Jews who had already fallen to the Chaldeans would abuse him. The prophet assured him that they would not and urged him to obey. The king nevertheless refused the way of escape set before him. The city was besieged until famine prevailed. Zedekiah fled by night, but the Chaldeans overtook him in the plains of Jericho and brought him to Riblah. His sons were killed before his eyes; then his eyes were put out, and he was bound and taken to Babylon. Jerusalem was burned as Jeremiah had warned. The king who feared the humiliation of surrender suffered a far greater calamity through resistance. God's warning had included mercy, but Zedekiah would not submit to receive it.

name: The captivity of Judah
text: Polluting the house of the Lord; mocking the messengers of God; refusing the Sabbath and the land's sabbaths. All the chief of the priests and the people transgressed very much after all the abominations of the heathen and polluted the house of the Lord. The Lord sent messengers because he had compassion; they mocked them, despised his words, and misused his prophets until there was no remedy. Judah's fall followed persistent transgression among rulers, priests, prophets, and people. They polluted the Lord's house, shed blood, practiced oppression, and failed to distinguish the holy from the profane. False prophets strengthened the corruption by speaking visions God had not given. The Lord sent His messengers repeatedly because He had compassion on His people and His dwelling place. They mocked the messengers, despised His words, and misused His prophets until there was no remedy. The sentence did not come without warning or opportunity to turn. The Chaldeans killed within the sanctuary, carried away its treasures, burned the house of God, and broke down Jerusalem's wall. Those who escaped the sword were carried to Babylon and served there until the Persian kingdom. The land lay desolate and enjoyed its sabbaths, fulfilling the word of the Lord by Jeremiah concerning seventy years. The captivity was not the end of God's word to Israel. In the first year of Cyrus, the Lord stirred the king to proclaim the rebuilding of His house at Jerusalem. The same account that records Judah's removal closes with an opening for return, showing that judgment did not annul God's faithfulness.

name: Nineveh under Jonah
text: Wickedness come up before the Lord. Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown. The people believed God, proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth from the greatest to the least; the king rose from his throne, sat in ashes, and decreed that man and beast cry mightily unto God and turn from the violence in their hands. Nineveh's wickedness had come up before the Lord. Jonah entered the city and announced that it would be overthrown in forty days. The king's own proclamation identified the needed change: each person was to turn from his evil way and from the violence in his hands. The people believed God, proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth. The king rose from his throne, laid aside his robe, and sat in ashes. His command joined crying mightily to God with abandoning violence. The outward humiliation was to accompany an actual change in conduct. God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way, and did not bring the announced evil upon them. Their deliverance was not credited to Nineveh's power, wealth, or former standing, but to repentance before the God who had warned them. Christ later declared that the men of Nineveh would rise in judgment against a generation that refused a greater witness than Jonah. Their response exposes the guilt of hearing God's warning without turning. A threatened judgment can be an opportunity for mercy when those who hear it believe and amend their ways.

name: Jeremiah
text: Speaking the word of the Lord faithfully despite persecution; not holding back when commanded to prophesy. Before Jeremiah was formed in the belly the Lord knew him, sanctified him, and ordained him a prophet unto the nations—set over kingdoms to root out, pull down, destroy, throw down, build, and plant. His own city conspired to kill him. The word burned like fire shut up in his bones. He was threatened with death, saved by Ahikam, and cast into a miry dungeon before Ebed-melech the Ethiopian drew him out. The word of the Lord came to Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee, and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations (Jeremiah 1:5). When Jeremiah protested he was a child, the Lord told him to go wherever he was sent and speak whatever was commanded. Be not afraid of their faces, for I am with thee to deliver thee (Jeremiah 1:7–8). The Lord put forth His hand, touched Jeremiah’s mouth, and said, I have put my words in thy mouth. See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant (Jeremiah 1:9–10). The commission was both destructive and constructive, and neither part could be refused. When Jeremiah prophesied in the temple court that this house would become like Shiloh, the priests and the prophets and the people took him and said, Thou shalt surely die. He answered that the Lord had sent him and that if they put him to death they would bring innocent blood upon themselves (Jeremiah 26:8–15). The hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with him, and they did not give him to the people (Jeremiah 26:24). Mocked and derided daily, Jeremiah resolved to stop speaking in the Lord’s name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay (Jeremiah 20:9). The word did not allow itself to be contained.

name: Pashur the son of Immer
text: Smiting the prophet and putting him in the stocks; prophesying lies. Pashur, chief governor in the house of the Lord, heard Jeremiah prophesy the city's fall, struck him, and put him in the stocks at the high gate of Benjamin overnight. In the morning Jeremiah gave him a new name. Pashur, the priest and chief governor in the Lord's house, heard Jeremiah prophesy and struck him. He put the prophet in the stocks at the high gate of Benjamin, using his office to punish the word he should have received. When Pashur released him the next day, Jeremiah did not withdraw the message. The Lord gave Pashur the name Magor-missabib, fear round about. His violence against the messenger could neither disprove the prophecy nor remove the danger it announced. The Lord declared that Pashur would become a terror to himself and his friends. Judah's strength and treasures would be given to Babylon. Pashur and his household would go into captivity, and he would die and be buried there with the friends to whom he had prophesied lies. The passage records this sentence against him; it does not give a separate account of its execution. The keeper of the stocks was warned of his own coming confinement. Authority in the sanctuary provided no exemption from answering for violence and false prophecy.

name: Jehoiakim
text: Building with unrighteousness; shedding innocent blood; burning the scroll of the Lord's words. Necho's puppet king built a great house with unpaid labor, killed the prophet Urijah for prophesying like Jeremiah, and when Jeremiah's scroll was read to him, cut it with a penknife leaf by leaf and burned it in the hearth. Neither he nor his servants were afraid. Jehoiakim enlarged his house through unrighteousness, using his neighbor's service without paying his wages. Jeremiah contrasted his display with Josiah's judgment of the poor and needy: that was to know the Lord. Jehoiakim's eyes and heart were set on covetousness, innocent blood, oppression, and violence. He also had Urijah brought back from Egypt and killed for prophesying against the city. He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem. He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David, and his dead body shall be cast out in the day to the heat and in the night to the frost. His son reigned three months and went to Babylon; his brother was the last king.

name: Hananiah the son of Azur
text: Prophesying a lie in the name of the Lord. In the temple, before the priests and all the people, Hananiah declared that the Lord would break Babylon's yoke within two years and bring back the vessels and the captives. He broke the wooden yoke from Jeremiah's neck to prove it. Hananiah announced in the Lord's name that Babylon's yoke would be broken within two years and that the temple vessels and captives would return. He broke the wooden yoke from Jeremiah's neck before the priests and people, making a visible sign serve his false promise. Jeremiah desired the people's restoration, but a desirable promise was not thereby a word from God. He reminded them that a prophet of peace would be known when the word came to pass. After Hananiah's display, Jeremiah went his way until the Lord gave him an answer. The Lord declared that the broken wooden yokes would be replaced by yokes of iron. Babylon's appointed rule would not end according to Hananiah's timetable. Jeremiah told him plainly that the Lord had not sent him and that he had made the people trust in a lie. Because he had taught rebellion against the Lord, Hananiah would die that year. He died in the seventh month, within the year of the confrontation. The prophet who promised swift release could not escape the swift judgment pronounced upon his own falsehood.

name: Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah
text: Prophesying lies in the Lord's name to the captives; committing adultery with their neighbours' wives. Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah prophesied lies among the captives and committed adultery with their neighbors' wives. The Lord named their sins and announced that Nebuchadnezzar would kill them and that their names would become a curse among the exiles. Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah prophesied lies in the Lord's name among the captives in Babylon. They also committed adultery with their neighbors' wives. God joined their public religious falsehood with the private wickedness they might have thought concealed. These were the two named prophets among the exiles, not the kings who bore the same names. The Lord declared that He knew and was a witness. Neither distance from Jerusalem nor the conditions of captivity put their conduct beyond His sight. The Lord announced that He would deliver them into Nebuchadnezzar's hand and that the king would kill them before the captives' eyes. Their names would become a curse among the exiles, recalling the two whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire. Jeremiah's letter records the announced punishment. Their position as speakers to the captive community made the lie no less accountable. God's people were to reject false promises and heed the word He had actually sent concerning their life in exile and His appointed time of return.

name: Shemaiah the Nehelamite
text: Sending letters from Babylon to have Jeremiah put in prison and in the stocks; prophesying a lie. From the first captivity Shemaiah wrote to the priests in Jerusalem, naming Jeremiah a madman and asking why he had not been put in the stocks. Zephaniah the priest read the letter in Jeremiah's ears, and the answer came back to Babylon: Shemaiah would have no man to dwell among the people, and would not see the good the Lord would do. Shemaiah sent letters in his own name from Babylon, urging Zephaniah the priest to restrain Jeremiah as a madman who made himself a prophet. He objected to Jeremiah's instruction that the captivity would be long and that the exiles should build houses and plant gardens. The message he attacked was the Lord's direction for the captives. Shemaiah sought to use priestly authority and imprisonment to silence it. Zephaniah read the letter to Jeremiah, and the Lord exposed Shemaiah as a man He had not sent, who had caused the people to trust in a lie. God declared punishment upon Shemaiah and his seed. He would have no man dwelling among this people and would not behold the good the Lord would do for them, because he had taught rebellion against the Lord. Shemaiah opposed the word governing the years of waiting and was denied a share in the promised good beyond them. His objection to a long captivity could not shorten the time God had appointed. The letter intended to procure Jeremiah's restraint instead became the occasion for a sentence against its author.

name: Jonadab and the Rechabites
text: Obeying the commandment of Jonadab their father for over two hundred years: no wine, no house, no vineyard, no field. The Lord had Jeremiah set wine before a whole clan in a chamber of the temple. They refused it: their father Jonadab had commanded them to drink none, build no house and sow no seed, and they had kept it all their days. The Lord held them up against Judah, who would not obey him though he rose early and spoke, and promised Jonadab a man before him for ever. The Rechabites refused the wine Jeremiah set before them in a chamber of the Lord's house. Jonadab their father had commanded them not to drink wine, build houses, sow seed, or plant vineyards, but to dwell in tents. They had kept his charge through their generations. Their presence in Jerusalem was explained by their flight from the invading armies, not by a claim that their ancestral way had been abandoned. Their refusal supplied the contrast God intended. The descendants of Jonadab observed their father's command, while Judah would not hear the Lord despite His repeated sending of prophets. The lesson did not make wine forbidden to everyone; it exposed Judah's refusal to obey the God who had spoken to them. Jeremiah announced that Jonadab the son of Rechab would not lack a man to stand before the Lord for ever, because his children had kept his commandment and done all he had charged them. At the same time, God declared the announced evil upon Judah and Jerusalem because He had spoken and they had not heard. The faithful household and the disobedient nation stood side by side, making clear that repeated access to God's word was no substitute for doing it.

name: Baruch the scribe
text: Writing the roll from the prophet's mouth and reading it in the house of the Lord, and writing it again after the king burned it. He wrote all the words of the Lord from Jeremiah's mouth on a roll, and because the prophet was shut up, he read it in the house of the Lord on a fast day in the ears of all the people. The princes heard it and told him to hide with Jeremiah. Jehoiakim cut the roll with a penknife and burned it leaf by leaf. Baruch wrote it again from Jeremiah's mouth, and many like words were added. He sought great things for himself and was told not to, and given his life for a prey. Baruch wrote the words Jeremiah dictated and read the roll in the Lord's house when Jeremiah could not go there. He then read it before the princes. The work required more than copying: he publicly delivered a warning that placed both him and the prophet in danger. After Jehoiakim burned the roll, Baruch wrote again at Jeremiah's mouth, preserving all the former words and many like words added. The king's attack did not cause him to abandon the charge. Yet Baruch also knew weariness and grief, crying that the Lord had added sorrow to his pain and that he found no rest. The Lord answered Baruch's distress by setting it within the judgment coming upon the land. What God had built He would break down, and what He had planted He would pluck up. Baruch was not to seek great things for himself amid that overthrow. God promised him his life for a prey in all places where he went. Preservation, rather than worldly advancement, was the particular mercy pledged to him. The faithful scribe was not promised freedom from the nation's troubles, but life through them.

name: Ebed-melech the Ethiopian
text: Going to the king for Jeremiah, and drawing him up out of the dungeon with old cast clouts and rotten rags. The princes had put Jeremiah in a dungeon of mire to die. A eunuch of the king's house, an Ethiopian, went out to Zedekiah at the gate and told him the prophet was likely to die of hunger where he was. The king gave him thirty men and he drew Jeremiah up with rags under his armholes. Before the city fell the Lord sent him his own word: thy life for a prey, because thou hast put thy trust in me. Ebed-melech, the Ethiopian eunuch in the king's house, heard that Jeremiah had been lowered into the dungeon and was sinking in the mire. He went to the king and plainly called the princes' action evil, warning that the prophet would die where he had been cast. With the king's permission, he took men and ropes to draw Jeremiah out. He also gathered old cast clouts and rotten rags and instructed Jeremiah to place them under his arms beneath the cords. His intervention joined courage before authority with careful treatment of the man being rescued. While Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison, the Lord sent him a promise for Ebed-melech. The announced evil would come upon Jerusalem, but Ebed-melech would not be delivered into the hands of the men he feared. God would deliver him, and his life would be for a prey because he had put his trust in the Lord. The approaching fall of the city did not prevent God from distinguishing the man who trusted Him. Ebed-melech's place in the royal household did not keep him silent when its princes acted wickedly.

name: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah
text: Murder of Gedaliah the governor at his own table; slaughter of the Jews and Chaldeans with him, and of seventy pilgrims. Of the seed royal, hired by the king of the Ammonites, Ishmael ate bread with Gedaliah at Mizpah and killed him, then killed the men with him, then killed seventy mourners on their way to the house of the Lord and threw them in a pit. He escaped to Ammon with eight men. Scripture records no sentence on him; it records what his deed cost the remnant. Ishmael came with ten men to Gedaliah at Mizpah and ate with him. During that hospitality he rose up and killed the governor appointed over the remnant, together with Jews and Chaldeans there. Gedaliah had previously refused to believe the warning of a plot against his life. Ishmael then went out weeping to meet eighty men coming with offerings to the house of the Lord. He drew them into Mizpah and killed seventy, casting their bodies into a pit. Ten were spared when they offered hidden stores of food. He took the remaining people captive and set out toward the Ammonites. His tears concealed violence, and the prospect of supplies determined whom he spared. Johanan and the captains pursued Ishmael. The captives rejoiced when they saw them and returned with Johanan, while Ishmael escaped to the Ammonites with eight men. The account records the breaking of his hold over the captives, but not his eventual death or a further punishment. His bloodshed left the remnant afraid of Babylonian retaliation and helped set the stage for their flight toward Egypt. His escape did not make his murders lawful, nor did it erase the injury done to a people already reduced by war.

name: Johanan and the remnant that went down to Egypt
text: Asking the word of the Lord, swearing to obey it, and refusing it; burning incense to the queen of heaven in Egypt. The remnant asked Jeremiah to pray for direction and swore to obey whatever the Lord said. Ten days later the answer came: stay in the land and I will build you; go to Egypt and the sword you fear will overtake you there. They called the prophet a liar, took him with them to Egypt, and there openly returned to the queen of heaven. Ye dissembled in your hearts, when ye sent me unto the Lord your God, saying, Pray for us unto the Lord our God; and according unto all that the Lord our God shall say, so declare unto us, and we will do it. In Egypt the men who knew their wives burned incense to other gods answered Jeremiah: we will certainly do whatsoever thing goeth forth out of our own mouth, to burn incense unto the queen of heaven, as we did in the cities of Judah; for then had we plenty of victuals. Then it shall come to pass, that the sword, which ye feared, shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine, whereof ye were afraid, shall follow close after you there in Egypt; and there ye shall die. I will take the remnant of Judah, that have set their faces to go into the land of Egypt, and they shall all be consumed, and fall in the land of Egypt; none shall return but such as shall escape. The sign given was Pharaoh-hophra delivered into the hand of his enemies, as Zedekiah had been.

name: Moab and Ammon
text: Magnifying themselves against the Lord and against his people; rejoicing over the sanctuary when it was profaned. Lot's two sons, neighbours to Israel from the wilderness on, are judged in Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos and Zephaniah for one long habit: pride against the Lord and gladness at Judah's ruin. Ammon ripped up the women with child of Gilead to enlarge its border; Moab said, Aha, against the house of Judah. We have heard of the pride of Moab; he is very proud: of his loftiness, and his arrogancy, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart. He shall be no more praised, because he hath magnified himself against the Lord. Of Ammon: because thou saidst, Aha, against my sanctuary, when it was profaned; and against the land of Israel, when it was desolate; and against the house of Judah, when they went into captivity. Amos: they have ripped up the women with child of Gilead, that they might enlarge their border. Moab shall be destroyed from being a people, because he hath magnified himself against the Lord. Yet will I bring again the captivity of Moab in the latter days. Of Ammon: I will deliver thee to the men of the east for a possession, and Rabbah shall be a stable for camels; Zephaniah: Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, even the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation. Nebuchadnezzar came through both.

name: Babylon, the lady of kingdoms
text: Showing no mercy to the captives; saying, I am, and none else beside me; trusting in her sorceries. Babylon was the Lord's hammer against Judah, and was judged for how she swung it: without mercy, laying a heavy yoke on the ancient, and saying in her heart, I shall be a lady for ever. Isaiah and Jeremiah both name the end before the beginning: the Medes, the sudden fall, the perpetual desolation. Babylon said that she would be a lady for ever. Though the Lord had delivered His people into her hand, she showed no mercy and laid a heavy yoke upon the aged. Permission to conquer was not permission for limitless cruelty. She trusted in wickedness, saying that none saw her, and let wisdom and knowledge turn her aside. Her boast, “I am, and none else beside me,” joined self-exaltation with confidence that she would never know widowhood or the loss of children. Sorceries and astrologers were summoned to secure a future she would not consider humbly. The Lord commanded her to sit in the dust and announced the loss of her former honor. Widowhood and loss of children would come suddenly despite her enchantments. An evil she could not ward off would expose the weakness of the wisdom in which she trusted. The astrologers would be as stubble before fire, unable to deliver even themselves. Those with whom she had labored would wander away, leaving none to save her. The oracle reverses Babylon's confidence at every point: power, learning, commerce, and sorcery could not exempt her from the God whose people she had oppressed.

name: The elders with idols in the temple (Ezekiel 8)
text: The image of jealousy; creeping things on the walls; women weeping for Tammuz; twenty-five men worshipping the sun with their backs to the temple. Carried in vision to Jerusalem, Ezekiel was shown four scenes of greater and greater abomination inside the house of the Lord: an idol at the gate, seventy elders with censers in a chamber of painted beasts, women mourning a pagan god, and men between the porch and the altar bowing east to the sun. The elders said, the Lord seeth us not. In Ezekiel's vision, the Lord showed him abominations within the precincts of the sanctuary: the image of jealousy, idolatrous pictures in hidden chambers, elders offering incense, women weeping for Tammuz, and men worshipping the sun with their backs toward the temple. Those practicing secret worship said that the Lord did not see and had forsaken the earth. The hidden rites stood beside violence in the land. The sanctuary's location did not sanctify what was being done within it. God brought the prophet through one disclosure after another so that the judgment could not be mistaken for an unprovoked abandonment. The executioners in the vision were commanded to begin at the sanctuary. A mark first distinguished those who sighed and cried over the abominations; proximity to the temple was not the distinction that preserved them. Judgment began with the ancient men before the house. Ezekiel also saw the glory of the Lord move from the threshold to the cherubims and stand at the east gate. The presence upon which Jerusalem presumed was departing. The vision exposed both the sins the people thought concealed and the false security they placed in the building they had defiled.

name: Pelatiah and the princes at the east gate
text: Devising mischief and giving wicked counsel in the city. In vision Ezekiel saw twenty-five men at the east gate of the temple, princes of the people, Jaazaniah and Pelatiah among them, who said, it is not near; let us build houses: this city is the caldron, and we be the flesh. He was told to prophesy against them. At the east gate in Ezekiel's vision stood twenty-five men, including Pelatiah, who devised mischief and gave wicked counsel. Their saying that the city was the cauldron and they the flesh was answered by the Lord, who knew the things that came into their minds. They had multiplied the slain and filled the streets with them. God reversed their image: the slain were the flesh within the city, while the counselors themselves would be brought out. Their confidence could not shelter the men responsible for bloodshed and corrupt counsel. The Lord announced that He would bring the sword they feared and judge them at the border of Israel. As Ezekiel prophesied in the vision, Pelatiah died. The prophet fell upon his face and cried out, fearing a full end of the remnant. God answered with a word concerning the scattered people. Though removed far away, He would be a little sanctuary to them and would gather them again. He promised one heart and a new spirit, that they might walk in His statutes. The fall of a corrupt counselor was thus followed by assurance that restoration would rest upon God's work and renewed obedience, not upon Jerusalem's boast.

name: Edom, in the day of his brother
text: Standing on the other side when strangers carried Jacob away; rejoicing over Judah's fall; cutting off those that escaped. When Babylon took Jerusalem, Esau's descendants looked on, entered the gate in the day of calamity, laid hands on the substance, stood in the crossway to cut off the fugitives, and delivered up those that remained. Psalm 137 remembers them shouting, rase it, rase it, even to the foundation. Edom's pride rested in its mountain strongholds, but its offense was also betrayal of its brother Jacob. When strangers carried away Jerusalem's forces, Edom stood on the other side and was as one of them. It rejoiced over Judah's destruction, entered the gate to take spoil, and stood at the crossroads to cut off those escaping and deliver up survivors. The calamity of a brother became an opportunity for gain. Neither distance from the original invasion nor the strength of its rock dwellings made Edom innocent of what it did to the defeated and fleeing. The Lord declared that He would bring Edom down even from a nest set among the stars. Its confederates would deceive it, its wisdom would fail, and its mighty men would be dismayed. The recompense followed its conduct: as it had done, it would be done unto it. Obadiah set this overthrow beside deliverance upon mount Zion and the possession of their inheritance by the house of Jacob. The kingdom would be the Lord's. Edom's expectation of profiting from Judah's fall could not prevail over God's judgment of its violence or His purpose for restoration.

name: The prince of Tyre
text: Saying, I am a God, I sit in the seat of God. Ezekiel's word to the ruler of the merchant city: because thine heart is lifted up, and thou hast said, I am a God, in the midst of the seas; yet thou art a man, and not God. Wiser than Daniel, richer by his traffick, and undone by both. Self-deification on the strength of trade. By the multitude of thy merchandise they have filled the midst of thee with violence, and thou hast sinned. Tyre had also rejoiced at Jerusalem's fall: aha, she is broken, I shall be replenished. They shall bring thee down to the pit, and thou shalt die the deaths of them that are slain in the midst of the seas. Wilt thou yet say before him that slayeth thee, I am God? Nebuchadnezzar besieged the mainland city; Alexander finished the island.

name: Pharaoh-hophra and Egypt
text: Saying, My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself; a staff of reed to the house of Israel. Judah leaned on Egypt against Babylon, and Egypt broke under the hand like a reed and ran into it. Ezekiel's word against Pharaoh is against the boast of ownership: the river was his, he had made it. Forty years of desolation were decreed, and Egypt was to be the basest of kingdoms afterward. The Lord addressed Pharaoh as the great dragon lying in the midst of his rivers, claiming the river as his own and saying that he had made it for himself. Egypt's strength had become a ground for boasting as though its provision came from Pharaoh's own power. Egypt had also been a staff of reed to the house of Israel. When they leaned upon it, it broke and injured them. The promised support encouraged a confidence it could not sustain. The remnant's later flight to Egypt repeated that misplaced reliance after the Lord had commanded them to remain in Judah. Ezekiel announced Pharaoh's removal under the image of hooks in the dragon's jaws. The oracle pronounced desolation, scattering, and afterward a regathering in a lowly condition, so that Egypt would no longer be Israel's confidence. These are the terms of the prophetic sentence, including the forty years named in it. Jeremiah gave the remnant a particular sign: Pharaoh Hophra would be delivered to his enemies and those seeking his life, just as Zedekiah had been delivered to Nebuchadnezzar. The kingdom chosen as a refuge was itself under judgment; its ruler could not guarantee the safety he could not secure for himself.

name: The shepherds of Israel
text: Feeding themselves and not the flock; scattering the sheep. Ezekiel 34 arraigns the rulers and pastors of Israel as shepherds who ate the fat and clothed themselves with the wool, but did not strengthen the diseased, heal the sick, bind up the broken, bring back the driven away, or seek the lost. The flock was scattered on every hill and became meat to the beasts. The shepherds of Israel fed themselves instead of the flock. They ate the fat, clothed themselves with the wool, and killed those that were fed, while failing to strengthen the diseased, heal the sick, bind the broken, bring back the driven, or seek the lost. They ruled with force and cruelty. The sheep were scattered and became prey because those entrusted with them sought their own advantage. The Lord also addressed the strong sheep that trampled the remaining pasture, fouled the waters, and pushed the weak aside. Exploitation was not excused merely because it occurred within the flock. God declared Himself against the shepherds and required His flock at their hand. He would remove their opportunity to feed themselves upon it and deliver the sheep from their mouths. He would judge between cattle and cattle, between the fat and the lean. The Lord promised to seek His sheep, gather them, feed them in good pasture, and bind what was broken. He would set one shepherd over them, His servant David, and make a covenant of peace. The remedy for abusive rule was not abandonment of the flock, but God's own intervention and the faithful shepherd He appointed.

name: Jonah
text: Fleeing from the presence of the Lord to avoid his commission; anger at God's mercy. Told to go east to Nineveh, Jonah bought passage west to Tarshish. A storm, a lot, and a fish brought him back. He preached, the city repented, and he was angry enough to die because God spared it. A gourd, a worm, and a wind finished the lesson. Jonah received the command to cry against Nineveh and fled toward Tarshish from the presence of the Lord. He confessed to the mariners that he feared the God who made the sea and dry land, even while his flight contradicted that confession. The storm endangered others as well as himself. After Nineveh repented, Jonah's anger disclosed his resistance to God's mercy. He said that he had fled because he knew the Lord was gracious and would turn from the announced evil. He preferred death to witnessing the sparing of the city he had been sent to warn. Jonah was cast into the sea, and the Lord prepared a great fish to swallow him. From that distress he prayed, acknowledging that salvation is of the Lord. God commanded the fish to release him and gave him the commission a second time. After the preaching, God corrected him again through the gourd, the worm, and the vehement east wind. Jonah pitied the plant that had sheltered him, though he had not made it grow. The Lord asked why He should not spare a great city with more than a hundred and twenty thousand persons unable to discern their right hand from their left, and much cattle. The book closes with God's question, not a recorded answer from Jonah.

name: Nineveh under Nahum
text: A bloody city, full of lies and robbery, mistress of witchcrafts. Nahum charged Nineveh with bloodshed, lies, plunder, and the corruption of nations. The Lord who is slow to anger would not acquit the wicked. The city's defenses, commerce, and commanders would fail, and the peoples it had injured would rejoice at its overthrow. Nahum charged Nineveh as a bloody city, full of lies and robbery, whose prey did not depart. Its power was pictured as a lions' dwelling filled with torn prey. Violence, deceit, and the entangling of nations had enriched the city and spread its injury abroad. The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace dissolved. Nineveh is laid waste; who will bemoan her? There is no healing of thy bruise. Tobit records hearing of its destruction by Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus before he died, and rejoicing over it.

name: The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin
text: Weakening the hands of the people; hiring counsellors against them to frustrate the building of the house of God. The people of the land offered to help build the temple and were refused, and turned to hindrance: hired counsellors, letters to Artaxerxes, and a stop-work order enforced by force and power. The work lay still until the second year of Darius, whose decree turned the tables: whoever altered it would be hanged on timber from his own house. The adversaries first offered to join the building, claiming to seek the same God. Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the chief fathers refused, declaring that they would build the house of the Lord according to Cyrus's command. The rejected offer was followed by open obstruction: the people of the land discouraged Judah, troubled the builders, and hired counselors to frustrate the work (Ezra 4:1-5). Ezra also records accusations against Jerusalem under later kings. Rehum and Shimshai represented the city as rebellious and warned that rebuilding would cost the king tribute and dominion. They obtained an order and enforced it by force and power (Ezra 4:11-23). Opposition clothed itself in concern for royal interests while working to weaken the returned people. When the temple work resumed under Haggai and Zechariah, the elders continued while the inquiry went to Darius. The eye of their God was upon them (Ezra 5:5). A search recovered Cyrus's decree, and Darius ordered the work left alone and its expenses supplied from the royal tribute (Ezra 6:1-10). His decree threatened severe punishment against anyone who altered it. The account does not record that penalty being executed upon the earlier adversaries. It records their obstruction overcome: the elders built, the house was finished, and the children of the captivity dedicated it with joy. The authority invoked to hinder the work now required that it be supplied.

name: Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest
text: Obeying the voice of the Lord by Haggai; rising up and working on the house of the Lord. Sixteen years the temple foundation lay bare while the people built themselves ceiled houses and said the time was not come. Haggai spoke, and the governor and the high priest with the remnant of the people obeyed and came and worked, twenty-four days after the word. The Lord said, I am with you, and by Zechariah, not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
