Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, with all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of the Lord their God, and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the Lord their God had sent him, and the people did fear before the Lord. And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel, and the spirit of Joshua, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people; and they came and did work in the house of the Lord of hosts, their God. Zechariah: Joshua stood before the angel clothed with filthy garments, and Satan at his right hand to resist him; and the Lord rebuked Satan and clothed him with change of raiment. Then spake Haggai the Lord's messenger in the Lord's message unto the people, saying, I am with you, saith the Lord. From this day will I bless you. In that day, saith the Lord of hosts, will I take thee, O Zerubbabel, my servant, and will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee. The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it. And the elders of the Jews builded, and they prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah, and finished it in the sixth year of Darius. Sirach names them together: Zorobabel, as a signet on the right hand; Jesus the son of Josedec, who set up the holy temple to the Lord.

name: Ezra
text: Preparing his heart to seek the law of the Lord, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments. A ready scribe in the law of Moses came up from Babylon with the king's letter and the king's silver, refused a guard because he had told the king the hand of God is on all that seek him, fasted at the river Ahava, and arrived. He read the law to the people from morning to midday, and they wept, and kept the feast of tabernacles as it had not been kept since Joshua. Ezra prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, to do it, and to teach statutes and judgments in Israel (Ezra 7:10). The charge of teaching began with the ordering of his own heart and conduct. Royal favor supplied authority and provisions, but his commission remained governed by God's law. At Ahava he gathered the travelers, obtained ministers for the sanctuary, and proclaimed a fast to seek a right way for the people, their little ones, and their substance. Having testified that God's hand was upon those who sought Him, he was ashamed to request soldiers for protection. He also weighed the treasure into appointed hands and required it to be watched and weighed again at Jerusalem (Ezra 8:21-34). Trust in God was joined to careful stewardship. The Lord delivered the company from enemies along the way. The treasure arrived and was counted and weighed in the house of God. The good hand acknowledged before the journey was acknowledged after it. At the water gate, Ezra read the law while the Levites gave the sense so the congregation understood. The people wept, received instruction to rejoice and share with those lacking provision, and kept the feast in booths (Nehemiah 8:1-18). The fruit of teaching was understanding followed by obedience, not merely the public reading of words.

name: The returned exiles who married strange wives
text: Mingling the holy seed with the peoples of the lands. Ezra was told that the people, priests, and Levites had taken wives of the Canaanites, Hittites, Ammonites, Moabites, and Egyptians, and that the princes and rulers had been chief in the trespass. He rent his garment and sat astonished until the evening sacrifice. A generation later Nehemiah found children who could not speak the Jews' language. The returned people, including priests and Levites, had joined themselves in marriage to the peoples whose abominations Ezra named. The princes and rulers were chief in the trespass (Ezra 9:1-2). Deuteronomy had warned against the marriages it forbade because they would turn Israel's children from following the Lord to serving other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4). Ezra's grief measured the offense against the mercy already received. God had punished them less than their iniquities deserved and given a remnant deliverance. To return to the forbidden alliances after that revival was to disregard both the command and the lesson of captivity (Ezra 9:13-15). The congregation wept and covenanted to put away the strange wives and the children born of them. The matter was examined at appointed times with the elders and judges, beginning in the tenth month and ending by the first day of the first month. Priests found guilty gave their hands to the separation and offered a ram for their trespass (Ezra 10:2-19). Later Nehemiah confronted renewed offenses and recalled Solomon, whom outlandish women had caused to sin. He drove away the priestly descendant allied by marriage to Sanballat (Nehemiah 13:23-29). The leaders' position did not exempt them from the covenant obligations they were responsible to uphold.

name: Nehemiah
text: Building the wall in fifty-two days with a sword in one hand; taking no governor's bread; forbidding usury; shutting the gates on the Sabbath; remember me, O my God, for good. A cupbearer wept for the walls of Jerusalem, prayed four months, asked the king, and came. He built the wall against Sanballat with half the people holding spears, made the nobles give back the usury they had taken from their brethren, refused the governor's allowance for twelve years, threw Tobiah's furniture out of the temple, chased Sanballat's son-in-law out of the priesthood, and shut the gates on the Sabbath. Four times his prayer is the same: remember me, O my God, for good. Nehemiah prayed before making his request to the king and credited God's good hand for the permission, letters, and timber he received. He inspected Jerusalem's broken walls before calling the people to build. Under threat, he joined prayer with a watch, stationed families with weapons, and arranged a trumpet signal so the scattered workers could rally (Nehemiah 2:4-18; 4:9-20). He also confronted oppression within Judah. The nobles could not be allowed to impoverish the brethren while others labored to restore the city. He required restitution and refused the governor's allowance because the people's burden was heavy (Nehemiah 5:6-18). Later he restored the sanctuary chambers and provision for the Levites and closed the gates against Sabbath trade. Rebuilding included the ordering of conduct within the walls. The wall was finished in fifty-two days. The surrounding enemies were cast down in their own eyes because they perceived that the work was wrought of God (Nehemiah 6:15-16). Threats, false reports, and invitations meant to draw him away had not stopped it. Nehemiah repeatedly committed his service to God's remembrance. His account shows the fruit in a completed wall, restored provision, and corrected abuses. He sought God's regard for work that required continued vigilance even after its most visible task was finished.

name: Sanballat, Geshem, and Noadiah
text: Mocking, conspiring, and hiring prophecy to frighten the builder off the wall. They laughed the work to scorn, then mocked it, then sent four times to draw Nehemiah down to the plain of Ono, then wrote an open letter accusing him of rebellion, then hired a prophet to make him sin in fear. Nehemiah answered every stage and finished the wall, and left their case with God. Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem mocked the rebuilding and represented it as rebellion. When ridicule did not stop the work, the opposition turned to conspiracy and intimidation. Sanballat and Geshem repeatedly invited Nehemiah to Ono, intending mischief; an open letter then accused him of seeking to make himself king (Nehemiah 2:19; 4:1-8; 6:1-9). Shemaiah urged Nehemiah to hide within the temple, but Nehemiah perceived that God had not sent him. Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him to induce fear and sin, providing grounds for an evil report. Noadiah and other prophets also sought to frighten him (Nehemiah 6:10-14). A claim to prophecy became another instrument in the effort to stop the work. Nehemiah refused the trap, denied the invented report, and prayed that God would strengthen his hands and remember the adversaries according to their works. The account names no executed personal sentence against these opponents. It does record the defeat of their purpose. The wall was finished, and the surrounding peoples recognized God's hand in it. Tobiah's correspondence and influence continued, but neither repeated pressure nor a religious disguise had made the accusation true or the work cease.

name: The nobles who exacted usury of their brethren
text: Lending on interest; taking brethren's lands and children for debt. During the rebuilding of the wall, the poor cried out that they had mortgaged their fields and vineyards and sold their sons and daughters into bondage to pay the king's tribute and the nobles' interest. Nehemiah was very angry and set a great assembly against the nobles and rulers. Families had mortgaged fields, vineyards, and houses for grain and borrowed for the king's tribute. Their children were being brought into bondage, and they lacked the means to redeem them because others held their property. The cry came against their own brethren, not merely against the foreign power taxing them (Nehemiah 5:1-5). Nehemiah rebuked the nobles and rulers for exacting usury. Some Jews were being redeemed from the nations while others were being sold by their own people. The lenders had no answer. Their conduct contradicted the fear of God and exposed the restored community to reproach before its enemies (Nehemiah 5:6-9). Nehemiah required immediate restoration of lands, houses, and the hundredth part of the money and produce exacted. The nobles promised to restore and require nothing further. He called the priests and bound the promise by an oath (Nehemiah 5:10-12). Shaking out his lap, he declared that God should likewise shake from house and labor the man who failed to perform it. The congregation answered Amen, praised the Lord, and did according to the promise. Correction reached the possessions taken and the practice that had taken them; a spoken apology alone would not have released the burdened households.

name: Eliashib and Tobiah the Ammonite
text: Lodging an Ammonite enemy in a chamber of the house of God; a priest's house allied to Sanballat. Eliashib prepared for Tobiah a temple chamber formerly used for offerings, vessels, and the ministers' portions. Nehemiah returned, cast out Tobiah's household goods, cleansed the chambers, and restored their proper use. He also confronted the neglect that had driven the Levites back to their fields. Eliashib, who had oversight of the temple chambers, prepared a great chamber for Tobiah. The space formerly held offerings, frankincense, vessels, and the portions appointed for the Levites, singers, porters, and priests (Nehemiah 13:4-5). Personal alliance displaced the use for which the chamber had been entrusted to him. Nehemiah discovered the arrangement after returning to Jerusalem. He also found that the Levites' portions had not been supplied and that those serving had gone back to their fields. The accommodation of Tobiah stood within a wider neglect of the Lord's house. In the priestly family, a marriage to Sanballat's daughter likewise bound office to an adversary's household. Nehemiah cast Tobiah's household goods out and commanded the chambers cleansed. The vessels, meat offering, and frankincense were brought back. He contended with the rulers, restored the ministers to their places, and appointed faithful treasurers to distribute the provision (Nehemiah 13:8-13). He also drove away the son of Joiada who had married Sanballat's daughter and committed the defiling of the priesthood to God's remembrance (Nehemiah 13:28-29). Restoration required both removal of the misuse and renewed attention to the service it had displaced.

name: The Sabbath traders of Jerusalem and Tyre
text: Treading winepresses, bringing in sheaves, and selling fish and wares on the Sabbath. Nehemiah saw men of Judah treading winepresses and loading asses on the Sabbath, and Tyrian merchants selling fish in Jerusalem on the holy day. He testified against the nobles, shut the gates at dusk, set his own servants to guard them, and threatened to lay hands on the merchants who camped outside. Nehemiah saw men treading winepresses, loading animals, and bringing produce into Jerusalem on the Sabbath. Men of Tyre sold fish and other wares to Judah within the city. He contended with the nobles because this trade profaned the day they were charged to sanctify (Nehemiah 13:15-17). He reminded them that their fathers' conduct had brought evil upon the city. Returning from captivity and rebuilding Jerusalem did not authorize a return to the practices for which it had suffered. Jeremiah had likewise warned against carrying burdens through its gates on the Sabbath (Jeremiah 17:21-27).

name: Bigthan and Teresh
text: Conspiring to lay hands on king Ahasuerus. Two chamberlains who kept the door were wroth and sought to lay hand on the king. Mordecai heard of it and told Esther, who told the king in Mordecai's name. They were hanged, and the thing was written in the chronicles, where a sleepless king found it years later on the night before Haman meant to hang Mordecai. Bigthan and Teresh were chamberlains entrusted with keeping the door. In their anger they sought to lay hands on Ahasuerus. Access given for the king's protection became an opportunity for a plot against his life (Esther 2:21). Mordecai learned of it and told Esther, who reported it to the king in Mordecai's name. The accusation was investigated and found true. The sequence distinguishes a discovered plot from a sentence resting upon an unexamined report (Esther 2:22-23). Both conspirators were hanged on a tree, and the matter was entered in the royal chronicles. Mordecai's service received no immediate reward, but the written record preserved his part in saving the king. Later, during a sleepless night, Ahasuerus heard that record read and asked what honor Mordecai had received. Haman arrived intending to request Mordecai's death and instead was commanded to honor him (Esther 6:1-11). The record of one defeated conspiracy helped overturn another. A service apparently forgotten remained available at the moment its remembrance would matter.

name: Haman the Agagite
text: Plotting the destruction of all the Jews; building a gallows for Mordecai. Because one Jew would not bow to him, Haman sought to destroy all the Jews in the empire, bought the decree with ten thousand talents, cast lots for the day, and built a gallows fifty cubits high for Mordecai. Esther exposed him at her second banquet. Mordecai's refusal to bow filled Haman with wrath. He scorned the idea of laying hands on one man alone and sought to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom. He represented their distinct laws as disloyalty and offered a vast sum to obtain their destruction (Esther 3:5-9). The sealed letters appointed a day to kill young and old, women and children, and take their spoil. Haman's personal resentment had become a decree against an entire people. Even his rank, wealth, and invitations to Esther's banquets gave him no satisfaction while Mordecai remained at the gate. He prepared a gallows for the man whose submission he could not obtain (Esther 5:9-14). Before Haman could ask for Mordecai's death, the king required him to proclaim Mordecai's honor. At Esther's banquet she exposed him as the enemy seeking her life and her people's. The king ordered Haman hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai (Esther 7:3-10). His estate and authority passed to those he had endangered. A further decree permitted the Jews to stand for their lives. Haman's ten sons were later killed and their bodies hanged. Purim preserved the remembrance of the appointed destruction turned against its deviser (Esther 8:1-11; 9:10-26).

name: Mordecai and Esther
text: Mordecai: bowing not to Haman. Esther: going in to the king against the law, after three days' fast: if I perish, I perish. A Jew in the king's gate would not bow to an Agagite, and the Agagite bought a decree to kill every Jew in the empire. His cousin the queen fasted three days with all the Jews of Shushan and went in to the king uncalled. Haman was hanged on his own gallows, the Jews were given the day, and Mordecai was next unto the king. The feast of Purim keeps it. All the king's servants bowed, and reverenced Haman: for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence; for he had told them that he was a Jew. Esther: Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish. Mordecai's word to her: who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this? So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king's wrath pacified. The king took off his ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it unto Mordecai. The Jews had light, and gladness, and joy, and honour. Mordecai the Jew was next unto king Ahasuerus, and great among the Jews, and accepted of the multitude of his brethren, seeking the wealth of his people, and speaking peace to all his seed. The Greek Esther adds Mordecai's dream and the Lord's answer: the Lord hath done wonders for his people.

name: Daniel
text: Purposing in his heart not to defile himself with the king's meat; praying three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem, decree or no decree. A captive boy in Babylon refused the king's meat and wine and asked for pulse and water; ten days later he looked better than the rest. Sixty years later, an old man under Darius, he kept his windows open and prayed as before, knowing the den was signed. He was in the den one night and the God he served shut the lions' mouths. Daniel purposed in his heart not to defile himself with the king's portion. He requested an alternative and proposed a ten-day trial, answering the officer's fear without abandoning his purpose (Daniel 1:8-16). Service in a foreign court did not require surrender of his obligations to God. Under Darius, his enemies could find no fault in his administration and sought occasion against him through the law of his God. After learning that the decree against petitioning any other than the king was signed, Daniel continued kneeling, praying, and giving thanks three times daily toward Jerusalem, as before (Daniel 6:4-10). The threat did not create his devotion, and it did not stop it.

name: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego
text: Refusing to fall down and worship the golden image; not careful to answer the king in this matter. Every people, nation and language fell down at the sound of the music. Three officers of the province of Babylon stood. Told they would go into the furnace and asked who was the God that should deliver them out of the king's hands, they answered that their God was able, and that if he did not, they would still not serve Nebuchadnezzar's gods. The furnace killed the men who threw them in and did not singe their hair. Nebuchadnezzar required the assembled peoples to worship his image at the sound of music, threatening the furnace for refusal. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego would not comply. Brought before him, they declared that their God was able to deliver them, but that even if not, they would not serve his gods or worship the image (Daniel 3:16-18). Their obedience was not conditional upon receiving an escape from suffering. The commandment against idolatry settled whom they would worship before the king decided what he would do to them. His question about a God able to deliver from his hands could not enlarge the authority of those hands over their worship. The king heated the furnace exceedingly, and its flame killed the men who carried them up. Yet he saw four walking loose within it, unhurt. The three came out with no hair singed, no change in their coats, and no smell of fire upon them (Daniel 3:19-27). Nebuchadnezzar blessed their God, acknowledging that they had trusted Him and yielded their bodies rather than worship another. He issued a decree against speaking amiss of their God and promoted them in Babylon. The king who demanded their bowing publicly acknowledged the deliverance his threat had declared impossible.

name: The Chaldeans who accused the Jews
text: Informing against the Jews to have them cast into the furnace for keeping the second commandment. Certain Chaldeans came near and accused the Jews, reciting the king's own decree back to him and naming the three men who would not bow. They did not come for an offense against themselves; they came because Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego kept the commandment, and the decree made that a capital matter. Certain Chaldeans approached the king with an accusation against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. They repeated the command to worship the image and its penalty, then named the Jewish officers as men who disregarded the king and did not serve his gods (Daniel 3:8-12). The charge made refusal of idolatry appear as disloyalty in office. The men had indeed refused the worship, but the king's decree could not make that worship righteous. The accusers invoked public authority to bring faithful servants under a sentence of death. The account records no personal punishment upon these accusers. The men killed by the furnace were those who carried the three bound servants into it; they are not identified as the Chaldeans who brought the accusation (Daniel 3:22). The accused emerged unharmed. Nebuchadnezzar blessed their God, declared that no other god could deliver in this manner, and promoted them (Daniel 3:28-30). The accusation succeeded in bringing them before the furnace but failed to accomplish their destruction. The king's public acknowledgment reversed the disgrace the charge had sought to fasten upon their refusal.

name: Nebuchadnezzar
text: Pride: is not this great Babylon, that I have built?. Warned by Daniel's interpretation of the tree dream to break off his sins by righteousness and his iniquities by showing mercy to the poor, the king walked on his palace roof twelve months later and took the credit for the empire. While the word was in his mouth a voice fell from heaven. Nebuchadnezzar received a dream warning that his greatness would be cut down until he knew that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men. Daniel interpreted it and counseled him to break off his sins by righteousness and his iniquities by showing mercy to the poor (Daniel 4:19-27). The warning offered instruction before the sentence fell. Twelve months later the king walked in his palace and boasted of Babylon as the work of his own might for the honor of his majesty. He treated entrusted dominion as an achievement belonging wholly to himself. The words were still in his mouth when the heavenly answer declared that his kingdom had departed (Daniel 4:28-32). He was driven from men, ate grass as oxen, and was wet with the dew of heaven until the appointed times passed. His dependence was exposed beneath the grandeur in which he had gloried. At the end he lifted his eyes to heaven, his understanding returned, and he blessed the Most High. His counselors sought him again, his kingdom was restored, and he confessed that the King of heaven can abase those who walk in pride (Daniel 4:33-37). The restored king's testimony gave God the honor his former boast had claimed for himself.

name: Belshazzar
text: Drinking from the temple vessels and praising the gods of gold and silver. At a feast for a thousand lords, Belshazzar called for the gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the house of God in Jerusalem, drank wine from them with his wives and concubines, and praised the gods of gold, silver, brass, iron, wood, and stone. Fingers of a man's hand wrote on the plaster. Belshazzar commanded that the vessels taken from Jerusalem's temple be brought to his feast. He and his company drank from them while praising gods of gold, silver, brass, iron, wood, and stone (Daniel 5:1-4). Holy vessels became instruments in a public display of contempt for the God whose house they had served. Daniel reminded him of Nebuchadnezzar's humbling and charged that he had not humbled his own heart though he knew it. The gods praised at the feast could neither see nor hear, while the God holding his breath and all his ways received no glory (Daniel 5:18-23). Knowledge of the earlier judgment increased his accountability. The writing on the wall announced that God had numbered and finished his kingdom, weighed him and found him wanting, and given the kingdom to the Medes and Persians. Gifts and advancement offered to the interpreter could not purchase a different interpretation. Belshazzar clothed Daniel in scarlet and proclaimed his rank, but that night the king was slain and Darius the Median received the kingdom (Daniel 5:25-31). The sentence reached the ruler while the honors he could distribute still appeared to be in his hand. His feast could not preserve the breath he had failed to acknowledge as God's gift.

name: Daniel's accusers
text: Conspiring by law against an innocent man. Unable to find fault in Daniel's administration, his enemies procured a decree forbidding petition to any god or man except the king for thirty days. They used his continued prayer to obtain his condemnation. God preserved Daniel, and the king turned the punishment upon the accusers. The presidents and princes searched Daniel's conduct for a charge and found neither error nor fault. They therefore devised a law aimed at his faithfulness: for thirty days, petition to any god or man except Darius would be punished by the lions' den (Daniel 6:4-9). They found Daniel praying as he had before and presented his devotion as disregard for the king. When Darius sought to deliver him, they pressed the rule that his decree could not be altered. Their scheme used the form of law to punish a man whose administration they could not impeach.

name: The priests who despised the Name
text: Offering polluted bread and blemished beasts; being partial in the law. After the return, the priests offered the blind, the lame, and the sick on the altar and said the table of the Lord was contemptible and its service a weariness. Offer it now unto thy governor, Malachi says; will he be pleased with thee? They also departed out of the way and caused many to stumble at the law. The priests despised the Lord's name by bringing polluted offerings and treating His table as contemptible. They offered the blind, lame, and sick, though such a gift would not please their governor. Their conduct withheld from the great King the honor they understood how to show to earthly authority (Malachi 1:6-14). I will curse your blessings; yea, I have cursed them already. I will spread dung upon your faces, even the dung of your solemn feasts. Therefore have I also made you contemptible and base before all the people, according as ye have been partial in the law.

name: Judah robbing God in tithes and offerings
text: Withholding the tithe from the storehouse. Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, wherein? In tithes and offerings. The returned community had left the Levites unsupported so that they fled to their fields, and the house of God was forsaken while every man ran to his own house. The Lord called the sons of Jacob to return from their departure out of His ordinances. They answered by asking wherein they should return and wherein they had robbed Him. The charge was direct: in tithes and offerings (Malachi 3:6-9). What they retained was not theirs to withhold merely because it remained in their possession. The neglect had practical consequences for God's house. Nehemiah found the Levites and singers gone to their fields because their portions had not been supplied. He confronted the rulers and restored both the ministers and the storehouses (Nehemiah 13:10-13). Provision for service was part of the people's obedience, not an incidental matter outside it. Malachi pronounced a curse upon the nation but joined the rebuke to a way of return. They were to bring the tithes into the storehouse so that there would be provision in God's house. The Lord promised opened windows of heaven, rebuke of the devourer, and preservation of the fruit of their land (Malachi 3:10-12). The promise addressed the covenant people and the provision they had withheld. Repentance required restoring that provision. God's call to return showed that the sentence was not an invitation to despair, but a summons to abandon the neglect and receive the blessing He offered.

name: Alcimus
text: Slandering Judas to the king; slaying sixty Asideans under a sworn peace; pulling down the wall of the inner court. Alcimus, who had defiled himself wilfully in the times of the mingling with the Gentiles, sought the high priesthood from Demetrius by accusing Judas Maccabeus of sedition. Sent with an army, he swore peace to the Asideans and killed sixty of them in one day. Later he commanded the wall of the inner court of the sanctuary pulled down, the work of the prophets. Perjury, judicial murder, and sacrilege by a priest. The people remembered the psalm over the dead: the flesh of thy saints have they cast out, and their blood have they shed round about Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them. As he began to pull down the wall, Alcimus was plagued; his mouth was stopped, he was taken with a palsy, and could no more speak or set his house in order. So Alcimus died at that time with great torment.

name: Aman, who ensnared Achiacharus
text: Treachery against the man who brought him up. Tobit's dying counsel to his son holds up one case: remember how Aman handled Achiacharus that brought him up, how out of light he brought him into darkness, and how he rewarded him again. Achiacharus, the king's cupbearer and Tobit's kinsman, had once interceded for Tobit himself. Ingratitude become betrayal, against a benefactor who stood as a father. The story assumed by the text is the tale of Ahikar: the adopted nephew who forged evidence to have his uncle executed. Achiacharus was saved, but the other had his reward: for he went down into darkness. Aman fell into the snare and perished. Tobit's moral: consider what alms doeth, and how righteousness doth deliver.

name: Andronicus
text: Murder of Onias the high priest under a sworn assurance. Onias, having exposed Menelaus' theft of the temple vessels, took sanctuary at Daphne. Menelaus persuaded the king's deputy Andronicus to lure him out; he came to Onias in deceit, gave him his right hand with oaths, and though suspected, persuaded him to leave the sanctuary, and shut him up immediately without regard of justice. A murder achieved by a false oath and the violation of asylum. Even the Greeks, the text says, were grieved for the unjust death of a man who had lived soberly and in virtue. When Antiochus heard of it he was sorry in his mind, and sent for Andronicus, stripped him of his purple, rent his clothes, led him through the city, and slew him in the same place where he had committed impiety against Onias. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.

name: Antiochus Epiphanes
text: Defiling the temple; forbidding the law; murdering the faithful. The Seleucid king outlawed the law of Moses, defiled the temple with an idol, and put to death those who kept the covenant. The books of Maccabees record both his persecution and his end. He forbade circumcision and the sabbaths, set up the abomination on the altar, forced sacrifice to idols, and killed mothers who circumcised their sons and families who kept the law in secret. Struck with an incurable disease of the bowels, worms rising from the living body, he died in a strange land in bitter grief, by the account, confessing at the last that it was right to be subject to God.

name: Apollonius
text: Falling upon Jerusalem on the Sabbath under a pretence of peace; slaying a great multitude; taking women and children captive. Sent by Antiochus with twenty-two thousand men, Apollonius spoke peaceable words to Jerusalem, waited for the Sabbath when the people would not fight, and slew them going out to see the show. Judas Maccabeus met him in the field, killed him, and carried his sword for the rest of his life. He came to Jerusalem, and speaking peaceable words unto them, but all was deceit: for when they had given him credence, he fell suddenly upon the city, and smote it very sore, and destroyed much people of Israel. He took the spoils of the city, set it on fire, and pulled down the houses and walls round about. He commanded his men to arm themselves, and to slay all those that went out to see the holy Sabbath, and there were slain great multitudes. Judas gathered those that were willing, and Apollonius gathered the Gentiles together, and a great host out of Samaria, to fight against Israel. Judas perceived it, and went forth to meet him, and so he smote him, and slew him: many also fell down slain, but the rest fled. Wherefore Judas took their spoils, and Apollonius' sword also, and therewith he fought all his life long.

name: Heliodorus
text: Attempting to plunder the temple treasury. Sent by King Seleucus on the information of Simon the temple governor, Heliodorus came to seize the money laid up in the treasury, though the high priest Onias told him it was the relief of widows and fatherless children and deposits held in trust. The whole city lay in sackcloth. He went in anyway. Sacrilege against the place, and theft from the poor the place protected. The law that forbids afflicting widows and the fatherless, and the law that makes God's house holy, were both in front of him. He proceeded as he had resolved. A horse with a terrible rider in golden armor struck him with its forefeet, and two young men scourged him without ceasing; he fell to the ground in darkness and was carried out on a litter. Onias offered sacrifice for his life, and he lived. He returned to the king and testified: if thou hast any enemy or traitor, send him thither, and thou shalt receive him well scourged.

name: Holofernes
text: Making Nebuchadnezzar a god; blasphemy against the God of Israel; lust and drunkenness. Nebuchadnezzar's captain, sent to make all the earth worship the king alone as god, cut down the groves and gods of every nation and besieged Bethulia. Who is God but Nebuchadnezzar, he asked, and told Achior that the God of Israel would not save his people. Judith came to his camp. Idolatry enforced by the sword, and contempt for the Lord spoken to his face through Achior. On the fourth night his heart was ravished with Judith and he was filled with wine, more than he had drunk at any time in one day since he was born. Judith took his own fauchion, smote twice upon his neck with all her might, and took away his head; his army, finding him headless in his tent, fled and was cut down. Judith's song: the Lord Almighty hath disappointed them by the hand of a woman.

name: Jason the high priest
text: Buying the priesthood; setting up a Greek gymnasium; drawing his countrymen to heathen customs. Onias' brother Jason obtained the high priesthood from Antiochus for three hundred and sixty talents and a promise of more, then built a place of exercise under the tower itself, brought the young men under the Greek hat, and had the priests neglect the sacrifices to hasten to the games. He sent silver for the sacrifice of Hercules. The narrator's summary: such was the height of Greek fashions, and increase of heathenish manners, through the exceeding profaneness of Jason, that ungodly wretch, and no high priest. A bought office, a foreign religion imported into the sanctuary's shadow, and the law despised for the sake of the games. Then Menelaus outbid him. Driven out, he attacked Jerusalem with a thousand men, slew his own citizens without mercy, and was driven out again. He fled from city to city, pursued of all men, hated as a forsaker of the laws; he that had cast out many unburied had none to mourn for him, and perished in a strange land.

name: Judas' soldiers with idol tokens under their coats
text: Carrying things consecrated to idols into battle. After the battle near Adullam, Judas and his company came to bury their dead and found under the coat of every slain man things consecrated to the idols of the Jamnites, which is forbidden the Jews by the law. Then every man saw that this was the cause wherefore they were slain. Deuteronomy: thou shalt not bring an abomination into thine house, lest thou be a cursed thing like it. Joshua's men had died at Ai for Achan's hidden spoil; these had died in a battle they otherwise won. The survivors praised the Lord, the righteous Judge, who had opened the things that were hid, and prayed that the sin might be wholly put out of remembrance. Judas took a collection and sent it to Jerusalem for a sin offering for the dead.

name: Lysimachus
text: Sacrilege: robbing the temple with Menelaus' consent. Menelaus' brother committed many sacrileges in the city by his brother's consent and carried away much gold. The multitude gathered against him; he armed three thousand men under a captain of years and madness and attacked the crowd. Plunder of the sanctuary treated as family business, then armed force against the people who objected. The narrator calls him the church-robber. The people took up stones and clubs and ashes, wounded many, killed some, put the rest to flight, and slew Lysimachus himself beside the treasury. Judgment executed by the congregation at the scene of the crime.

name: Menelaus
text: Buying the priesthood over Jason; stealing the temple vessels; procuring the murder of Onias; bribing his way past the king's judgment. Sent by Jason to carry the king's money, Menelaus outbid him by three hundred talents and came back high priest, though he was not of Aaron's line by the account. He stole gold vessels from the temple to pay his debt, had the righteous Onias murdered for exposing him, and bought off the king when the Jews accused him. Second Maccabees lists him as the cause of all the mischief: a great traitor to the laws and to his own country, bringing nothing worthy the high priesthood, but having the fury of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast. The bribe that acquitted him sent his three accusers to death instead. At last the King of kings moved Antiochus Eupator against him. In Beroea he was thrust into a tower of ashes fifty cubits high, the death for sacrilege, not having so much as burial in the earth: for inasmuch as he had committed many sins about the altar, whose fire and ashes were holy, he received his death in ashes.

name: Nicanor
text: Blasphemy against the temple; breaking covenant with Judas; resolving to attack on the Sabbath. Demetrius' general, having sworn friendship to Judas and broken it at Alcimus' instigation, stretched out his hand toward the temple and swore that if Judas were not delivered to him he would burn the house and build a temple to Bacchus. He resolved to attack on the Sabbath; asked if there were a Mighty one in heaven who commanded the day, he answered that he was mighty on earth. Contempt for the sanctuary, for the Sabbath, and for the God of both, spoken aloud as policy. The priests prayed at the altar for vengeance on the blasphemer; Judas' army prayed the prayer of Hezekiah against Sennacherib. Nicanor fell first in the battle at Adasa, and his army fled. They cut off his head and the right hand which he stretched out so proudly, cut out the tongue of the blasphemer, hung the head from the tower over against the temple, and ordained the day a yearly feast, the day before Mordecai's day.

name: Ptolemy the son of Abubus
text: Murdering Simon the high priest and two of his sons at a banquet in his own castle. Simon's son in law, captain of the plain of Jericho, wanted the country and the crown. He received Simon and his sons Mattathias and Judas in the castle of Docus, made them a great banquet, and killed them when they had drunk well. He sent men to kill John Hircanus too; John was told first and killed the messengers. Ptolemeus the son of Abubus, being made captain in the plain of Jericho, had abundance of silver and gold, for he was the high priest's son in law. Wherefore his heart being lifted up, he thought to get the country to himself, and thereupon consulted deceitfully against Simon and his sons to destroy them. When Simon and his sons had drunk largely, Ptolemee and his men rose up, and took their weapons, and came upon Simon into the banqueting place, and slew him and his two sons. In which doing he committed a great treachery, and recompensed evil for good. He wrote to the king to send him an host and deliver him the country, and sent others to take Jerusalem. One ran before to Gazara and told John that his father and brethren were slain, and he laid hands on them that came to destroy him, and slew them. The first book of the Maccabees ends there; the murderer's sentence is not in it. Deuteronomy's is.

name: Simon the governor of the temple
text: Betraying the temple treasury to the king out of a private quarrel; slandering Onias the high priest. Falling out with Onias over the market of the city, Simon of the tribe of Benjamin told the governor of Coelosyria that the treasury at Jerusalem was full of infinite sums and could be brought under the king's power. That report sent Heliodorus. When it failed, Simon slandered Onias as the author of the mischief and had a man of his party commit murders. Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, who was made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about disorder in the city. When he could not overcome Onias, he went to Apollonius the son of Thraseas and told him that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money. Afterward he slandered Onias, as if he had terrified Heliodorus and been the worker of these evils, and so proceeded in his malice that murders were committed by one Apollonius, a furious man. Onias went to the king, not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all. Scripture does not record Simon's end; it records that his brother Menelaus bought the priesthood with the same appetite, and how that ended. The law's word on the man who takes a bribe against the innocent, and on the false accuser, stands over him unrecorded.

name: The Hellenizers who forsook the holy covenant
text: Covenanting with the heathen; removing circumcision; profaning the Sabbath; sacrificing to idols. In the days of Antiochus, wicked men went out of Israel persuading many to make a covenant with the heathen round about. They built a place of exercise at Jerusalem, made themselves uncircumcised, forsook the holy covenant, and were sold to do mischief. When the king's decree came, many Israelites consented to his religion. First Maccabees calls them sinners and wicked men; Second Maccabees traces the profaneness to Jason. Every mark of the covenant was surrendered by choice: circumcision, Sabbath, sacrifice, food, and the company of the nations. Mattathias and his friends smote sinful men in their anger and wicked men in their wrath; the rest fled to the heathen for succour. Judas burnt up those that vexed his people, and the wicked shrunk for fear of him. After Antiochus, the ungodly out of Israel who sought Alcimus' priesthood found Judas had taken vengeance on their sort.

name: The Jew who sacrificed at Modin
text: Sacrificing on the heathen altar at the king's command. The king's officers came to Modin to compel sacrifice and offered Mattathias silver, gold, and the title of king's friend to go first. He refused for himself and his sons. A Jew stepped forward in the sight of all to sacrifice on the altar according to the king's commandment. Deuteronomy 13 and 17: the man who serves other gods, or entices to it, in Israel shall be put to death, and the hand of the witnesses first upon him. He did it publicly, for reward, to lead the rest. Mattathias was inflamed with zeal, ran upon him, and slew him at the altar, and the king's commissioner with him, and pulled down the altar. Thus dealt he zealously for the law of God, like as Phinees did unto Zambri. The revolt began there.

name: The men of Joppa
text: Drowning two hundred of the Jews that dwelt among them, under a pretence of peace. The men of Joppa invited the Jews living in their city, with their wives and children, into boats they had prepared, as though they meant them no hurt. The Jews accepted by common decree of the city, suspecting nothing. When they were out in the deep, the Joppites drowned no less than two hundred of them. They prayed the Jews that dwelt among them to go with their wives and children into the boats which they had prepared, as though they had meant them no hurt. Who accepted of it according to the common decree of the city, as being desirous to live in peace, and suspecting nothing: but when they were gone forth into the deep, they drowned no less than two hundred of them. The invitation itself was the weapon; the men of Jamnia were minded to do in like manner. When Judas heard of this cruelty done unto his countrymen, he commanded those that were with him to make them ready, and calling upon God the righteous Judge, he came against those murderers of his brethren, and burnt the haven by night, and set the boats on fire, and those that fled thither he slew. He came upon the Jamnites also by night and set fire on their haven and navy, so that the light of the fire was seen at Jerusalem two hundred and forty furlongs off.

name: The priests of Bel
text: Deceiving the king and the people with an idol that seemed to eat. The Babylonians spent twelve measures of fine flour, forty sheep, and six vessels of wine daily on Bel, and the king asked Daniel why he would not worship a living god who ate so much. Daniel laughed. Ashes strewn on the temple floor showed the footprints of the seventy priests, their wives and children, who came in by a secret door under the table every night. Priests feeding themselves on offerings made to a lump of clay and brass, and threatening Daniel with death to protect the trade. The Epistle of Jeremiah describes the same racket: as for the things sacrificed unto them, their priests sell and abuse. Therefore the king slew them, and delivered Bel into Daniel's power, who destroyed him and his temple. When Daniel then destroyed the dragon, the Babylonians forced the king to throw him to the lions; he came out unharmed, and those that were the cause of his destruction were cast into the den and devoured in a moment.

name: The two elders who accused Susanna
text: Attempted adultery by extortion; false witness against an innocent woman. Two elders of Babylon's Jews, appointed judges, hid in Joacim's garden, tried to force his wife Susanna, and when she cried out, accused her of adultery with a young man. The assembly believed them, as elders and judges, and condemned her to death. Daniel stopped the execution and examined them apart. Lust turned to extortion and then to perjury: they perverted their own hearts and turned away their eyes that they might not look unto heaven nor remember just judgments. Examined separately, one said the pair were under a mastick tree and the other under a holm tree. Their own mouths convicted them of false witness. According to the law of Moses they did unto them in such sort as they maliciously intended to do to their neighbour: and they put them to death. Thus the innocent blood was saved the same day. Deuteronomy 19 is the statute; this is its clearest case.

name: Timotheus
text: Gathering the heathen to root out the Jews; a second campaign after being once spared. Timotheus raised the Ammonites and Arabians against the returned Jews, was beaten at the river and shut up in Gazara, and was let go alive when he pleaded his hostages. He came again with a hundred and twenty thousand, and Judas's men found him hid in a pit and slew him. Timotheus, whom the Jews had overcome before, when he had gathered a great multitude of foreign forces, and horses out of Asia not a few, came as though he would take Jewry by force of arms. He had boasted over the Jews and blasphemed, and the Jews would not spare his men who had provoked them. Judas and his company, calling upon the Lord, came to the Jews' ease: Timotheus and his host were overthrown at Raphon and thirty thousand slain. Timotheus fell into the hands of Dositheus and Sosipater, whom he besought with much craft to let him go with his life, and they let him go for the saving of their brethren. At last, in the second campaign, he fled to Gazara, and Judas's men, finding Timotheus hid in a certain pit, killed him and his brother Chereas, and Apollophanes.

name: Tryphon
text: Taking Jonathan the high priest by treachery under a covenant of friendship; slaying him and the young king Antiochus. Tryphon set up a boy king to reach the crown himself, feared Jonathan would not suffer it, and took him at Ptolemais with fair words and a thousand men, killing the rest. He took Jonathan's sons as hostages, took a hundred talents for his release, kept both, and killed Jonathan on the way home. Then he killed the boy. Tryphon went forth to deceive Jonathan: he said, Why hast thou brought all this people to so much trouble? Send them home, and choose a few men to wait on thee, and come thou with me to Ptolemais. When Jonathan entered, they of Ptolemais shut the gates and took him, and all them that came with him they slew with the sword. Afterward he sought to slay Simon's men as well, and having deceived Simon of the hundred talents and the children, went and slew Jonathan at Bascama. Tryphon dealt deceitfully with the young king Antiochus and slew him, and reigned in his stead, and brought a great calamity upon the land. Scripture records his crown, not his sentence: Antiochus the son of Demetrius came against him, the men of war forsook him, he fled by ship to Orthosias, and the book leaves him running. The law's sentence on the murderer and on the man who breaks a covenant of peace is written elsewhere and does not run out.

name: Eleazar the scribe
text: Choosing to die gloriously rather than eat swine's flesh, or pretend to, at ninety years old. One of the principal scribes, an aged man and of a well favoured countenance, was compelled to open his mouth and eat swine's flesh. He spat it out. Old friends offered to let him bring his own meat and only pretend. He refused, so that the young would not be deceived by Eleazar, being fourscore years old and ten, into thinking he had gone over to a strange religion. He went to the torment and died leaving his death for an example. But he choosing rather to die gloriously, than to live stained with such an abomination, spit it forth, and came of his own accord to the torment. Being fourscore years old and ten: it becometh not our age in any wise to dissemble, whereby many young persons might think that Eleazar was now gone to a strange religion. For though for the present time I should be delivered from the punishment of men: yet should I not escape the hand of the Almighty, neither alive, nor dead. Wherefore now, manfully changing this life, I will shew myself such an one as mine age requireth, and leave a notable example to such as be young to die willingly and courageously for the honourable and holy laws. And thus this man died, leaving his death for an example of a noble courage, and a memorial of virtue, not only unto young men, but unto all his nation. When he was ready to die with stripes, he groaned, and said, It is manifest unto the Lord, that hath the holy knowledge, that whereas I might have been delivered from death, I now endure sore pains in body by being beaten: but in soul am well content to suffer these things, because I fear him. The blessing recorded is the memorial: his name and his refusal, kept by his nation for ever, and the resurrection the next chapter's martyrs claim aloud.

name: Judas Maccabeus
text: Going to battle with prayer and the law, keeping the ordinances of war, and cleansing the sanctuary. Mattathias' third son gathered those that kept the law, sent home the fearful and the newly married as Deuteronomy commands, prayed before every battle, and beat Apollonius, Seron, Gorgias, Lysias and Nicanor with a fraction of their numbers. He cleansed the sanctuary on the twenty-fifth of Chislev, three years to the day from its defiling, and ordained the eight days of Dedication. His prayer for the dead after Adullam is the plainest hope of resurrection in the Old Testament. It is no hard matter for many to be shut up in the hands of a few; and with the God of heaven it is all one, to deliver with a great multitude, or a small company: for the victory of battle standeth not in the multitude of an host; but strength cometh from heaven. He commanded, according to the law, those who were building houses, or had betrothed wives, or were planting vineyards, or were fearful, to return home. He gave the army the watchword, The help of God. And Judas and his brethren said, Behold, our enemies are discomfited: let us go up to cleanse and dedicate the sanctuary. He made a reconciliation for the dead, that they might be delivered from sin. So Judas fell upon them, and they fled; and the fame of him was spread abroad even to the utmost part of the earth. They built the sanctuary anew and offered sacrifice according to the law upon the new altar of burnt offerings; and there was very great gladness among the people, for that the reproach of the heathen was put away. Judas and his brethren with the whole congregation of Israel ordained, that the days of the dedication of the altar should be kept in their season from year to year by the space of eight days. Onias and Jeremiah appeared to him in a dream, and Jeremiah gave him a sword of gold: take this holy sword, a gift from God, with the which thou shalt wound the adversaries.

name: Judith
text: A widow who feared God greatly, fasting all the days of her widowhood; going out to Holofernes in the name of the Lord. When Bethulia's elders promised to surrender in five days if God did not help, a widow who had fasted since her husband died told them they were tempting the Lord. She prayed, put off her sackcloth, went out to the Assyrian camp with her maid, ate only her own clean food, and came back with the head of Holofernes in a bag. Israel praised her, she gave the spoil to the temple, and no one made the Israelites afraid in her days. She was a widow three years and four months; she fasted all the days of her widowhood, save the eves of the sabbaths and the sabbaths, and the eves of the new moons and the new moons. She feared God greatly, and there was none that gave her an ill word. To the elders: who are ye, that have tempted God this day, and stand instead of God among the children of men? In the camp she would not eat the meat of Holofernes, but ate of her own that she had prepared, and went out every night to the valley to pray. Then she took his sword, and she smote twice upon his neck with all her might, and she took away his head from him. Blessed art thou of the most high God above all the women upon the earth: and blessed be the Lord God, which hath created the heavens and the earth, which hath directed thee to the cutting off of the head of the chief of our enemies. Thou art the exaltation of Jerusalem, thou art the great glory of Israel, thou art the great rejoicing of our nation. Judith dedicated all the stuff of Holofernes unto the Lord. And there was none that made the children of Israel any more afraid in the days of Judith, nor a long time after her death.

name: Mattathias
text: Zealous for the law: refusing the king's commandment at Modin, and executing the apostate on the altar as Phinehas did Zambri. The king's officers came to Modin to make the people sacrifice, and offered Mattathias the priest wealth and the king's friendship to go first. He answered that though every nation obeyed, he and his sons would walk in the covenant of their fathers. When a Jew came forward to sacrifice, Mattathias killed him on the altar, killed the king's commissioner, pulled the altar down, and fled to the mountains with his sons. The Maccabean deliverance began there. Though all the nations that are under the king's dominion obey him, and fall away every one from the religion of their fathers, and give consent to his commandments: yet will I and my sons and my brethren walk in the covenant of our fathers. God forbid that we should forsake the law and the ordinances. We will not hearken to the king's words, to go from our religion, either on the right hand, or the left. He ran and slew the Jew upon the altar, and killed the king's commissioner, and the altar he pulled down. Thus dealt he zealously for the law of God, like as Phinees did unto Zambri the son of Salom. And Mattathias cried throughout the city with a loud voice, saying, Whosoever is zealous of the law, and maintaineth the covenant, let him follow me. His deathbed roll of the fathers is the blessing he claimed: Phinees our father in being zealous and fervent obtained the covenant of an everlasting priesthood. Daniel for his innocency was delivered from the mouth of lions. And thus consider ye, throughout all ages, that none that put their trust in him shall be overcome. He blessed his sons and was gathered to his fathers, and all Israel made great lamentation for him. Judas and Simon after him took the city and the temple back, and the feast of the dedication is kept to this day.

name: Onias the high priest
text: Godliness and hatred of wickedness, so that the laws were kept very well and the city lived in peace. While Onias was high priest the holy city was inhabited with all peace and the laws kept very well, and even the kings of the nations sent gifts to the temple. When Heliodorus came to rob the treasury, Onias' prayer and the priests' brought the horse and the two young men that scourged him, and Onias' sacrifice restored him. He was murdered afterward under a sworn peace; Judas saw him after death, praying for the people. Because of the godliness of Onias the high priest, and his hatred of wickedness, the holy city was inhabited with all peace, and the laws were kept very well. When Simon slandered him, he went to the king, not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both publick and private; for he saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, without the king's providence. When the king's messenger was struck down in the treasury, the high priest, fearing lest the king should misconceive that some treachery had been done to Heliodorus by the Jews, offered a sacrifice for the health of the man. Then the high priest offered sacrifice for the health of the man; and the Lord restored Heliodorus to life. Heliodorus testified to all men the works of the great God, which he had seen with his eyes. After his murder, Judas saw in a dream Onias, who had been high priest, a virtuous and a good man, reverend in conversation, gentle in condition, well spoken also, and exercised from a child in all points of virtue, holding up his hands and praying for the whole body of the Jews. The blessing recorded is a city at peace under the law, a martyr's honour, and a place among those who pray for the people.

name: Susanna
text: Choosing to fall into the hands of the elders rather than sin in the sight of the Lord. Two elders and judges of the people caught her alone in her husband's garden and gave her a choice: consent, or be accused of adultery and put to death. She cried out. They testified, the assembly condemned her, and she cried to the Lord on the way to die. Daniel, a young man, separated the witnesses and caught them in a lie about a tree. They died by the law of Moses for false witness, and the innocent blood was saved. Susanna sighed, and said, I am straitened on every side: for if I do this thing, it is death unto me: and if I do it not I cannot escape your hands. It is better for me to fall into your hands, and not do it, than to sin in the sight of the Lord. With that Susanna cried with a loud voice. Condemned, she cried out with a loud voice, and said, O everlasting God, that knowest the secrets, and knowest all things before they be: thou knowest that they have borne false witness against me, and, behold, I must die; whereas I never did such things as these men have maliciously invented against me. And the Lord heard her voice. Therefore when she was led to be put to death, the Lord raised up the holy spirit of a young youth whose name was Daniel. Under what tree sawest thou them? Under a mastick tree. Under an holm tree. With that all the assembly cried out with a loud voice, and praised God, who saveth them that trust in him. And according to the law of Moses they did unto them in such sort as they maliciously intended to do to their neighbour: and they put them to death. Thus the innocent blood was saved the same day. Therefore Chelcias and his wife praised God for their daughter Susanna, because there was no dishonesty found in her.

name: The seven brethren and their mother
text: Refusing to taste swine's flesh under torture, seven times over, in hope of the resurrection. Seven brothers and their mother were taken and compelled by the king to taste swine's flesh, and tormented with scourges and whips when they would not. One after another they were flayed, dismembered and fried, each speaking the law and the resurrection to the king before he died. The mother watched all seven and exhorted them in her own language, and died last. Their hope is written plainly: the King of the world shall raise us up, who have died for his laws, unto everlasting life. We are ready to die, rather than to transgress the laws of our fathers. Thou like a fury takest us out of this present life, but the King of the world shall raise us up, who have died for his laws, unto everlasting life. The mother: I cannot tell how ye came into my womb; the Creator of the world, who formed the generation of man, will also of his own mercy give you breath and life again, as ye now regard not your own selves for his laws' sake. To the youngest: fear not this tormentor, but, being worthy of thy brethren, take thy death, that I may receive thee again in mercy with thy brethren. The blessing they claimed is the one the law's own words hold out: everlasting life, and to be received again with their brethren. The seventh: our brethren, who now have suffered a short pain, are dead under God's covenant of everlasting life. The chronicler: let this be enough now to have spoken concerning the idolatrous feasts, and the extreme tortures. Hebrews remembers them without naming them: others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection. Antiochus' own end is his own case, and it followed within the year.

name: Tobit
text: Walking in truth and justice all his days; alms, tithes, and burying the dead of his people at the risk of his own life. A captive of Naphtali in Nineveh, he went alone to Jerusalem for the feasts when all his tribe went to Dan's calf, gave the double tithe, fed the hungry, clothed the naked, and buried the men Sennacherib killed even after it cost him everything he owned. He was blinded by sparrows' dung and prayed to die. The angel Raphael was sent, his son came home with a wife and the money, and his eyes were opened. I Tobit have walked all the days of my life in the ways of truth and justice. I alone went often to Jerusalem at the feasts, as it was ordained unto all the people of Israel by an everlasting decree, having the firstfruits and tenths of increase, with that which was first shorn; and them gave I at the altar to the priests. I gave many alms to my brethren, and gave my bread to the hungry, and my clothes to the naked: and if I saw any of my nation dead, or cast about the walls of Nineve, I buried him. Alms doth deliver from death, and suffereth not to come into darkness. Raphael: When thou didst pray, and Sara thy daughter in law, I did bring the remembrance of your prayers before the Holy One: and when thou didst bury the dead, I was with thee likewise. I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels, which present the prayers of the saints, and which go in and out before the glory of the Holy One. The whiteness pilled away from the corners of his eyes: and when he saw his son, he fell upon his neck. He was an hundred and eight and fifty years old, and buried honourably; and before he died he saw Nineveh destroyed as Jonas had said, and rejoiced.

name: Barabbas
text: Insurrection and murder. A notable prisoner, lying bound with them that had made insurrection and had committed murder in the insurrection. Pilate offered the crowd a choice between him and Jesus; the chief priests moved them to ask for Barabbas. He was released and Jesus was crucified. Rebellion against the government and murder, both capital under the law of Moses and of Rome. Peter states the exchange to the men of Israel: ye denied the Holy One and the Just, and desired a murderer to be granted unto you. Released, by the custom of the feast and the demand of the crowd. The guilty man walked free because the innocent was condemned in his place; the gospels leave the figure there and say no more of him.

name: Caiaphas and the council
text: Seeking false witness against Christ; condemning him by night; delivering him to the Gentiles; forbidding the apostles; stoning Stephen. Caiaphas had already ruled that it was expedient one man die for the people. The council sought false witness to put Jesus to death and found none that agreed; then the high priest adjured him and condemned him for his answer. They delivered him to Pilate, chose Barabbas, and afterward beat and forbade his apostles, and gnashed on Stephen and stoned him. Every rule of the court broken in one night: witnesses suborned, testimony not agreeing, a capital sentence at night by the accusers themselves, and the prisoner condemned by his own compelled confession. Stephen's charge to them: ye stiffnecked, which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted? and ye have been now the betrayers and murderers of the Just One. Christ told them the kingdom would be taken from them and their house left desolate; Paul says the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost. Peter to their faces: the stone which was set at nought of you builders. Within the generation the temple in which they sat was rubble.

name: Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum
text: Not repenting after the mighty works done in them. Most of Christ's miracles were done in three towns on the north shore of Galilee, and they did not repent. He measured them against Tyre, Sidon and Sodom and found them worse off in the judgment, because more had been shown them. Capernaum, exalted unto heaven, was to be brought down to hell. Then began he to upbraid the cities wherein most of his mighty works were done, because they repented not. If the mighty works, which were done in you, had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Capernaum had heard the sermon in the synagogue, seen the centurion's servant healed and the paralytic carried down through the roof, and stayed as it was. Woe unto thee, Chorazin! woe unto thee, Bethsaida! It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment, than for you. And thou, Capernaum, which art exalted unto heaven, shalt be brought down to hell: for if the mighty works, which have been done in thee, had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. It shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment, than for thee.

name: Herod Antipas and Herodias
text: Taking his brother's wife; beheading John for saying so. Herod the tetrarch married Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, and John told him it was not lawful. Herodias wanted John dead; Herod feared him and heard him gladly, but at his birthday feast swore to give her dancing daughter whatever she asked. She asked for John's head on a charger. Leviticus twice: thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy brother's wife. Then a rash oath kept at the cost of a prophet's life, for the sake of them which sat with him. Christ called him that fox and would not answer him at his trial. Scripture records no sentence on Herod or Herodias; the gospels leave them at Christ's trial, mocking him. History records Antipas exiled by Caligula at his wife's ambition. The record here is the crime and the statute.

name: Herod the Great and the children of Bethlehem
text: Slaying all the male children of Bethlehem from two years old and under. Mocked by the wise men who did not return to report the child, Herod was exceeding wroth and sent and slew all the children in Bethlehem and its coasts from two years old and under, according to the time he had inquired of them. Matthew hears Rachel weeping in Ramah. Innocent blood on a scale of a town, from a king's fear for his throne. The children's only crime was their age and their address. Matthew records only that Herod died and Joseph brought the child back from Egypt. Scripture pronounces no sentence on him; secular history records a hideous death. The law's word on innocent blood stands over the case regardless.

name: Jerusalem, that killeth the prophets
text: Killing the prophets and stoning them that are sent; not knowing the time of her visitation. Christ wept over the city and told it what was coming: thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and lay thee even with the ground, and thy children within thee, because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation. He said not one stone of the temple would be left on another, and that this generation would see it. The blood of all the prophets shed from the foundation of the world, from Abel to Zacharias, required of this generation; and the rejection of the one who would have gathered her children as a hen her chickens. Daniel had said the people of the prince that shall come would destroy the city and the sanctuary. There shall be great distress in the land, and wrath upon this people. And they shall fall by the edge of the sword, and shall be led away captive into all nations: and Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled. Deuteronomy 28 had described the siege in detail.

name: Judas Iscariot
text: Theft from the common purse; betraying innocent blood for thirty pieces of silver. One of the twelve, keeper of the bag, and a thief who took what was put in it. He went to the chief priests and asked what they would give him; they weighed thirty pieces of silver. He delivered Christ with a kiss. In the morning he brought the silver back: I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood. Covetousness ripened into treachery. Zechariah had priced the shepherd at thirty pieces of silver, the price of a gored slave. His own confession names the statute: cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. Christ: good were it for that man if he had never been born. The priests would not take the money back; he cast it down in the temple, went and hanged himself, and the silver bought the potter's field. Acts adds that he fell headlong and burst asunder. Peter, citing the Psalms, says he went to his own place, and his bishoprick passed to another.

name: Nazareth, his own country
text: Being offended at him; seeking to cast him down the hill. In the synagogue where he had been brought up he read Isaiah and said the scripture was fulfilled that day. They marvelled, then asked if this was not the carpenter's son, then were filled with wrath and led him to the brow of the hill. He did no mighty work there, and passed through the midst of them. Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary? And they were offended at him. When he reminded them that Elijah was sent to a widow of Sidon and Elisha cleansed a Syrian, all they in the synagogue were filled with wrath, and rose up, and thrust him out of the city, and led him unto the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong. A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house. And he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief; he could there do no mighty work, save that he laid his hands upon a few sick folk, and healed them; and he marvelled because of their unbelief. He passing through the midst of them went his way, and Nazareth kept what it had chosen: a carpenter's son and no miracles.

name: Peter's denial
text: Denying Christ three times with cursing and swearing. Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee. Before the cock crew twice he had denied him three times, the last with oaths and curses, to a maid and to bystanders in the high priest's courtyard. The Lord turned and looked upon Peter, and he went out and wept bitterly. Whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father. Peter did it three times and sealed it with a false oath. The sin was foretold, and so was the mercy: I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not. No sentence but the look and the tears. After the resurrection Christ asked him three times, lovest thou me? and three times restored him: feed my sheep. Peter's godly sorrow worked repentance; Judas' sorrow worked death.

name: Pontius Pilate
text: Condemning a man he had three times pronounced innocent. Pilate found no fault in him, said so three times, was warned by his wife's dream, and offered the crowd Barabbas instead. When they threatened that he was not Caesar's friend, he washed his hands, said, I am innocent of the blood of this just person, and delivered Jesus to be crucified. The judge who justifies the wicked and condemns the just is an abomination; the judge who follows a multitude to do evil is forbidden by name. He knew, he said so, and he signed. Water does not answer for a sentence. Scripture pronounces nothing on Pilate personally; Acts names him with Herod and the Gentiles and the people of Israel as gathered together against the Lord's holy child, to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done. Paul cites his court as the place where Christ witnessed a good confession.

name: The chief priests, and the watch at the sepulchre
text: Paying the soldiers large money to report a lie about the resurrection. They had asked Pilate for a watch so the disciples could not steal the body and say he is risen. When the watch came into the city and told them all the things that were done, they assembled with the elders, took counsel, and bought the story they had set the guard to prevent. The chief priests and Pharisees came to Pilate saying, Command therefore that the sepulchre be made sure until the third day, lest his disciples come by night, and steal him away; so they sealed the stone and set a watch. When some of the watch came into the city and shewed all the things that were done, they were assembled with the elders, and had taken counsel, and gave large money unto the soldiers, saying, Say ye, His disciples came by night, and stole him away while we slept — and promised, if this come to the governor's ears, we will persuade him, and secure you. No sentence is recorded on them here. The record instead marks how long the purchased lie outlasted the purchase: so they took the money, and did as they were taught: and this saying is commonly reported among the Jews until this day. They bribed the witnesses of the thing they most needed not to be true, and the men they hired were the only witnesses they had.

name: The penitent thief
text: Robbery, under sentence of crucifixion. Two malefactors were crucified with Christ. One railed on him; the other rebuked his fellow: we indeed justly, for we receive the due reward of our deeds, but this man hath done nothing amiss. Then: Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. Matthew calls them thieves, Luke malefactors; the man's own confession is that the sentence was just. He owned the law's verdict on himself in the hour of its execution. The sentence of the state was carried out; he died on the cross that day. The sentence of heaven was reversed in the same hour: verily I say unto thee, to day shalt thou be with me in paradise. Isaiah had said the servant would be numbered with the transgressors.

name: The Samaritan village, and the sons of thunder
text: Refusing to receive him because his face was toward Jerusalem; James and John asking for fire from heaven. A village of Samaria would not take him in, and James and John asked leave to call down fire as Elias did. He rebuked them, not the village: ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of; the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them. They went to another village. They did not receive him, because his face was as though he would go to Jerusalem. And when his disciples James and John saw this, they said, Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did? He turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them. And they went to another village. The village was spared a sentence, and the disciples were taught the difference between Elijah's day and theirs; one of those two sons of thunder later went down to Samaria with Peter to lay hands on believers there.

name: The scribes and Pharisees
text: Shutting up the kingdom against men; devouring widows' houses; tithing mint and omitting judgment, mercy and faith; whited sepulchres. They sat in Moses' seat and were to be heard; their works were not to be followed. Eight woes in Matthew 23 name the crimes, and the sentence at the end gathers all the righteous blood from Abel to Zacharias on that generation: your house is left unto you desolate. They bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers. Ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men. Ye devour widows' houses, and for a pretence make long prayer. Ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith. Ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones. Ye are the children of them which killed the prophets. Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell? Behold, I send unto you prophets, and wise men, and scribes: and some of them ye shall kill and crucify; that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias. Verily I say unto you, All these things shall come upon this generation. Behold, your house is left unto you desolate. Forty years later the house was.

name: The traders in the temple
text: Making the house of prayer a den of thieves. Twice Christ found the temple court full of those that sold oxen, sheep, and doves, and the changers of money sitting. He made a scourge of small cords, drove them out, poured out the changers' money, overthrew the tables, and would not suffer any man to carry a vessel through the temple.
